articles.title: The secret to “Silicon Valley” is Buddhism
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.text: Silicon Valley is a magical place. It's the birthplace for some of the world's most impressive innovations and a breeding ground for leading technology companies. We often refer to it as an _technology ecosystem._ In essence this means a well-functioning community consisting of all critical players needed to bring technology from idea into global phenomena - entrepreneurs with bold ideas, capital (angel and institutional investors across the various stages of a company lifecycle), big companies (with an understanding of and respect for technology and innovation), talent (from universities, big corporations, and other startups) and service organizations (accelerators, advisors, co-working spaces, events, etc.). Many regions around the world, including my home-turf Stockholm, are trying to learn what they can do to resemble Silicon Valley in their respective part of the world_._ Some of it comes down to politics like eliminating friction of starting and running a company, some of it comes from creating role models to inspire the next generation of entrepreneurs, and some of it comes with scale of simply having more of all the pieces to the puzzle. But the most important thing is very intangible. It's something any developing ecosystem around the world can start embracing today. It's the mindset of मुदिता. मुदित is Sanskrit for _[Mudita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudita)_, which is an important Buddhist term and way of life which means "appreciative joy". Living mudita essentially suggests you enjoy the pleasure from other people's success - the opposite of [schadenfreude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schadenfreude). Silicon Valley long time ago realized that with true innovation the overall pie grows. It's not about elbowing your way and grabbing slices of the pie from others. Sure individual companies may compete and disrupt an industry moving capital from one incumbent to the new entry. But when considering the macro impact, innovation not only creates _new_ but also _more_ capital. With individual success, there's more for everyone. Your success increases opportunities for my success. Hence, the mudita mindset in Silicon Valley allows for a very inclusive community. There is cross-functional and cross-industry sharing, and an inherent true desire to help others. People are constantly open for new relations and there's a focus on giving rather than taking. Those with success pay it forward to those who are growing up through the community. Hierarchies becomes fluid, with old and young loosing its meaning. And for anyone with intellectual curiosity the environment becomes truly inspirational as there's always something new to learn. Wherever you are in the world, you can start your path to Silicon Valley by embracing mudita. (This is by no means a claim that Silicon Valley is a perfect functioning society; a region struggling with massive issues of homelessness, mental illnesses, and huge difference between the privilege rich and the poor.) <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2FTZFsJcj0Whc88%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&src_secure=1&url=http%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fgifs%2FTZFsJcj0Whc88&image=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FTZFsJcj0Whc88%2F200.gif&key=d04bfffea46d4aeda930ec88cc64b87c&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="" height="232" width="435"></iframe>

articles.title: Most startup events are a waste of time
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Here’s how to pick the right ones
articles.text: Conferences, meet-ups, formal networking groups, casual dinners, fitness classes with industry peers, etc. There are many events within startup communities around the world. These events are integral parts of the community which is our core as early stage technologists. Some of these events are awesome and the ecosystem needs them. It's one way for serendipitous networking and relationship building, for role models to inspire next generation entrepreneurs, and for the exchange of experiences. But as a founder it's easy to get caught in the event circus. You get flattered when asked to speak at an event, and it's also one of few places where you get patted on the back from the industry for your success after your high-level response to the questions like "How are things going for your company?". But more often than not, the value of attending these events is simply a confidence boost with marginal upside for the growth trajectory of your company. The value of attending events has to be put in relation to the time commitment needed; an average meet-up is 2h and a conference in another city or country is a minimum 1-day commitment. This is time which should carefully be weighed against the opportunity cost elsewhere in your company or even personal life (like working out ). My advice is not to avoid events completely. The important thing is rather to be _very_ selective about what events you choose to attend and the reasons therefore. And don't overdo it. Think about what you and your organization mostly need right now. Avoid becoming what [Mark Suster](None) calls a [conference ho](https://bothsidesofthetable.com/be-careful-not-to-become-a-conference-ho-8add822b2c75#.4n6xc9ud3)... If you're a startup, my general recommendation is to avoid generic startup events and rather focus on _deep topics_. Deep topics should be either specific industry events where you meet your **relevant customers** and peers (one of my company Wrapp's best conferences was the International Gift Card & Couponing Summit in Wiesbaden...far from the glamour of startup hype), or technical developer conferences where you can showcase your technical achievements with purpose to **attract talent** __ and **lear**_n_ from others. Only pay for events where there's is such imminent value. Generic startup conferences are only useful if you have a speaker slot so you can get **massive exposur**e. But beware that even in such cases the value of them can often be disappointing unless you come well-prepared with a disciplined agenda of meetings with other attendees who you have pre-vetted. Don't go to an event and simply believe in serendipity. And in very few instances would I recommend any entrepreneur to ever pay to attend generic startup conferences! (The above advice doesn't relate to VCs as we need to market ourselves broadly to the ecosystems we focus on, meaning you'll see us schmooze at more events than I would advise any single founder to attend.) Where I live in Silicon Valley there are startup events every single day. And because of this region's global allure, many entrepreneurs fly in from all around the world to attend such events. But don't waste your time flying here for anything random. I want to highlight the few major events over here with high enough caliber worth travelling in for. There are of course other events which are very valuable and relevant for your specific business. Most of them will be smaller industry events. For example [Founder Field Day](https://rothenbergventures.com/founderfieldday) for anyone in AR/VR. Focus on them. The good ones are amazing and definitely worth the trip. But for the majors ones, very few are and here's that list. ### Developer conferences - **[F8](https://www.fbf8.com/) -** Facebook's annual event for anyone who is building upon the FB platform and who want's to learn where the world is going when it comes to social. - **[WWDC](https://developer.apple.com/wwdc/) -** Apple's equivalent of F8 for anyone building mobile products (should be most of you) but also people building on top of any of the other operating systems of (OS X, watchOS, tvOS). - **[Google I/O](https://events.google.com/io2016/) -** The annual developer conference of the tech industry's third [aircraft carrier](https://medium.com/creandum-family/the-importance-of-aircraft-carriers-abf6c721c4b9#.6ip05k84g), where you learn where they see the world going when it comes to web, mobile and enterprises applications. - **[Amazon Re:invent](http://reinvent.awsevents.com)** - The largest event for the cloud computing and the AWS community powering most tech products we love. ### Industry events - **[SXSW](http://www.sxsw.com)** - A massive show for any company operating in music and media but even general consumer internet products. Actual conference pass not always required since so much activities are happening outside of the conference venue all across the city. (in **** Austin) - **[GDC](http://www.gdconf.com/)** - The most important conference for game developers and gaming studios. - **[Money 2020](http://money2020.com) -**Where the fintech industry of small startups and large incumbents meet. (in Las Vegas) - **[CES](http://www.ces.tech)** - The number one event for showcasing the future of consumer electronics and technology. A must for any consumer hardware manufacturer. (in Las Vegas) ### Others - **[Dreamforce](https://www.salesforce.com/dreamforce/) -** An enormous sales and marketing conference put on by [SalesForce](http://salesforce.com) to learn about the latest in things like sales automation and sales operations. 120,000 (!) attendees means hotel rooms and Airbnb are sold out across the city. - **[Launch](http://launchfestival.com) -** The only generic startup event listed and worth mentioning only because it's free to attend for most early stage companies. Mostly focus on scaling companies and fundraising. Not critical enough to solely fly into but a great reason for you to come to town and sch

articles.title: I’m a fraud!
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: My dealings with imposter syndrome
articles.text: There are so many people that I know who are more competent than me... Generally, I'm a reasonably confident person, but throughout my life and especially my career I have always asked myself questions of _how_ and _why_. How did I get here, and why was I picked? Do I really deserve this? Why did I get this job, make this sale, raise this capital, etc. More times than others my answers have been that **luck** and **timing** played a big part of it. If I were to summarize what my mind has been asking me at various stages of my career, it would sound something like this: ### First job out of school. _"How did I get this job? I must have been so lucky to pass through that case interview. And my market size guesstimate was way off. They must have had very few other candidates to choose from."_ ### First company. _"I can't believe clients are buying this from me. This business feels just like a house of cards. Isn't this whole thing just duct taped together? I'm sure the client is just doing this as a nice gesture to a young entrepreneur."_ ### Second company. _"Wow, how are investors willing to trust us with this amount of money? How can anyone take this much risk in us? There's so much uncertainty and I've never done anything at this scale before. When will they realize that there are many others in the world who are way more experienced in doing this than I am?"_ ### Being a VC. _"I'm not an oracle. I can't predict the future. How would I know what company will be successful in 5 years from now? And what do I really know that can help a company to grow? What do I do in the board room? I don't know their business at depth. Why would anyone pick me as an investor and advisor?"_ <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2FyoJC2NhEwhBSQhu6WY%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&src_secure=1&url=http%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fgifs%2Ffraud-yoJC2NhEwhBSQhu6WY&image=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FyoJC2NhEwhBSQhu6WY%2Fgiphy.gif&key=d04bfffea46d4aeda930ec88cc64b87c&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="" height="244" width="435"></iframe> These vicious thoughts are known as [Imposter Syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impostor_syndrome), which is a mental state when a person has difficulties to internalize their accomplishments and instead fear of being exposed as a fraud. This is not a new thing and psychologists have researched it for decades, but when I learned about it it was a huge sense of mental relief for 2 reasons. First of all because the description was so spot on. This was exactly what I had and was experiencing. I finally could point these thoughts to something that felt tangible. I could put a name to it. By realizing this was a "thing" I could understand myself much better whenever these thoughts surfaced. Secondly I also understood how common this was. As much as [70% of the population](http://crl.acrl.org/content/75/3/255) are affected by it. So I started asking around and realized that most, if not all, of the people I admire for their professional accomplishments were processing the exact same thoughts as I did. Especially amongst what looked to be confident and successful entrepreneurs. In our own heads, we were all faking it and lucky no one caught us yet. I still have Imposter Syndrome. I doubt I'll ever get rid of it. The risk is that you also have it. And it's all in your heard. After many years I've learned (to some extent) to tame it. And here are my 5 tactics for you to do the same: 1. **Recognize it.** Whenever you question yourself and your accomplishments, realize it's Imposter Syndrome. Learn to identify the signals your mind is sending you. Remind yourself that it's a "thing" and the thing has a name - Imposter Syndrome. And this thing happens to your role models, idols, peers, and co-workers. Recognizing it helps you stop it. 2. **Eliminate fear.** The fear of being exposed as a fraud will limit you to stay within your comfort zone. Push yourself into new environments and you'll prove to you have strengths and that you still can grow, learn and accomplish. 3. **Don't compare.** Your personality and achievements are built up by an endless amount of different input. Comparing your specific weakness to someone others' strengths does not give you justice. Your skills and capabilities are unique. And that's what makes you perfect for this opportunity. 4. **Remember your achievements.** Remember how hard you worked to get here. You earned it. You are worth it. Have a list of things at hands where you have walked the extra mile. What you've done for others, your company and yourself. We all exceed expectations from time to time. That is what brought you here. 5. **Talk about it.** Speaking to others will eradicate the demons. Find a trusted group of people to converse with. You will understand how others are feeling, but you will also experience this group lifting you up and highlighting your achievements. Always remember to fake it. Not until you make it. Until always. It's what everyone else does... ![An imposter.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1pROxVwT0jT9NOhSZhyEM1/1f2eaa9666bd00c444e3419d6fb01448/image_336.gif)

articles.title: The best VC returns are created at Series A
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.text: Venture capital is a business of funding milestones. Companies raise capital to take themselves from point A to B. And most VCs invest at a dedicated point during these companies' life-cycles (Series A, B, C and D+). The stage of where a VC invests is rooted in their strategy and believes as to where one can yield best risk-returns. But at what funding stage do VCs experience the highest valuation multiple increase? As a VC, what stage is really "best" __ to invest in? By looking at some interesting funding data just release by the law firm [Cooley](https://www.cooleygo.com/trends/) we can try to answer this. ![Median pre-money valuation over time and funding stage.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3jUDW7FnxIpa4vz9rZoUDt/a8dd3a55c862bc8bc02382aa32933e11/image_335.png) Series A valuation have not changed dramatically during the past 2 years, and is dancing around the $15M mark. Series B and C have fluctuated a little more and is around $50M and $100M respectively. Series D+ however shows significantly larger historical changes, with a huge spike in early 2015 having fallen about 50% to $190M since its peak with late stage funding drying up. When comparing data across the funding stages we can see the expected relative valuation increase. - **A-to-B:** 3.4x in 2016 Q2; 3.25x average - **B-to-C:** 1.94x in 2016 Q2; 1.6x average - **C-to-D+:** 1.94x in 2016 Q2; 3.15x average The biggest relative valuation increase happens between Series A and B with a 3.4x valuation increase during the latest quarter and hovering just below that as average across the entire historical data set. Investing in Series B rounds seems to create significantly less relative valuation increase of <2x, with Series C expected returns being unpredictable considering the late stage funding ups and downs the world experienced in the past years. So there you have it - the best relative returns are created when investing at Series A stage. If you also take into account that you continue to create returns from subsequent rounds of funding, when you stick it out, the Series A stage becomes even more appealing. Luckily, this is also the [Creandum Funds](http://creandum.com)' sweet spot as happy investors at the seed and A stage. ...however, although interesting to see what valuation multiple happens between funding rounds this whole blog posts comes with a massive caveat_._ I've not taken into account things which really matters for VCs like size of fund and portfolio, loss risk ratio, superior dealflow access, and many other things. The analysis is based on medians and averages. And as a matter a fact, VC returns are not determined by median and averages. It's all about _[power law distribution](https://www.cbinsights.com/blog/venture-capital-power-law-exits/)_ - the best investment in a successful fund often equals or outperforms the entire rest of the fund combined. So whatever stage VCs invest in, it's all about hitting the home run. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2Fsk6rprwHWnm6I%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&src_secure=1&url=http%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fgifs%2Fhomerun-sk6rprwHWnm6I&image=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2Fsk6rprwHWnm6I%2F200.gif&key=d04bfffea46d4aeda930ec88cc64b87c&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="Empire home run." height="245" width="435"></iframe>

articles.title: Kry fills all the boxes of our healthcare checklist
articles.text: _By [Fredrik Cassel](None)_ Most consumer service areas have already been transformed by technology, but as a relative latecomer you can easily see health care will undergo massive changes in the coming years. I don't think any of us can wait - so much time, value and agony is just waiting to be saved. We have been following the space closely and met tens if not hundreds of companies, many with interesting ambitions in changing the healthcare experience. Until meeting Stockholm-based [Kry](http://kry.se/), our checklist hasn't been filled. This is what we've been looking for: A team **putting the consumer experience first**. This means meeting users and patients on their own terms. Providing an efficient and predictable experience. Mobile focused. Not complex. Quick and adaptive. Loved by users. **Frugality**. Transforming the healthcare market will take time. The time until proper reimbursement for the general consumer is widespread may be long. Awaiting this kind of structural adaption with a high burn-rate will kill the best product team. **Just enough healthcare experience.** Using Kry as an example this means wide enough to understand the priorities and what a virtual doctor's meeting is best suited for. But also not so wide and influential that the company holds back the product ambition to realize the efficiency gains that the new platforms hold, such as video, text, and artificial intelligence. Creandum has now found a team that checks all these boxes and - also important - together with Index Ventures and Project A, a syndicate of investors that can really make the best of this opportunity. Very exciting times ahead. Stay tuned for more news from Creandum and Kry! _For more info on our team and the fund's investments, head on over to [Creandum.com](http://creandum.com)_

articles.title: Ready to hire
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: 4 things to prepare you for organizational growth
articles.text: _This is the first part in a 3 post series related to startup hiring and growing your organization._ You started off with your co-founders working out of your kitchen. The dreams about what you together could build carried you through the days with brutally scarce resources. So far you hadn't been punched in the face by the entrepreneurship war. It was all about the possibilities. And your co-founding team were so in sync pushing towards your dream it felt like you had mastered the art of telepathy. Now enter phase 2 of your company's lifecycle. You just raised some and you're looking to increase your output velocity by making a few key hires. Sh*t is getting real! When going from extreme scrappiness to finally having resources available to execute your dream, it's not uncommon to see entrepreneurs rushing into scaling their team. And speed is always essential for any startup. But take a deep breath, and don't just go out there and try to bring in the best functional talent you can find. Hiring is expensive...salary, insurance, equity grants, laptops and cellphones are just the basic direct costs. But this is just the tip of the iceberg, when you also consider costs associated to your team involved in interviewing, onboarding, training and managing the new hire. Hiring the right people for the right jobs is by far the most important thing you do in your company. Don't underestimate it. It takes time and requires preparations. At any time your company enters an organizational growth phase you need to be sure you're ready for it. You have to be _ready to hire_. To help you understand this, together with Bay Area recruiter [Tim Farrelly](https://www.linkedin.com/in/timfarrelly) at the [Coit Group's](http://www.coitgroup.com/) we've identified the 4 most critical items you need to define and articulate before you start hiring: **1 - Identify your _true_ organizational needs.** The first an most fundamental question to ask yourself is, do I actually need to hire or am I simply doing something poorly? Before you hire make sure you understand your operational processes. We often see organizational problems originating in teams that are unnecessarily inefficient, that can be easily fixed by adjusting workflows - not by adding more people. Also understand the work distribution in your current team as some people may be swamped, while others are bored from not having enough work. Some problems may be solved by simply shifting tasks amongst your existing team. Throwing more people at an inefficient process can be devastating. Don't recruit to fix. Only recruit to scale. If you bring in an external recruiter to help you fill your hiring needs, the first thing they should do is to learn about your company structure - not just to understand the culture, but to identify and target organizational inefficiencies and bottlenecks. - Tim Farrelly, Coit Group **2 - Prioritize cost and benefits.** Even companies with funding have a limitation to its resources and need to make hard priorities around what roles to fill first. Don't try to recruit for all your needs at the same time. Focus and prioritize on filling roles where you expect the impact and benefit to be greatest. Don't always default to hiring more engineers because your backlog is long. Often the right choice is getting more clients in through the door and you need to focus on sales and marketing. Furthermore, rarely does the biggest benefit come from hiring senior management. Most early stage companies need doers. Another useful exercise to help you prioritize is considering the costs of NOT hiring for a specific role. Compare what the the overall impact on your company would be if you did not have the various roles filled within the next 6 months. Open positions which are not actively destructive can be pushed into the future. **3 - Decode the foundation.** Once you understand what you really need more people for, you have to recognize how the all the roles will fit and operate in you organization. Regardless if you use a conventional pyramid hierarchy or a [holacracy](http://www.holacracy.org/how-it-works/), you will need clearly defined rules around how people are organized and operate. The essence is to define an environment which is _predictable._ Predictable for both new and existing hires. Uncertainty will create friction. Eliminate uncertainty by articulating "hard elements" like organizational charts, role descriptions for all roles (even those who have been with the firm up until now), career paths, compensation benchmarks, etc. And never forget the "soft elements" like culture values (an entire series of blog posts could be written around the topic of culture). Once you have all of this, make sure the rest of the organization understands this. Bringing in new people may have impact on some existing people's jobs, where a redistribution of responsibilities may feel like a demotion. Predict where people will be impacted. And communicate, communicate and communicate. **4 - Define the process.** Before bringing people in for interviews, make sure you have articulated what the hiring process look like ahead of time. Who is involved at what stage, what is the evaluation focus at each stage of the process, how is debriefing done after each stage, etc. Make it a team effort. Way too many startups have non-existing recruiting processes creating a time consuming, unprofessional and unstructured experience for not only the candidate but also your team members. Yet again, make this predictable. It's the only way to make it efficient. But don't settle to define the process of interviewing. Think about what you do before and after interviewing. What can you do before a candidate meets with your team, to build a pipeline and a pool of talent. Top talent is rarely out looking for jobs, and you can only win them by building relationships over time. Furthermore, make sure to define what your company does after interviewing those you decline. Ideally ever

articles.title: Winning the war for talent
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: 5 ways to improve your hiring process
articles.text: _This is the second part in a 3 post series related to startup hiring and growing your organization. If you didn't read the first part [check it out here](https://medium.com/creandum-family/ready-to-hire-4-things-to-prepare-you-for-organizational-growth-c891a3ee911f#.ng3tih758)._ The tech industry in Silicon Valley is one of the world's most competitive recruiting markets. And hiring the right people for the right job is the single most important thing you do as a founder. So once you've [prepared yourself and you're ready to start hiring](https://medium.com/creandum-family/ready-to-hire-4-things-to-prepare-you-for-organizational-growth-c891a3ee911f#.ng3tih758), how do you actually win the best candidates? Much of this comes down to having a well-managed hiring process. Together with [Creandum's](http://creandum.com) friends at the Bay Area search firms [Riviera Partners](http://rivierapartners.com/) and [True.](http://truesearch.com/) in this post I've tried to highlight some important learnings and best practices to use to improve your hiring process. ### 1 - Be inclusive. This sounds like the most obvious advice, but leverage your network of employees, board members and trusted people to find candidates. Don't only involve the engineering team to hire for engineers. Be inclusive. And don't limit yourself in using more people to access potential talent, but also to vet, build references, and close candidates. Not only can this be one of the best qualifiers of candidates in terms of culture fit and gaining new perspectives, but this will also signal to your candidates that by working with you, they'll get access to a network that will help them further down their careers. Remember the hiring process involves a huge part of selling the opportunity of working for your company so use your best sales tool - your extended team. ### 2 - Avoid tribal hiring. To pull in the best available talent to your company, you have to keep an open mind with the types of candidates that you're willing to recruit. If you've started off your company in a kitchen with a couple 20-something-year-olds, it's easy to fall into the trap of looking for more people that are exactly like you. It's a very common mistake for immature managers and this truly self-limits the amount of talent available to bring into your company. This is what's known as _tribal hiring._ Tribal hiring really limits your company's ability to scale. Hire for the needs of the role and the opportunity for growth it provides - do not hire someone because they look and talk like you. - Austin Brizendine, Rivera Partners This shouldn't be confused with hiring for culture fit, where you look for a foundation of shared values. With tribal hiring you rather look for identical functional skills and background to yourself. ### 3 - Test. People can be great communicators and salesy. Especially candidates who are actively interviewing tend to be very polished in their way of articulating their background and skill set. But how do you ensure someone has the skills they say they do? The answer is by testing them. Tests can be written, role-plays, or simulations of a typical work situation. These tests don't need to be elaborate, but they do need to be able to differentiate the candidates who have the necessary skills from those who don't. Depending on the role you may want to give a heads up about the test and allow the candidate time to prepare, while many tests can be done on the spot. Some roles are easier than others to test, but _all roles can be tested for_ whether junior or senior. Presentations & case studies have become commonplace in almost every search we do. CEO candidates are asked to present their vision to the Board while VP candidates are asked to present a 100 day or 1 year plan to fully flesh out their understanding of what they have learned throughout the interview process and demonstrate how they will address the strategic and tactical needs going forward. This is an especially valuable exercise to gauge how you will work with one another in future, to ensure thoughts & vision are aligned and test for depth of understanding in all key areas required for success in the role. - Mark Jacobson, True. However, know when in the process you want to introduce a test. At the time of testing the candidate should ideally already be sold on the opportunity to work for you and also have a deeper understanding about the expectations on the role. Hence, tests should not be used during the first stage of the hiring process but rather towards the latter part. Also remember each candidate should be given the exact same parameters and, ideally, everyone who will be part of picking the candidate is present during the delivery so you can comment consistently on all candidates in organized debriefs. ### 4 - Use momentum. Once you find a candidate that fits your position there's no sense in wasting more time. As the recruiting adage goes, "time kills all deals". Use momentum to move fast. There are some companies in the Valley who have "hacked" this part of the process very well by using social pressure (getting everyone from the company involved in the recruiting process to personally reach out to the candidate and congratulate them before they have signed the offer) and bells & whistles (bringing in a cake at the end of the last round of the interviews with the candidates name on and "celebrate" that they now are joining). Some of these things may very well be what brings over a candidate who are evaluating different offers, and it obviously communicates a huge commitment from the company making the candidate feel wanted. Also be somewhat opportunistic for certain roles where you repeatedly are hiring, e.g. sales and engineering. If you find amazing talent but there's no exact short-term fit, it may still be the right decision to bring them on. Dare to pull the trigger and move beyond the exact role description on amazing people you meet. Great companies a

articles.title: The importance of the beginning
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: 4 must-dos to improve employee onboarding
articles.text: _This is the last part in a 3 post series related to startup hiring and growing your organization. For full context check out part 1 about [preparing and getting ready to hire](https://medium.com/creandum-family/ready-to-hire-4-things-to-prepare-you-for-organizational-growth-c891a3ee911f#.ng3tih758) and part 2 on [how to improve your hiring process](https://medium.com/creandum-family/winning-the-war-for-talent-5-ways-to-improve-your-hiring-process-eda5e5d42068#.7dxexdxyt)._ Sourcing, interviewing, evaluating, negotiating and closing candidates is what most people define as recruiting. But one of the most fundamental parts of any complete recruiting process also involves onboarding the new hire onto your organization. Onboarding is the structured way get a new employee to a fully contributing team member. During this time period, an employee's output is often negative because they consume resources from the rest of the organization. But don't do the common mistake of disregard the onboarding process' importance. In hard financial terms, you need to invest in your new hire to make a return. This post gives you some best practices I've used together with input from prominent Bay Area search firms [Caldwell Partners](http://caldwellpartners.com) and [Swing Talent](http://swingtalent.com). Successful onboarding requires a strong foundation and a transparent plan. This requires a commitment on the part of the full organization. - Mercedes Chatfield-Taylor, Managing Partner at Caldwell Partners. ## 1 - Start before the start. Onboarding starts the day you sign the offer letter with your new hire. Not the first day on the job! When they have signed an offer letter they have made a crucial decision in their life. They have chosen to embark down a path together with your company. This is huge for you and them! But new employees more often than not are worried about the unknown of joining your company. Will they truly fit in? Who exactly of all people they met during recruiting will they be working with? How is working close to this founder really going to be when the honeymoon is over? You bridge this worry instantly by inviting the new hire into the team upon signing the offer letter. They are now part of your family, even if they aren't yet operational. Hence invite them to company events, townhall meetings, team dinners, Slack groups, etc. Assign them a buddy or mentor so they have someone to chat to about any type of questions that comes up. And do this before they start. But don't put pressure on the new hire making these things mandatory. Simply open the gates to the inside rooms of your company and invite them in. The longer time you have between the offer and start date, the more important this becomes. ## 2 - Set goals. Get wins. The uncertainty for an employee starting a new job is often derived from a combination of i) not knowing exactly what to do, and ii) not knowing exactly what the organization expects the person to do. On the first day for the new hire proactively manage this by creating a clear plan with 30, 60 and 90-day goals. This is something you often see executive preparing themselves when taking a new job, but it's something which should be used for _all_ hires. The difference is that the respective manager should create this in tandem with the new hire. This creates valuable transparency regarding the organization's expectations on the new hire and helps with setting priorities. And in such a plan, make sure to define goals which give the new hire ownership and a few quick wins. Ownership creates a purpose and quick wins build extremely valuable confidence and operational momentum. Make sure you have fully functioning feedback loops and communicate these wins to the new hire, whether in a 1-on-1 or more publicly within the organization. And regardless how fast everything is going and how many fires you have to put out, always, always, always create a plan together with the new hire! ## 3 - Beware of the culture sponge. From a cultural aspect, the onboarding period is the most important time during an employee's journey at your company. This is the time the employee absorbs and learns the ways of your organization. This is where they act as a sponge for culture. Anything which happens in your organization during the onboarding, whether intentionally or not, will be something the new hire adds to their organizational culture framework. At this point of time for the new hire, there is no norm and anything goes. This is where you need to demonstrate your organizational role model behavior. Make sure the new hire's buddy, manager and team member explicitly enforces your organization's culture. When explaining operational processes be clear to anchor them in cultural values. When making decisions involving the new hire be clear to articulate the cultural rationale behind the decision. Over communicate culture norms with behavioral examples. Articulate the role model behavior. It is a million times more difficult to change cultural norms after they have been developed, so this is truly your time to shape new hires into the organizational culture you want. ## 4 - Leverage momentum of excitement. Starting a new job is EXCITING! New hires come in with dreams and hopes of what to become, how they will grow, and the fun and challenging things they will working on. It's also an event which impacts the social circle around the candidate. Family and friends are also excited and curious. This is where the value of your corporate swag truly comes to play. Give your new hire the ability to show off their new career path. T-shirts, pens, stickers, coffee mugs, etc. Things which play a minor role on their own, but when used at the right time becomes something tangible for your new employee to articulate the pride they feel about embarking on this new career journey. If your burn rate allows you to, give the new hire swag to share amongst their friends and family as well. New hires aren't jus

articles.title: Why AI is (and sure isn’t) Magic
articles.text: As quickly as we entered it, we're out of the "Uber for X" era and have landed into the "AI solution for Y" one. I am particularly excited about this trend in startup pitches because I'm one of the very few VCs in Europe who have been working in this field, and I've seen firsthand that there's huge potential here. I would have to guess even most Danes haven't heard of startup I co-founded, Alipes, which uses natural language processing and machine learning to analyse the stock market, but we've been pretty successful thanks to AI. While it's easy to get starry eyed when entrepreneurs come up to you and say, "check this out: we have a machine... that learns," there's more to it than that. AI is hard, requires the right team, and there are definitely still things that AI cannot do. ### Why AI deserves the hype It is very exciting what AI can do today, and amazing progress has been made just these last few years. Just the fact that computers can now recognize images ([Clarifai](https://www.clarifai.com/)), engage in meaningful conversations ([x.ai](http://x.ai)), do accounting ([Dooer](https://www.dooer.com/)), and drive cars ([Zoox](http://zoox.co/)) is staggering, and if and when these services reach a critical level of performance, we will see a massive shift away from having humans do these tasks. That, of course, is the real benefit of AI - that computers are starting to do the tough, "smart", human things that once took lots of man hours to complete. It's huge value to many industries by not only saving employee resources, but being able to scale up tasks quickly and seamlessly. ### Why you have to stay grounded At the same time, it's important to keep in mind that there is a limit to what AI can do. It's not an automatic value driver for any industry, sometimes because the market is very competitive (recommendation engines), other times because they add dubious value (chatbots). But more importantly AI is tough. The most bewildering thing to me is that somehow people have this notion that machine learning is magic and yet at the same time that it's somehow easy to do: "We'll just hire a machine learning guy who will build an algorithm that predicts exactly which product our users want to buy". The truth is that if machine learning is key to your business (and to most businesses, it's not) then you need to have machine learning expertise in your founding team. By now, simple predictive regressions are commonplace. Equally important to consider is that AI never works 100% of the time, and there are many cases where the best algorithm in the world applied to the same data maybe works 10% better than a simple algorithm applied properly. So say you were planning on adding some heavy machine learning to an e-commerce solution to predict what shoppers want, you might go from 5% predictive power to 5.5% predictive power. ### The magic is only in the problem you're solving I love technical founders who can build stuff themselves and iterate superfast to hit product market fit. And even more so for machine learning based startups, where actually solving the technical challenge is a very big part of getting to product market fit. The downside that I see from some technical founders is that some of them fall in love with a technology, which causes them to not make good decisions. "I just want to use this cool deep neural network for something" or "I can build this really awesome scraping technology" is not the right starting point. Start with a problem you want to solve. Then build technology to solve that problem. Cut corners as much as possible, don't insist on using some specific piece of technology, use existing solutions as much as you can, especially for stuff that's not your competitive edge, and build the scrappiest, simplest hack of a solution first, then test it with the market before making it more elegant, scalable and sophisticated. That's where the magic is.

articles.title: Five questions to ask yourself before entering the US market
articles.text: Out of the four years, I've been with Creandum, I've spent more than 2.5 years in Silicon Valley focusing on working with European entrepreneurs. During these years I've spent hours and hours discussing US expansion strategies with startups, and boiled these discussions down to a framework based on five questions: - Why would it make sense for your business to establish operations here in the US? - When is right timing to establish operations in the US? - Where should your US operations be based? - How should your US organization be structured? - What are the main risks and how can you mitigate them? No matter the answers to the questions above, something I recommend everyone is to start to feel out the US market early. Visit different startup cities like San Francisco and New York, preferably with a relevant business purpose but could also be a "worcation" where you are visiting an important event for instance. That will help you build a better understanding to answer the questions: ## Why would it make sense? As the world is getting more flat, it is possible to build big companies from basically everywhere in the world with a bit of traveling. There is a storm of challenges and risks associated with establishing operations in the US so make sure that you have a credible purpose - a lot can be accomplished with frequent trips. Common primary purposes are being close to important customers (marketing/sales) and to build deep partnerships (platform relations). Secondary reasons are access to experienced talent and funding. ## When is right timing? It always takes significantly more time and resources than you've planned - take into consideration that it takes 6–12months before you will see any significant business impact. The key here is to have a good foundation before making a move. A good action plan before making a move is to: - Travel frequently early on to [1] test hypotheses (e.g. ensure product-market-fit), and [2] get to know, evaluate and select service providers to work with as working with the right service providers truly can accelerate your progress and [3] start build your network with customers, platforms, VCs, angels (also to evaluate your hypotheses) - Build strong routines for communication already before you have moved over - communication is extremely challenging so start early with weekly meeting with obligatory participation (physical or video), and with communication tools like Slack, and don't take lightly on documentation (meeting notes, CRM, etc.) - Ensure that you have a good company foundation that can handle the gap from losing the people that will move over - Secure and allocate enough resources - the amount differs between companies, but I would not recommend making a move if you have less than 12 months of runway including the budget for the US establishment + 1 x your estimated budget need for the US establishment as a reserve. I'll repeat: do not underestimate the time and resources needed to establish your operations ## Where should you be based? Go back to your purpose: where your customers/partners are - most possible if you are in tech San Francisco, New York, Seattle, LA, Austin or Boulder. To briefly zoom in on the two most common cities: **San Francisco** Here you are close to the main US platforms, most of the top tier VCs and talent. But, there is always a but: there is a very limited time overlap with Europe. In general, San Francisco is a good fit if you are within Social/Messaging/Community, Dev tools, and deep tech like AI, databases, etc. **New York** Here you have some great VCs and some great talent, but the 3 hours makes a huge difference, both regarding office hours overlap and also significant less jetlag when you are traveling back and forth. In general, a good fit if you are working with ad-tech, media/entertainment, fashion, e-commerce or fin-tech. ## How should your organization be structured? The recommended setup differs a lot depending on the company and the purpose of the US operation. If it is a really early stage, i.e. before you have a good foundation, the best setup might be to move the whole team. The most common setup for European startups, however, is to have the CEO moving over to establish a marketing/partnership office in the US while continuing building dev and product in Europe. Some general guidelines: - Move over the CEO, or at least one of the founders to ensure that someone that understands the culture and company vision fully is a part of building out the operations - Ensure right staffing - do not be alone: it is usually challenging to recruit local talent, especially in the beginning, so many companies bring at least a second co-worker from the original office - Recruit local talent, especially for sales - great successful local hires will help you progress faster regarding to know the market in-depth - Budget for mistakes - recruiting in a new market is very tough so plan for that you will have to make some people go ## What are the main risks? Besides the previously mentioned risks, common risks include - Relying too much on a product-market-fit in your home market - it is far from a given that your local product-market-fit is a product-market-fit for the US market - Besides general communication challenges, it often becomes a gap in the local organization when someone of the founders move over - you might think that you will be able to have the same responsibilities that you used to have but it is so much more challenging to manage people and projects on distance, and also when you are spending so much time and energy learning about the new market - As you grow, you need to embrace the local cultural differences within your multiple offices and make it work - e.g. in San Francisco the salary level is significantly higher than in Sweden, while in Sweden you have 30 days vacation of which four weeks are spent without answering emails during the summer, etc. Additional input?
