articles.title: The Creandum Funds invest in KNL Networks to provide Internet Anywhere
articles.author: Daniel Blomquist
articles.text: We're very happy to announce that the Creandum Funds are leading a $10 million Series A investment in [KNL Networks](http://www.kyynel.net/) together with existing seed investors Inventure and Butterfly Ventures and prominent angels including John Lindfors from DST Global. Most of us take fast, reliable internet access at a reasonable cost for granted. While this is true for people living in cities, for the majority of the world's land and sea areas, this is most certainly not the case. KNL Networks is solving exactly this by providing fast, global, always-on, secure data communication at a reasonable rate for users anywhere in the world. When Simon and I first met with Toni Lindén, CEO and co-founder of KNL Networks, we immediately got very excited by the big and hard problem he and his team are tackling by trying to provide internet anywhere. You need to combine unique radio technology competence, world-class software development and hardware engineering. Working in stealth mode for several years, the KNL founders Toni, Matti Raustia and Teemu Vanninen and the KNL team built a patented communication systems based on a fully automated software-defined radio that can receive and transmit data communication over many thousands of kilometers at unparalleled reliability and speed. This means that the $200 billion container shipping market now can have continuous internet access needed for streaming critical operations data from sensors and engines. It means that the $300 billion public safety and security market can have a reliable, always-on and secure two-way communication mean in cases of emergencies or catastrophes. We believe that KNL has the potential of disrupting communication services for many sectors including maritime, offshore, IoT, public safety, defence and security. Today, most users outside wifi and cellular-covered areas rely on satellite communication. By contrast, KNL's terrestrial peer-to-peer network offers superior reliability, coverage, data speeds and security at a fraction of the cost. The need for data in many of these sectors and industries is exploding and satellite communication just cannot deliver a good enough service for many users. As an example, people that we have talked to testify to situations where they are stopping their ships at sea in order to transfer data or take costly detours to not lose data connectivity and in many areas have no data access at all. As for the business model, KNL Networks is operating a network while providing users with long-commitment data subscriptions. This is an attractive model but typically the problem is that it requires a lot of capital to build the infrastructure needed to provide the service. Another problem is that while on one hand one needs to build critical mass of users to recoup the big infrastructure investments, on the other hand typically the service degrades the more participants that are on the network. KNL Networks has an opportunity to overcome all of these problems. The cost of building out the communication network is a fraction of the cost of satellite technologies. Also, by offering a peer-to-peer network where all participants help build out capacity, KNL's network gets better the more users that are on it. So, we're super excited to help the KNL team deliver its very big ambition of providing internet anywhere to companies around the world! _For more info on our team and the fund's investments, head on over to_ [creandum.com](http://www.creandum.com)

articles.title: The value isn’t your algorithm, it’s your data
articles.text: Before becoming a VC at [Creandum](http://creandum.com) (and a stint building up Rocket Internet's Vaniday) I started Alipes, a tech company that uses machine learning and natural language processing to find insights about the stock market. A very ambitious task, especially in 2008 when the markets were crashing, machine learning wasn't yet cool, and there was no such thing as fintech. To get off the ground we needed data. For us, this required reading and marking up a ton of financial news to train the algorithms on. As we had zero resources apart from ourselves, for the first year or so we would each spend an hour per day or more doing this. It was insanely boring, but there was no other option. We even convinced our little brothers to help us for free in exchange for excellent recommendation letters, and my little brother famously stated that "this is the kind of stuff they have you do at Guantanamo". It was pretty crazy. But since it was such a crazy thing that no one in their right mind would do, it meant that before not too long we had the best data set in the world. As we began seeing results and scaled up, we hired people in India to do that work. Training them was super difficult - being extremely detail oriented when doing something that is very boring is really hard for the human brain. But persistence paid off, and we now have an amazing team there, steadily building up a database no one else in the world has access to, which allows us to build a better product than anyone else. ### The magnificent data network effects The point of this example is that for almost all machine learning startups the value is not the algorithm. If you have access to more (and better) data than the competition, then you can build a better product than them. What you should ultimately strive for is to get this data from your customers' use of your product: x.ai is a great example: Whenever one of their customers use their virtual assistant they get additional insights into the intricacies of meeting scheduling discussions, which lets them improve their algorithms. Tesla is another one: all Teslas have sensors that constantly record their surroundings, which means that Tesla now has the best dataset in the world for training a self driving car algorithm. The beauty of this is that this gives you defensibility at scale: you can have data network effects. Like normal network effects, but through the data you get from them. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/795iC9hPlLh6bdz3jNR3Fd/8d1a24709aaef49650a8ad1991aa8132/image_334.jpg) The end goal is to reach a point where this makes your business a natural monopoly, as you can build products that are better than anyone else because you have data that no one else has. This means higher profit margins and a more sustainably valuable business. ### Data cleanup will always be important Now, data quality is key to success. Raw data is almost always messy and has errors in it. Because of that, you need to spend resources to clean up your data. And, before you have customers providing you with data, go out and get some the old fashioned, manual way. Manually tagging data at any decent scale seems like such an insane thing to do that very few actually do it. Even though it is actually very doable. Which is what gave us an opportunity. To drive this point home, Facebook's head of News Feed has famously stated that a logistic regression is as good as any sophisticated algorithm, just have enough data to train it on. Recent developments in deep neural networks for things like natural language processing and image recognition may mean this holds true less than it used to, but what still holds is that any algorithm will become a commodity sooner than you think. The algorithm is not your unfair advantage. The data is your unfair advantage. Now go out there and get it.

articles.title: Part 1: The awesome power of moats
articles.text: _This is part 1 in a two post series._ We all know that the most important factors that VCs look for in startups are [team, product and market](http://pmarchive.com/guide_to_startups_part4.html). But there is actually one more thing that we obsess about and are always discussing when evaluating deals, but isn't something many first time founders think about when starting a company. My cofounders and I definitely didn't when we started our company 8 years ago; we just wanted to build cool technology that would work and make money. It goes by many names: unfair advantage, defensibility, competitive edge, but I will use the term that Warren Buffett made famous in his [talks about how he invests in businesses](http://www.businessinsider.com/buffett-on-moats-2016-4?r=US&IR=T&IR=T): The Oracle From Omaha - and VCs - look for **moats**. For those of you who are not native english speakers and also not medieval architecture buffs, a moat is the ring of water surrounding a castle that protects it from attackers. ## So what is a moat in business? Just like how it protects a knight in a castle, a moat is something that protects your business from competition. However, your moat is not that you have an amazing team. Your moat is also not your amazing product or technology. Instead, your moat is something inherent in your business model that means that once you have reached a certain size it will be very hard for others to compete with you. Really, your moat is your key to sustainable high profit margins and long term revenue growth, and because of that, they are critical in determining which revenue and earnings valuation multiple your business has. Here are the most important moats in business: ## Patents Patents are the most obvious moat: You get a government mandate that your company is the only one that can build your product, and if someone else does it you can take them to court. Patents are crucial in pharma companies and are important in hardware. But it's generally not possible to patent software. And because of that, patents are not really important in the kind of companies that Creandum backs. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/55BnobUdjo1Afke9V5ZSaC/13658469ff7ebd0c23d268d386933d9c/image_328.jpg) ## Regulation This is comparable to patents: The government specifies certain requirements - for capital, training, or for filling out various forms - in order for a company to operate in a certain market. A couple of good examples are banking and taxis. While it's a hassle to fulfil those requirements, once you do, they act as a barrier to any new entrant competing with you. Regulation is one of the reasons why financial services were some of the last to be disrupted by technology, as it acted as a moat for the incumbents. While regulation can be a powerful moat, it is sometimes not as wide as it may appear. When a regulation in place starts not making much sense, businesses and consumers begin to simply disregard it, which can quickly erode the advantage you get from it. And it's very much out of your control. Just look at the [taxi industry](http://nypost.com/2016/07/05/city-lets-uber-and-lyft-cannibalize-the-american-dream/). ## Brand Brand can be a very powerful moat: Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble are fantastic businesses because they are amazing at branding their products. Brand is most important for fast moving consumer goods businesses: In these markets, products are fairly similar in terms of quality and price, and purchases happen frequently. When this is the case, a strong brand is an excellent way to get consumers into a habit of buying the same product again and again. In technology businesses, brand is less important, and a requirement for having a strong brand is to have an amazing product. Look at Apple and Spotify: both companies have fantastic brands, but those are driven by their amazing products much more than they are driven by cool ads with people listening to music. ## Scale Scale is when your cost per item goes down when you sell more items. How this works in practice varies massively between industries. From economic theory: it depends on whether the bulk of your costs are fixed or variable. The part that's not in the theory is that your operational complexity increases as you scale, which increases cost per item. These two effects - fixed vs variable costs and operational complexity - are one of the key determinants for how big companies tend to be in different industries. In shipping, most of the costs are for buying and operating the vessels, which means that your average cost doesn't really drop as you add more vessels once you have a handful. This is (one of) the reasons why shipping companies all struggle to make money. A similar thing applies to airlines, where companies also suffer from the massive complexity of operating a large fleet. The opposite example is software, where in theory the marginal cost is 0, there are no variable costs, and all the costs are fixed. This is actually the key reason why VCs like software companies: it's an attractive business to be in because it scales so well. And it means that the more revenue you have the more money you can put into product development - a fixed cost - and thereby create a better product than the competition. In reality, even software companies tend to have customer acquisition costs (CAC) above 0, which means that some of the costs are in fact variable. The reason why VCs always ask you about CAC, and how they relate to customer lifetime value, is exactly because it tells us a lot about how much profitability will improve as you scale. ![Robots in an Amazon Fulfilment Center](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/39creCsDPZdkkoEt3Yu7s7/8932ced934958c8e91416c592eeb29aa/image_329.jpg) Because of the moat that is scale, some companies proactively work to turn variable costs into fixed costs. A great example of this is Amazon - by far the tech giant that I'm most bullish about. By building larger and larger war

articles.title: Part 2: What you need to know about network effects
articles.text: I already discussed the value of moats in business, and listed the key ones. But I left out one. The most powerful of them all. The mythical network effect. Network effects in its simplest form means that the value of a product increases when more people use it. The most obvious example here is the telephone: A phone is useless if nobody else has one as there would be nobody to call! Network effects are so important that when discussing a deal, VCs often say stuff like "Yeah sure it's a great team, but are there any network effects in this model?" This post is about network effects, which forms they come in, and why they are so powerful. ### Direct network effects The simplest, most obvious network effect is the _direct network effect_: where the value increases directly as more people use a product. The phone is still a good example here, as are social media and messaging platforms (Facebook, Pinterest, Whatsapp, Snapchat, Wechat, Slack...). You mostly see direct network effects in products that are about interacting directly with others, and for the individual user, the value add of an additional user depends heavily on who that additional user is. Whether or not my friends are on Facebook matters deeply in how valuable it is to me, whereas I don't really care whether people I don't know are on there. ![The value of the network increases faster than the size of the network](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4wQapJCjpjP9ySlAW4wU6g/ee93f8c8c62335ab4f2dafaff9afd5a8/image_325.png) Direct network effects are not limited to social networks. The Creandum portfolio company [KNL Networks](http://www.kyynel.net/) uses radio waves to transfer data, and gives the shipping industry global internet access for their vessels, with each individual vessel being a node in the network, and the network coverage improving as more vessels join. ### Marketplaces Marketplaces are businesses where different parties meet to make some form of transactions. Ebay coined the term in the 90s, and some of the most successful companies made in the last decade are marketplaces: from food delivery (Just Eat, Grubhub and Deliveroo) to ride hailing and sharing (Uber and BlaBlaCar) to apartment sharing (Airbnb). The network effects in marketplaces are _indirect_: I don't get any direct benefit from more people using Uber. But more people using Uber means that it's more attractive to become an Uber driver, which means better availability for me. This is why once a ride hailing platform has a certain size in a city, it's very hard to compete with it. Which is why [Uber is spending like crazy](https://techcrunch.com/2016/06/01/uber-takes-its-most-significant-investment-yet-at-3-5-billion-from-saudi-arabia/): they want to grab as many cities as possible, and they know from their most mature cities how profitable a city at scale is, and roughly how big an investment it takes to get there. The indirect network effects of a marketplace are sometimes referred to as _supply side economies of scale_, and they can really be just as powerful as the direct kind. One form of marketplaces are GDS's (Global Distribution Systems). They are central platforms for booking tickets for flights, hotels and more. [Amadeus](http://www.amadeus.com/) is a famous one in the airline industry. Launched by a number of airlines in the 80s as a joint project, the airlines since sold it as a separate company. Guess what? Amadeus is now worth more than all the airlines that launched it combined! The network effect means that being the central hub for booking tickets is much more valuable than actually operating airplanes, where you are easily replaced and mostly need to compete on price. It was clearly a topic of conversation when discussing [Distribusion](http://distribusion.com/), a GDS for the bus industry, which Creandum backed last year. ### Platforms A platform is something that others build stuff on top of. They are somewhat similar to marketplaces, and also have indirect network effects, but rather than just being a place where people buy and sell stuff, a platform is a place that products and businesses are built on. A big reason why users flock to a platform is if it has the best products - even if those products are built by other companies. And the best products are usually built for the platforms that have the most users. This creates a flywheel effect that can be extremely powerful. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6l338Vxr93t4jsw5tKRTns/08210803989954e512433624553df4b0/image_326.jpg) Operating systems like Windows and iOS are obvious platforms, but the list also includes [Unity](https://unity3d.com/) (a platform for game development), [Wechat](http://www.wechat.com/en/) and [Slack](https://slack.com/) (chat applications that you can build apps inside), [Fulfillment by Amazon](https://services.amazon.com/fulfillment-by-amazon/benefits.htm) (ecommerce infrastructure for third party ecommerce companies) and [AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/) (cloud infrastructure). Most big software companies aspire to become platforms, because it is such a powerful position to be in. Indeed, Salesforce, Zendesk, Shopify etc all have app stores: they fear being disrupted by nimbler, leaner startups like they disrupted the companies that came before them, and hope that the power of being a platform, and having useful third party apps to offer to their customers, will let them better sustain their market position. Platforms are some of the most difficult businesses to build, but once you have made it, they are the most powerful business models out there. Microsoft was the most important technology company in the world for 20 years because they owned the main computing platform (Windows), and only lost the position when mobile replaced PC as the main computing device. And the four most valuable companies in the world today - Apple, Google, Microsoft and Amazon - are all platform companies. ### Data network effects The final type of network effects is _data netw

articles.title: Why we think Pleo is the perfect Fintech company
articles.text: — By Creandum's Johan Brenner and Bjarke Staun-Olsen The first sign that we knew [Pleo](http://pleo.io) was onto something big was a year ago at a Bloomberg startup event in Copenhagen. Jeppe, Pleo's CEO, did a great pitch on their smart company payment cards. When it was time for questions, Theis, one of the [Vivino](http://vivino.com) founders (Vivino is a Creandum portfolio company), immediately raised his hand and asked when he could get his hands on the product. Now that we can announce Pleo has raised €5.5 million with a new investment from Creandum Fund IV, we're excited to get our hands on it too. Pleo does two important things: it makes it easy for companies to get a handle on employee spending all while streamlining the process of tracking receipts. When a new employee joins, you simply add an additional card online, and get a virtual card instantly, and a physical one in the mail within a few days. This is a stark contrast to when Bjarke joined Creandum, where our office manager had to send a paper application to the card issuer and I waited 6 weeks for the card to arrive. Managers and finance departments can set spending limits for each card, and get a live dashboard so they can track everything employees buy in real time. This added transparency and control has convinced many Pleo customers to give cards to everyone in the organisation, instead of only giving them to top management and make everyone else lay out money personally. Pleo is a big plus for employees as well. With a card in their pocket they've got less friction to buy things they need to do their job, and the Pleo app instantly reminds them with a push notification to take a picture of the receipt when they use their card. Pleo also integrates with customers' accounting system, so all transactions including receipts are sent there directly, which means that with Pleo, we can finally stop wasting time doing expense management. We think this hits the sweet spot of Fintech for three reasons. First, it's a problem that touches just about every business on earth. Employee spending and tracking receipts are one of those problems that every business knows they have, but are unaware that there's a beautiful solution out there. We've personally seen how once companies find out about Pleo, they come knocking down their door until they get it. Second, it's super easy for organizations to adopt. The secret here was for Pleo to solve this problem through credit cards, which are easier to plug into than switching to a brand new bank account and overhauling the company's financial backend. And third, we see Pleo getting even smarter. Looking at their product roadmap we have a strong feeling that Pleo will completely change business' relationship to employee spending, just like Slack did with employee communication. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/scUtD9duLr5w0MsuBQa8r/85860640323c169a322411ff7dd2f38b/image_324.jpg) And as always, the most important thing is the team. CEO Jeppe Rindom has deep hands-on experience as CFO of Tradeshift, one of the most successful Fintech companies coming out of the Nordics. Meanwhile, CTO Niccolo Perra has serious experience in the technical side of Fintech from his work on the core team behind massively-used products like Mobilepay and the payment service provider DIBS. It's no irony that this is being written while staring at a pile of receipts on our desks - we just received our monthly reminder that we need to organize receipts for our colleague in the back office, who then needs to process them. In Fintech, Creandum strives to find companies that has the best mousetrap to attract customers whether they are consumers or businesses. A great mousetrap is usually a very focussed product attacking a profitable niche and beautifully solves a huge problem for the user. — For more information on [Pleo](http://pleo.io), check out their website. Or learn more about [Creandum](None) at [Creandum.com](http://creandum.com) or by following Creandum on medium.

articles.title: The Creandum Funds invest in Armada Interactive — where mobile gaming is heading
articles.author: Daniel Blomquist
articles.text: It doesn't feel like a long time ago, but I first met Samuli Syvähuoko, CEO and cofounder of [Armada Interactive](https://armadainteractive.com/), 6–7 years ago in Ruoholahti, right next to Supercell's second office. At the time, Samuli was mapping out the Finnish game ecosystem, and there couldn't be a better person doing it given Samuli's involvement with the scene since the early 90's as a serial entrepreneur behind Finnish game companies like Remedy, Fathammer and Recoil, and an organizer of the legendary Assembly Computer Festival. We continued to stay in touch as he was building two more game companies. First Helsinki GameWorks that merged with NextGames, and eventually Armada. Now I am very happy that we finally have come to a working relationship as the Creandum Funds join Korea Investment Partners as new investors in Armada. Mobile games is a massive business today with revenues around $40Bn (representing close to 50% of global games revenues) and growing $5–10Bn per year. But it is also an industry dominated by a few very successful companies and even games, and it has been very hard for new companies to enter the top-grossing charts the last few years and frankly there have not been much of innovation in terms of gameplay and mechanics. We think Armada has the potential to change that. The team is a great example of what we look for in game companies: successful and experienced game developers and company builders. It also checks the box of a big untapped market opportunity as we feel that there is a big potential providing core gamers with a mobile game experience that can rival or surpass what they are used to on PC and console. Samuli and his co-founders have built an impressive team who are working on a very ambitious and truly unique game concept that combine immersive and competitive gameplay with highly innovative new mechanics and UX. It is extremely fun and engaging to play but also engaging and addictive to watch. I would not be surprised if it can become the first massively popular mobile e-sports game. Game on!

articles.title: Virta Health — Reversing Diabetes
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.text: **In** 2000 I was diagnosed with Diabetes. Every day since then, I have injected insulin at least four times per day. And many more times than that, I've pricked my fingers to measure my blood glucose level to find out if the insulin dosage was the right one. Now if you think that the associated discomfort with pinpricks are the main issue for me as a diabetic - think again. The bigger problem with diabetes is that, all other factors equal, it can impact your long-term health significantly. I monitor the leading indicator of how well I manage the disease regularly, and trust that the positive indications I get mean less long-term impact on my health. The diabetes I have, Type 1, is a chronic disease. Reversing it remains a dream, albeit one that I share with many hundreds of thousands of patients around the globe. When I first heard black belt entrepreneur and elite triathlete Sami Inkinen tell his story about himself becoming pre-diabetic and committing to build a company that could reverse diabetes, I felt deep in my heart that Creandum should get involved. Virta is truly remarkable for being able to _reverse_ type 2 diabetes without all the risks, costs, or side effects of medications or surgery. The disease Virta Health has started to address is Diabetes Type 2. It's root cause is different from Type 1 but patients share a lot of the long-term negative health effects. The treatment is also similar: tens of millions of patients use medication - pills and insulin - as help to lead a normal life. It's a multi-billion dollar cost to society and equally big market for the pharma industry. But instead of helping to managing the disease with medication, Virta is truly remarkable for being able to _reverse_ type 2 diabetes without all the risks, costs, or side effects of medications or surgery. You may have seen articles suggesting that some people have found ways to manage their Type 2 diabetes through a diet and treatment plan. Virta health takes it to the next level by building on decades of research into the topic and turning it into the Virta clinic managed by medical professionals. ![The new tool used to reverse Type 2 Diabetes](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/12be75nw5Kbb8G9MQPNlyp/f6b7936ded0a328b493e6c092972bc79/image_323.png) Here, Virta does two big things. First, they take an individualized approach to metabolic health by focusing on carbohydrate intake and nutritional ketosis to address the underlying biochemistry of diabetes. It is stunning to see the impact of Virta Health's treatment - many patients lose their dependence on drugs or insulin altogether. And second the clinic is further improved by artificial intelligence, so that the healthcare team can provide round-the-clock care to their patients, feeding information directly to Virta's physicians and health coaches. Rather than most diabetes patients seeing their doctors once every six to twelve months, those suffering from type 2 diabetes now have access to continuous individualized remote care of the highest possible standards. From my own experience, I can tell how dramatically different and very valuable to the patients this is. Virta Health is a massive paradigm shift for people suffering from diabetes, and it's a huge opportunity for the company - people spend over $300B+ on diabetes and prediabetes prevention combined. Creandum has been backing Sami and the team ever since the seed round because Virta Health, to us, defines what medicine should look like in 2017. More: [Virta Health Launch Blogpost](http://blog.virtahealth.com/we-are-on-a-mission-to-reverse-type-2-diabetes/) — At Creandum, we believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. Check out our [website](http://creandum.com) or follow [Creandum Family](http://medium.com/creandum-family) on Medium to learn more.

articles.title: What comes next after Nordic.AI?
articles.text: I was excited when I jumped on yet another very early morning flight last week to go to Copenhagen for the first [Nordic.AI](http://nordic.ai) conference. Excited because AI is a technology that is very quickly in the process of changing the world, and because it's a field that I spend a lot of time on, having built my first company on Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence. The lineup was one of the most interesting I've seen at a startup conference, and it shows how much great talent we have in the Nordics. Andreas Mattsson from [Spotify](http://spotify.com) uncovered some of the magic under the hood that drives all my personalised weekly playlists and daily mixes. Danny Lange, [Unity's](https://unity3d.com/) Head of Machine Learning, who used to run Machine Learning at Uber, talked about how enterprises can and should use AI to enhance their products. And Lars Maaløe, Head of Machine Learning at [Corti](http://cortilabs.com/), laid out radical new applications of AI in the healthcare space. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1JFQFXT62gtCCOO7banP3l/438539c5afec781dbf14423b8a90e8bf/image_322.jpg) I was part of an investor panel with [Azeem Azhar](https://twitter.com/azeem), [Nathan Benaich](https://twitter.com/NathanBenaich) and [Hampus Jakobsson](https://twitter.com/hajak), where we discussed what an AI-first startup should focus on. I laid out my view - [as I've done before](https://medium.com/creandum-family/the-value-isnt-your-algorithm-it-s-your-data-dda4a1bf688b#.s4mccqcc9) - that even though you are AI first, you should focus on solving one important problem for your customers, build a full stack solution and not just the AI part, and make sure that you gather data through your product that nobody else has access to. Azeem, who is one of the world's leading authorities on AI, didn't fully agree: his point was that by getting together a group of insanely smart AI researchers, and focus on building bleeding edge technology, you can do very very well for yourself by aspiring to being acquired by Google or Facebook. And he's absolutely right, although there is a risk of limiting the upside potential with that strategy. The big question now is what comes next. In order to succeed with this mission of making the Nordics into a global AI hub, we need to do the following things: - **Get organised**: everyone involved in AI, machine learning, data science, quantitative research and whatever it's called, sign up for the [Nordic.AI](http://nordic.ai) newsletter, follow it on Twitter, and be active participants in making AI a group conversation. - **Celebrate the big successes**: Inspiration is key to get more people to aim for greatness. Share great news, and use the #Nordic_AI hashtag on Twitter and elsewhere. - **Strengthen the ties between academia and business, particularly startups:** There is so much we can learn from each other, and with a groundbreaking field like AI we need to be sure we're communicating to universities what talent we're looking for. - **Improve access to talent**: Continue to push our politicians to make it easier to allow brilliant minds from all over the globe to move here. Big things will be happening in this space in the years ahead!

articles.title: Elevating Creandum to the next level
articles.author: Daniel Blomquist
articles.text: After 7 years of being part of building a fast-growing VC-backed software startup and then almost 10 years as a VC focusing on software and game investments at Creandum, I am today starting my new professional life as Operating Partner at Creandum. Since I joined Creandum soon ten years ago, we have grown along all possible dimensions. Bigger team, more LPs, portfolio companies and funds under management, and now 3 offices. At the same time, there's much more competition and capital available for Europe's best entrepreneurs. Venture really is about finding and being allowed to invest in a few breakaway companies and sometimes it can feel at bit random but the best firms in the industry have been able to do this repeatedly and systematically. And while it's true that success breeds success and that some top firms have been able to sustain stellar performance, others have not. Our ambition is to be one of the leading VCs in Europe and we have now reached a point where all building blocks are in place for that - investments in some of Europe's most successful companies and strongest entrepreneurs, top-industry performance and returns, and a great team in Stockholm, San Francisco and Berlin. But to be successful over time, we need to double down on how we operate so we can offer such a great service and experience to top entrepreneurs, that they choose Creandum as their preferred partner when building their companies. This means that we need to continuously work harder and step up our efforts. Four years ago, we started an office in San Francisco to better help entrepreneurs successfully build their companies in the US. Recently, we opened an office in Berlin to be better partners for entrepreneurs in Germany and continental Europe, and we will continue to do what's necessary to assist ambitious European entrepreneurs looking for building globally leading companies. As Operating Partner, I will lead many of the efforts aimed at providing the best possible support for entrepreneurs. I will manage our operations, LP relationships, investment advisory process, and fund strategy making sure that we optimize the returns of the Creandum funds as well as the experience and service provided to entrepreneurs and investors. I will remain on the board of most of the Creandum portfolio companies that I have been working with and I will continue to assist the investment team in areas of my expertise but I will no longer be involved in new investments on behalf of the Creandum funds. While I have highly enjoyed this part of being a VC, I also very much look forward to making Creandum the top choice for entrepreneurs and investors alike.

articles.title: 10 years later: Getting to know Spotify before Series A
articles.text: We first met Spotify in spring of 2007, and later Creandum Fund II led the firm's first venture round of funding. Ten years later we're hearing Creandum partner Fredrik Cassel brag too much about being user 700-something, so we we decided look at that moment where we first signed up. This interview [can also be found on our website](https://www.creandum.com/stories/spotify). **Creandum:** So take us back and give us the Creandum/Spotify story. Thinking about timing, Creandum had just raised Fund II where the firm could start focusing on software and web, rather than the old focus on semiconductors and hardware in Fund I. **Fredrik Cassel:** Yeah it was a wild start. I can still remember it because I've thought about it so many times. It actually all started at my old school - the KTH school of Technology in Stockholm where I was sourcing new deals. I was watching a webcast of what had happened earlier in the day and there was this guy Andreas [Ehn, the first CTO of Spotify] on stage pitching this new company. He wasn't saying anything about what they were doing but somehow it seemed very interesting. And I could tell from the audience that they had a lot of respect for the guy and the venture he was building, even though he didn't say too much. So I reached out to learn more. He said that the company was called Spotify but he wasn't the guy I should speak to, I should talk to someone called Daniel. He put me in touch, I gave Daniel a call, and he asked me "Creandum - who are you guys?" and I gave the backdrop and told him what we were up to: changing the fund focus and really swinging for the fences. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/2juiONIb8OsGKr47aVi6xX/dc6ab2f20ea2980bd6473dfddbec1f81/image_320.png) And that was the start of a relationship that is still stands firm ten years later. So this was in February 2007 (edit: April! [Thanks Sriram for hosting Hej](https://twitter.com/_fredrik/status/971704415882285056?s=12)!)and we ended up following the company for a good 18 months before the fund finally invested. Those were 18 months followed by ups and downs in the relationship, but also plenty of back and forths in negotiations. And ultimately as it became very clear how the relationships with the rights holders would look, we were closer to the company than nearly anyone else in the venture scene which allowed us to pull the trigger and actually invest. **Creandum**: Tell us about Spotify back then. Because in 2007 Napster was shut down, but it was almost the cultural peak of Bittorrent use and every magazine was predicting the death of the record industry. How did you believe that these guys could not only get people to start paying for music, but overcome the technical challenges and negotiate with these rights holders to make it all work? **Fredrik**: The first thought was, "This is impossible, right?" As you were downloading your MP3 files you would then un-RAR them, rename them, try to get some order into that crazy mess. And here was a company saying, "We have all the world's music, it's searchable, and it plays instantly." It was impossible, right? It sounded completely impossible. And then we tried it out. I think I'm user number 704, or something? And it worked! It was just fantastic. The pitch already from the start was, "This needs to be better than piracy," and of course anyone who tried it knew that it was. It was just better. But at first - just hearing about the product - I thought it couldn't really work. And then I tried it out at my first meeting with Daniel and Martin. I sat in the room and they asked me to name any song I could think of. And I pulled this thing out of my pocket which was a super small Swedish artist called The Bear Quartet. They sold maybe 5 thousand CDs per release in those days. Martin asked, "What was that? Beer-chord?" and Daniel corrected him and said, "No, Bear Quartet. They're from Luleå." And Martin entered it and of course all their songs were there. I was blown away. So they also overshot significantly when it comes to minimum viable product. It was everything. So that was the first sensation that the impossible seems to be true. The second extraterrestrial experience was when we had the first demo with their mobile product. You know, quite frankly when Daniel told us they were doing an app for mobile phones that would have the same functionality as the desktop, nobody believed that it could be done. This was back in the era of Nokia's dominance. So the first Spotify mobile app that was ever made was a Nokia Series 60 app. Daniel demoed it and everyone's jaws dropped to the floor like, "How the fuck could this work on a cell phone?" and it worked seamlessly! And eventually over time they hacked their way onto the iPhone, pre app-store, to demo an even better experience. And then I still remember the first day walking from my home to the office listening to Spotify over 3G on my cellphone and I thought "Ok. This is a new world now." Today you think about it as something that is ubiquitous. But back then it was like, "This is the next generation." Fantastic. **Creandum**: Tell us more about Martin Lorentzon and Daniel Ek. How did you perceive them as entrepreneurs? **Fredrik**: We got to know them over those 18 months after my first reaching out. I believe I was one of the first VCs to reach out to them, ever. And then doing the deal we got to know them as a couple that complemented each other super well, but who both really had the power and integrity to say no to deals that they didn't want. And that impacted us, of course, because there were many moments over those 18 months where we wanted to invest but there just wasn't a deal on the table that they would accept. But it also made them ultimately do the right deals for the company. They didn't compromise or take shortcuts in any significant way. They knew what they wanted and they went after that. So we got to know them as counterparts in a pretty intense negotiation over a long per

articles.title: Tech in China
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Learnings from scratching the surface of a new world
articles.text: As Venture Capitalists we search for change and disruption. We have seen much of that coming out from our home markets in Europe and of course Silicon Valley. But recent years China has grown into to a serious contender or true innovation! Let's face it - China's startup scene is growing at an unparalleled pace in some of the most interesting sectors to VCs these days. In 2015, [4.44 million companies were set up in China](http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2016twosession/2016-03/03/content_23729043.htm), which averages out to 12,000 (!) a day. Therefore, a few weeks back the whole investment advisory team of Creandum passed through Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Beijing to learn from the local players. Talking to giants like [Alibaba](https://www.alibaba.com/), [Baidu](http://baidu.com), and [Tencent](http://www.tencent.com/index_e.shtml), and key investors like [Sequoia China](https://www.sequoiacap.com/china/en/), [DST](https://angel.co/dst), [HAX](http://hax.co), [Innoway](https://qz.com/534956/inside-innoway-chinas-36-million-government-backed-startup-village/), [Legend Star](http://www.lstar.vc/) and [Zhenfund](http://www.zhenfund.com/en/) we've come away with some key takeaways that we feel are important for the modern European entrepreneur. **There are two internets on the globe** **— the Chinese internet and everything else beyond the great firewall.** All services you know of in Europe and the US exist in China with their own domestic version. For Chinese internet users, there are limited reasons to use VPN services to access our part of the internet since everything already exist on their side of the wall. As proud backers of [Vivino](http://Vivino.com) we even stumbled upon a huge ad campaign for the domestic equivalent [Wine World](http://www.wine-world.com/). ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/13Rfg2iYrsYxlpGRQ6YeS8/738d46f94f81f7d74e4778e96b1b58c5/image_317.jpg) Due to the size and unique differences most Chinese entrepreneurs still focus is on the domestic market, but they are increasingly looking [beyond their borders](http://technode.com/2017/03/28/ofo-overseas-expansion/) - especially in consumer internet and for mobile services. The situation in enterprise software is however significantly different since big parts of the Chinese market leapfrogged directly into mobile without a heavy desktop legacy. This has resulted in the domestic enterprise software sector significantly lagging behind on the international front...for the time being. **All the stories you've heard about cutthroat competition in China's internet are true**. Things move _fast_ in China! As soon as a service gains traction, you will see numerous teams going up head-to-head against you. There are so much entrepreneurial execution capabilities in China waiting to be deployed when the right idea comes along. Furthermore, the three big players in China referred locally as BAT: Baidu (search engine), Alibaba (ecom), and Tencent (social), are highly focused on the domestic market where they expand deep into their verticals and beyond. All these three players have their unique strengths but they also compete head to head across most verticals. There's not one independent Spotify in China which dominates the market, but rather 2–3 Spotify equivalent services who are deeply integrated and bundled into the respective BAT services. And bundling is the core part of Chinese product development and distribution. This also explains why competition becomes so fierce in China, as the most unexpected platforms broaden their offering with anything that gains traction in the market. Any European startups looking at China should seriously consider how they can partner with any of the BAT for access and distribution, as they are a necessity to scale services in China. For products and services with low barriers of entry, it seems to be literally _crazy_! We became blown away how all metropolitan areas in major Chinese cities are invaded by bike sharing companies. Each one with their unique color there are at least 5 well-funded companies fighting it out, and easily 100 smaller players trying to get their slice of the pie. We met with [Ofo](https://www.ofo.so/), the bike rental company that spits out 1,800 bikes an hour from its factory and turn up on every street corner to be unlocked by smartphones. Ofo has some 20M users, after only 18 months of operations. A truly amazing achievement. Entrepreneurs should know that making a dent in China with products with low barriers of entry takes A LOT of cash. Ofo have raised at least $450M already and they're just getting started... ![Source: [http://english.sina.com/china/s/2017-01-16/detail-ifxzqnim4542559.shtml](http://english.sina.com/china/s/2017-01-16/detail-ifxzqnim4542559.shtml)](https://miro.medium.com/1*xqgjl0riigkmDf3oIOTT3Q.jpeg) **Beijing is the true startup hub in China.** Sure, you've heard about Shenzhen's hardware heaven and what's going on in Shanghai and Hangzhou, but Beijing is where the big tech players all meet. 4 of the world's top 10 valued startups are based in China, and 3 of them in Beijing alone. Beijing also is the true Sand Hill Road of China's startup space, with 60% of Chinese venture capital originating there. If you come to China on tech business, you can't miss the capital. **Trends are global.** The investor landscape in Silicon Valley and Europe at the moment get very excited about companies within AI, VR/AR and autonomous driving. The same exists in China. Just as much innovation is happening within these deep tech and platform developments in China as elsewhere in the world. A big advantage and factor behind these specific fields for China is because the hardware required to prototype and sell these products can be found right in your backyard. To wrap up, we paired our excitement with how fast things were moving in China with questions of what the next steps are for our firm and portfolio (to no fault of all the great people that took time ou

articles.title: Cornershop raising a $21m Series B
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Doing it like Uber. But in LatAm. And in groceries.
articles.text: In the past recent years, some of the biggest entrepreneurial muscles have focused on the logistics and transportation sector. André The Giant of private companies, Uber - [a $69B "startup"](https://www.bloomberg.com/gadfly/articles/2017-03-16/uber-needs-to-get-real-about-that-69-billion-price-tag), captured massive value by creating a magical experience of having a car appear to take you home with the tap of a button. About a year ago Creandum backed a company building a similarly magical experience for grocery shopping in Latin America. With a few taps on your phone, [Cornershop](http://cornershopapp.com) gets groceries delivered to your home within 90 minutes. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4F6M32mfXlzuIrFKG1Aghc/393af65222952fbc4225145d0581e40c/image_315.png) During the past year we have been honored to witness an impressive growth journey with Cornershop, and today we're excited to announce...drumroll ... Cornershop just secured $21M in a Series B round led by [Accel](http://accel.com). Getting backing from Silicon Valley's finest for a company in LatAm is no easy feat and a true testament to how amazingly the team has executed this business so far. ### So how did the company get to here? At the time of Creandum Fund's [original investment in 2016](https://medium.com/creandum-family/groceries-beyond-europe-f5be8cdd9432) the company was experiencing a nice trajectory, but were losing money on each bag of groceries they delivered. We realized building a delivery business on top of razor thin margins in this industry would be difficult, but if anyone could figure it out it would be [Oskar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/oskarhjertonsson/), [Daniel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/danielundurraga/) and [Chaq](https://angel.co/chaq). The bet was also that the LatAm market had a unique combination of regional purchasing power and cost of labor which could lead to healthy unit economics. As part of that we identified 4 major milestones to achieve using the Series A financing: 1. Prove the business model with profitable unit economics 2. "Win" the Mexican and Chilean markets for online grocery 3. Secure partnerships with leading grocers 4. Significantly grow GMV Looking at the company today, roughly 12 months later, we can conclude that they checked all the boxes. With scale, amazing ops and impressive tech the company operates with very healthy unit economics, is significantly larger than the closest online grocer startup in the region, have several exciting established grocer partnerships in the region. All these achievements while growing GMV 400% in a year! And for the record, scaling a grocery business like Cornershop is not like growing a pure software company. The complexity to meet demand by deploying just the right amount of fulfillment workforce throughout a week, and how you have to tighten every little step in the value chain in order not to screw up your slim margins is very tricky. ### And, what about the Uber comparison? Uber's recent PR issues and the lofty valuation and burn aside, the company's ability to scale was inconceivable until now. It. Is. Impressive. And much of Uber's growth was enabled by these 3 things: 1. Uber didn't need their own car fleets and other physical infrastructure to take advantage of transportation demand. 2. Uber took advantage of a flexible labor supply, motivated by earning some extra spending money in their free time at their own terms. 3. The Uber experience compared to any pre-existing services was better across all dimensions. Uber truly redefined the taxi experience. Outside of an amazing team, Cornershop's growth is also enabled by very similar elements: 1. Instead of building up its own physical infrastructure, Cornershop relies on and partner with your local grocery stores as local warehouses. A significantly more capital efficient and scalable model compared to building your own distribution centers and warehouses. 2. Cornershop uses a fulfillment team of contractors, which dynamically resizes based on demand cycles over the day and weeks. 3. Most previous online services were associated with insane lead times and unreliable quality. Cornershop redefined the grocery shopping experience through transparency, high quality and rapid on-demand service using an intuitive and beautiful interface. Those who try it very much make Cornershop part of their grocery shopping routine. We see a massive opportunity for Cornershop to become a leading online grocer and tech company in Latin America, and we remain exceptionally excited for this $500B+ market opportunity. As a European VC we happily back our region's best entrepreneurs regardless where they find opportunities, and in this case, the Swedish co-founder Oskar identified a market on the other side of the globe from us but with unique characteristics to create a giant. The journey is still only getting started and we would like to extend a big toast and congratulations to the team for securing financing to continue to scale and take the Cornershop service across the rest of Latin America! ![ groceries.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/71HaLsdbzGEW0KFslh6PLK/2998eb2b5b0ee6099a42ad879953abe8/image_316.gif)

articles.title: The iZettle story with cofounder Magnus Nilsson
articles.text: We caught up with Magnus Nilsson, COO and cofounder of iZettle, the payments solution that has become the one-stop-shop for small businesses. Between a few good laughs we found the story of how iZettle beat industry experts (and our) expectations. This interview [can also be found on our website](https://www.creandum.com/stories/izettle). **Creandum Partner Johan Brenner:** Creandum participated in your A round but we should have invested in your seed round. As I recall it, we did some due diligence and we felt that the regulatory environment was initially too big of a burden. In retrospect I think [iZettle](http://izettle.com) has proven - more than many others - how important the team has been. **Cofounder and COO Magnus Nilsson:** You know, just to take a look at that decision, Jacob and I quickly decided that I would be the hardware expert. And that was somehow based on the fact that I had been in charge of importing GPS equipment from China at my previous company. I set out to find someone who could make hardware, and, looked all over the world to see who could do a an EMV certified chip card reader for us. And I found a company very early on that was making all the e-banking devices that were used to put in chip cards. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7zFnRErw6SlRoPoXtuI0td/32c93c00adaa521744412ea8f4689026/image_313.jpg) I found through the CEO the person to talk to and called the guy, and I have never, in my entire business life, been treated that way. Before or after. So I call this guy, he's an expert on chip and EMV, and I tell him, "This is our game plan". We started this company and we want to do this payments system. We're doing it with without magstripe, we're doing it for chip cards only, and I believe that you would be the perfect partner for us to produce our hardware. And you could hear a deep sigh on the other end of the line. He says, "You know, how long have you been in this business?" And I said, "Not for very long, as you can tell. But I really believe this will fly. I have some proof points, but there are some hurdles to overcome." He says, "Magnus, do you know how many cab drivers there are in China?" I said, "No." "There are 6 million cab drivers in China. Isn't that amazing." "That's amazing," I said "And he said, "Well, don't you think they would like a product like this? Well they would love a product like this! You know why they don't have it? Because it can't be done. So I only have one advice for you. And that is to close down this company. It's never going to work. And trust me, I've been in this business for a long time." ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7LBhpm0p5fmXyWKJzvM6Xi/fa53d1adb75c3346f092361c5e8e62bc/image_314.jpg) I said, well, you know, that's a pretty hard statement to give someone who's just started a company.
