articles.title: The Future of Flexible Staffing — Creandum Backs Syft
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.text: Technology has long opened up non-traditional forms of employment, and today it's in our face more than ever. Whether you're booking a ride or getting food delivered, you're likely to interact with a non-traditional employee. Someone who fits buzzwords like "freelancer", the "gig economy", and "the agile workforce". Driving demand for this style of employment is the desire for greater income, flexibility, and freedom. While much of the gig economy is relatively new, there is another form of flexible employment that has been around for centuries: temp staffing. ### The Temporary Staffing Market Temp staffing is a staggering $400 billion market worldwide. It's a highly fragmented market of approximately 260,000 temp staffing agencies who can be described as being high-touch (i.e. labour intensive) and low-tech. It's a model that effectively kills the drivers of greater income, flexibility, and freedom. Temp agencies are run by arbitrary command and control. There is no consideration to personal preferences or schedules - no freedom, no flexibility. What makes sense to an agency often makes little-to-no sense to the workers and the employers. This is evident in the high, close to 12% no-show rates that surround the industry. Furthermore, traditional temp agencies do not account for individual skills or experience. Temp workers are treated as a commodity - every barista, every bartender, every hostess, etc. is treated the same. As a result, temp agencies post wages corresponding to low skill levels, which in turn limits the market. On top of that, temp agencies need to recoup their high operating expenses, which translates into very high fees for employers on hiring temp staff. Typically between 25% to 50% or more on top of the pay rate. Despite all of the above, the market exists, and is growing. It exists out of necessity. Traditionally, temp workers have been used as a stopgap solution to replace permanent employees (e.g. in case of illnesses, temporary leaves of absence, etc.). But increasingly, temp workers are also used to increase capital efficiency in industries that face high seasonal fluctuations (e.g. anything from warehousing to hospitality to sports or other event organisers). ### [Syft(ers)](https://syftapp.com) to the Rescue With the shortcomings of traditional temp agencies in mind, we are excited to announce that Creandum Fund IV is leading a £6m series A round in [Syft](https://syftapp.com) - a marketplace for flexible staffing. At Creandum we have not only spent a lot of time thinking about [how the future of work shapes up to be](https://medium.com/startup-grind/adapt-or-die-5-changes-in-the-workplace-which-will-impact-all-organizations-375409605408), but also the forces driving this change. Creandum have long been exposed to various services surrounding the hospitality industry (one of the big Syft verticals) through [Bookatable](http://bookatable.com) that I co-founded years ago, as well as Creandum Fund's investments in [Planday](https://www.planday.com) (workforce management solution for shift-based businesses). ![Syft's applications to manage every aspect of temp staffing](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7w316AI4waONcJ3Slz9nCm/2959c4509828b50587343bac66361a02/image_295.jpg) Syft was founded by [Jack Beaman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jackbeaman) and [Novo Abakare](https://www.linkedin.com/in/novoabakare) in London - home to the largest market for temp staffing in Europe. A strong team of entrepreneurs who we believe have what it takes to define the future of flexible staffing. In a short while, they have built a strong platform with a mission to replace the gatekeepers- the traditional temp agencies. Syft is a win-win proposition for everyone. Except, perhaps, for the temp agencies. What excites us about Syft is their win-win proposition for both the temp workers and the employers that enables Syft to disrupt the traditional agencies. Syft brings the drivers that have shaped other industries towards flexible forms of employment also to the temp staffing market. Syft shifts control and choice from temp agencies to employers and temp workers. Temp workers can choose when, where, and for whom they want to work. Employers, on the other hand, can easily and quickly (i.e. within hours) hire temps, and also choose to work with their regulars. This results in significantly lower no-show rates than the current industry average. Syft aims to decommoditize the market - help employers find temp staff with appropriate skill sets, and enable skilled workforce earn wages corresponding to their skill sets. This unlocks the temp staffing market to a much wider audience than only people willing to work for a minimum wage. To top it off, Syft's low-touch and high-tech solution enables them to pay temp workers higher salaries, all the while being a cheaper solution for the employers. It's really a win-win. If you are as excited as we are about the future of temp staffing, [Syft is hiring for various roles](https://syftapp.com/careers-at-syft/). Alternatively, you can use their platform to [hire flexible staff](https://syftapp.com/employers/) or [work a shift yourself](https://syftapp.com/job-seekers/). _At Creandum, we believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. Check out our [website](http://creandum.com) or follow [Creandum Family](http://medium.com/creandum-family) on Medium to learn more._

articles.title: ICOs and what makes financial markets work
articles.text: [Initial Coin Offerings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_coin_offering) (ICOs) are the hottest thing in tech right now. Countless cases of founders raising tens or hundreds of millions of dollars weeks after launching their companies have made people ask: Is this the future of fundraising? Will VCs be out of a job soon? And will existing stock markets be replaced? Being a tech dude, I'm very excited about the potential for technology to revolutionise how financial markets work. But as a former finance guy who played around with credit derivatives on the London trading floor of Goldman Sachs during the financial crisis of 2007 and 2008, I know that most of what is happening with ICOs now has happened before. And it did not end well. ![This was the kind of place I worked](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/54w6JxUB581ZqFrbM6u180/30ee1251240dac1d5fad2395157ce859/image_292.jpg) ### Here's where it goes wrong People who follow ICOs will know that [buyers in an ICO do not buy equity](https://news.21.co/thoughts-on-tokens-436109aabcbe), but rather buy the right to use the future product that the people behind the ICO are going to build. This makes ICOs similar to Kickstarter campaigns, with an important difference: The right is freely transferrable, and the future price of the product is not fixed, but rather will depend on future supply and demand for the product. Unlike shares of stock in startup companies, there are no restrictions on who can participate in an ICO. And at the same time, they can be used for speculation: buy the token and hope it appreciates in value. ICO pundits talk about how this is revolutionizing how to start companies: that VCs will be out of business soon, and that this new technology has made it possible to raise money in minutes instead of months. There's just one problem with this logic: The reason ordinary people cannot buy shares in the newest hottest startup is not because nobody thought that that could be cool before 2017. It also has nothing to do with the blockchain somehow making it all technologically possible to make trades: On the US public equity markets, average trading costs are 0.01%, with billions of trades and billions of dollars worth of stock changing hands daily. This infrastructure is built for massive scale, volume and stability, and could handle ICO volumes in a heartbeat. Instead, the reason why there is no market for buying and selling shares in new and hot young startups comes down to two things: - **Regulation:** Authorities are explicitly preventing it - **Counterparties:** There are not enough investors to trade with for the market to function Let's dig into each of these two separately. ### Regulation It may surprise some people that the [SEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission) is not preventing the public from investing in startups to prevent them from getting rich. Rather, it put regulations in place because without lots of rules, it is impossible to avoid scams in markets with massive asymmetric information: where some people - insiders; company management, board members etc - know much more about the company than the general public. ![Stock trading in the 1920s was wild!](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/34I2oQCJsWW3ws1ipU01Za/b95145b0224bc47bafee390ac519bbad/image_293.jpg) This goes back to the 1920s: Before the Great Depression, the stock market was free for all. And it was not pretty. CEOs who knew their company was in grave trouble could freely sell all their shares to the unknowing public before the market crashed. Worse than that, rings of sophisticated investors perfected pump and dump schemes: they would trade a given stock with each other at higher and higher prices while spreading hype to the public, and at some point, after it had gone up by a factor of 5 or 10 or 20, they would offload it to the public. The stock would soon experience a crash back to ordinary levels now that the artificial buying had ceased. A lot of ordinary people lost a lot of money. A lot of fraudsters made a lot of money. And most importantly, the public had little faith in the stock market, which meant that companies couldn't use it to raise money as efficiently as they otherwise would have to finance legitimate operations. After the Great Depression, President Roosevelt set up the SEC in 1934. Rules have been adjusted along the way, but the general logic is this: - Very tight **restrictions on how insiders are allowed to trade** in their stock: they are not allowed to trade on specific information that is not known to the general market, there are restrictions on when they are allowed to trade (eg. they cannot trade immediately before an earnings report), and their trading activity is made public. - **Market manipulation is illegal**, which means that you are not allowed to do trades or spread outright lies with the explicit intent to manipulate the market, which covers the pump and dump schemes mentioned above. - Clearly defined rules on what and how listed companies **need to report how they're doing** (mainly financially), so the public can properly assess whether they would make good investments. - Companies that can not or will not adhere to these requirements can only sell shares to sophisticated investors that know exactly which minefield they are going into. ![The SEC Headquarters in Washington, D.C.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/f1m1qL5amGfgwNqHljuP3/cc4e111c9d80ea48e73b5d1ffb44b165/image_294.jpg) It's counterintuitive for proponents of free markets that you need all these restrictions to get markets to work well. But there is just no way the market can take care of this by itself: the individual CEO or investor that can manipulate the market can make so much money in that one transaction that it won't matter if their reputation is destroyed. In less developed markets these principles are not followed as stringently, and because of that, they have poorer functioning stock markets. This e

articles.title: Backing Taxfix — The Tax Accountant for Everyone
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.text: This isn't news to anyone, but getting your taxes done in Germany is a hassle. It takes an average of 6 hours to complete your yearly duty - and at least three strong drinks worth of willpower. Laws are continuously changing, yearly updates to any tax software you might own are still sold on DVDs, and the average German quite reasonably doesn't see the point given how much effort it takes. Thanks to this, roughly 6 million Germans don't even hand in their taxes and just let the government figure it out. This is despite the fact that the average taxpayer gets back 900€ by the government! Of course you could hire a tax accountant, but that can be costly, bothersome, and really not focused on the average German; most tax accountants focus their services on white collar workers. Simply put, there's no modern and intelligent solution for the average German to handle taxes by themselves. That's why we're excited to be backing Taxfix, the automated tax accountant for everyone, in a €2 million round. **Not your typical Fintech company.** Those in the Berlin startup scene may recognise the founders, [Mathis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mathisbuechi/) and [Lino](https://www.linkedin.com/in/linoteuteberg/) as the founders of SmallPDF, the platform that makes it super easy to convert and edit all your PDF files. Thanks to these roots, Taxfix is not a typical taxation company or even your typical fintech company. It's a technology company for putting legal frameworks into practice. Over the last year, the founders have developed a unique backend that enables their inhouse tax accountants to create taxation logic within the app - without the help of developers. This is a huge shift in the way tax software is built. Rather than needing developers to understand taxes, regular tax accountants can build the app themselves. Thanks to this framework, the software can adapt to local needs, languages, and yearly changes to the tax law with unparalleled speed and scalability. Currently Taxfix is only available in Germany, but we look forward to it coming to your country. **User experience as a DNA.** Another important point is that the founders strive for excellence in user experience. Coming from their SmallPDF roots, the goal of Taxfix is to minimize time, hassle and burden for the user. One great example of this user experience is how Taxfix OCRs their users' yearly income statement. Just take a picture of the yearly statement your employer send you, and it will pull out 70 data points that it would otherwise have to ask each user. By leveraging this technology, the app only asks the relevant questions and minimizes data input. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.youtube.com%2Fembed%2Fgt3l1g37ijk%3Ffeature%3Doembed&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.youtube.com%2Fwatch%3Fv%3Dgt3l1g37ijk&image=https%3A%2F%2Fi.ytimg.com%2Fvi%2Fgt3l1g37ijk%2Fhqdefault.jpg&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=youtube" title="" height="480" width="640"></iframe> At the end of the process, the app calculates the amount the state owes to the user (or the amount the user owes to the state), and users can easily hand in their tax declaration through their phone. And best of all, Taxfix takes risk out of doing your taxes. Users only have to pay Taxfix a small fee if they get money back from the government. **Learning from their customers.** One of the most important things Taxfix is doing is building an intelligent tax accountant that proactively, asks the right questions from the right people. While your typical German tax advisors are optimized for men in corner offices, Taxfix is able to learn what their customer group - the other 80% - need and can declare to the state. Over the time the system gets better and learns what line items a user should declare. Did you know you can deduct the costs of laundering your dirty clothes as a construction worker? Or that there is a standard deduction for every trip to the doctor? Well, the app does. And it's happy to tell you. We see this as a huge opportunity for growth. Now for the first time, the average man on the street has access to a mobile-first tax accountant who's optimized for their needs. **Our hypothesis.** Personal finance is going more and more mobile. First it was banking, then insurance, and now finally taxes. We know that declaring taxes in most countries is right up there with going to the dentist. Solving the issue through an intelligent, beautifully designed user experience will build very valuable connections with its users. And why wouldn't it? It's saving them money. On the other side of the coin, Taxfix is able to collect meaningful data that can optimize the user experience in the next tax year, or provide adjacent products and services that are designed for each user. Taxfix is a product that we see only getting better and better. We are very excited to work with [Mathis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mathisbuechi/), [Lino](https://www.linkedin.com/in/linoteuteberg/), and the team, and t[here](https://taxfix.de/en/jobs-at-taxfix/)'s a chance for you to work with them too. Check out their open positions here. Read what others have written: [Tech.eu](http://tech.eu/brief/taxfix-funding/) (English), [Wirtschaftswoche](http://gruender.wiwo.de/steuer-start-ups-taxfix-greift-auf-einem-komplizierten-terrain-an/) (German), [Handelsblatt](http://www.handelsblatt.com/finanzen/banken-versicherungen/fintech-ticker-per-chat-zur-steuererklaerung/13863370.html) (German).

articles.title: Looking beyond Berlin in the German Startup Ecosystem
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Berlin is unarguably the center of german startup scene. Over the years it has drawn in talent from across Germany and Europe, and has built a name-brand reputation in the global startup ecosystem thanks to a consistent lineup of great startups. Since joining Creandum's Berlin office, I began to realise how easy it is to put up blinders and ignore the rest of Germany (and some do), but doing so would be a mistake. Other hubs also have much to offer: innovative startups, universities with top talent, and entrepreneurial support programs plugged into powerful industries. Having a look beyond the 3.5m inhabitants capital of Germany is worth it! For my own sake as a VC I decided to pull back and look at Germany as a whole: how are the Startups distributed among the country? What clusters can you find? How do they differ in funding or focus? And: What does this mean for Creandum? **Regional clusters** To narrow it down from an investor perspective, I focused on all Startups that raised more than $500k (with funding rounds recorded Crunchbase). As expected Berlin is by far off, the #1 in terms of number of startups and total funding amount, but there is an ambitious follower. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4HtJ6VX6SHR6GDg2HJXAil/a59b473a2de72401f9bce5706ac5c82b/image_286.jpg) **Number of startups with >$500k funding**: As expected, more than half of the startups with more than a small angel round of funding have their base in Berlin. Munich, Hamburg and Cologne are following, but in absolute numbers are still quite small. Further hubs, yet significantly smaller are: Frankfurt, Bonn, Stuttgart, Dresden as well as Aachen and Karlsruhe, who are known for their renowned technical universities. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6fUizPymgPt8c7jnDtnAdv/93a10794ad86ab8656b51c2059a107a6/image_287.jpg) **Startups per Capita (>$500k funding):** Relative to its inhabitants, Berlin and Munich have ~4x respectively 3x higher rates of startups per 1000 inhabitants than the smaller hubs. I believe this stems from a mix of local talent/universities, existing startup ecosystem and high quality of life of the cities, that attract founders. **Funding size** ![Note: Startups with >$500k funding](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/fWO104uBWYVJI4pwjtpwS/1c7f0431a33ddf172fb0570b952d7b7c/image_288.jpg) ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4m337FyKBRd6WgKa8d3aSJ/903c4cbace46b08814af0052f873188a/image_289.jpg) Berlin's large amount of funding relative to other cities is driven by both quantity of funding rounds in total as well as the amount of individual funding of some very large startups. Some of the best funded ventures have passed the actual startup stage: Berlin's unicorns - Delivery Hero, Zalando, Auto1 and HelloFresh - account for roughly one third of all funding in Berlin. However, looking at a the median funding size per company, Munich, Frankfurt and Berlin are roughly on par with ~$4M in funding per company. Bonn, Dresden and Aachen's high median can be explained by the low number of startups that passed the $500k threshold. However, the few who passed received quite significant funding, e.g. Nawabi (e-commerce, based in Aachen, >$25M funding in VC funding), BlueYonder (big data/ predictive analytics, based in Karlsruhe, >$50M in growth funding) or Sunfire (energy - liquid fuels and combustibles, based in Dresden, >$15M in VC funding). **Startups with the highest total funding per region** The distribution of startups in Germany becomes more tangible when mapping out large funded startups on a regional level. Again, the picture is relatively clear: Berlin → Munich → Hamburg → other Hubs There are several notable companies that did not make it to the map, due to inclusion criteria (e.g. founded within past 10y, funding level before exit) but should be mentioned here, as they contributed considerably to the local ecosystem: a.o. Wunderlist (Berlin), Quandoo (Berlin). Trivago (Düsseldorf), Check24 (Munich), Scout24 (Munich) **Industry: B2B vs. B2C** The major hubs vary by industry and focus. ![Source: DSM 2016](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/TNPnxt37QJ3NlVXlJG2yY/5a94be874a6dc3f79a0d1a6294b740b1/image_290.jpg) Berlin: Compared to the German average (35% B2C), Berlin has a higher proportion of B2C startups (>40%). This is also reflected by its unicorn flagships all coming from the B2C area. Yet Berlin is the largest hub and has upcoming startups across all industries. It is attracting talent from all over the world and I expect that also more large B2B startups will come from Berlin in the future. Hamburg: Traditionally a media and trade city, Hamburg is also home to the German headquarter of multinational tech giants like Google, Facebook and Twitter. Industry wise there is not a clear direction in the startup world, but some of it's most prominent startups are in Fintech (Kreditech, Deposit Solutions, Finanzcheck) and in E-commerce (Dreamlines). Munich: Bavaria is a powerhouse for the industrial sector in Germany. This is also reflected in the stronger B2B focus of startups. The focus can be explained by both proximity to potential customers as well as the technology driven talent coming out of the technical university (TUM). Standing out is the region's relative strength in IoT (e.g. Tado, Konux), as well as hardware driven high-tech startups such as Lilium (electric jet), Bragi (wireless earphones), Franka Emika (robotics) or Magazino (robotics). **Local vs. International funding:** International VC money is more focused on Berlin, and represent nearly 40% of venture capital invested. US-based VCs account for the largest chunk(12%). The share is slightly lower in Munich (< 30% international) and Hamburg (<25% int.). ![Source: DSM 2016](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4eCXHXbFyeGHqAB62dp04m/5dd9ecd2db6d36f2113673b5980c05c9/image_291.jpg) **Concluding** Have a look beyond Berlin. Germany's other ecosystems are growing and should be followed closely. Where to go? That is a case by ca

articles.title: Should you build machine learning in-house?
articles.excerpt: Probably not
articles.text: About two weeks ago, Box announced that they are [launching a new set of machine learning services](https://techcrunch.com/2017/10/11/box-skills-applies-ai-and-machine-learning-to-growing-content-store/). The customers of the enterprise cloud storage and collaboration giant are now able to search inside the content of photos ([announced in August](https://techcrunch.com/2017/08/26/ai-will-fundamentally-change-how-we-manage-content/)), audio and video using image and speech recognition. The fact that Box launches these products is no surprise, and goes very much along the thesis that I (along with everyone else) have that machine learning will become a component of every product and service in the world. The big surprise, at least to me, was that instead of building this themselves, Box has decided to completely outsource the machine learning to Google Vision API, Microsoft Azure Cognitive Services and IBM Watson. This is new! ### The theory Standard business logic tells us that you should build in-house things that fit these two conditions: - You can do this better than anyone else - It makes a big difference for your customers ![Until 10 years ago, launching a startup meant buying and operating your own servers](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3ofgaYToh9PSBbBXQRdGaI/4b2c0a038f7bd2dadcbeff6805a8e0a6/image_285.jpg) This is why companies usually outsource electricity production, email clients, cleaning, and server hosting and management. There is simply no way that a company can build a better email client in-house than Microsoft or Google. Even if companies could probably get a higher quality of cleaning by doing it themselves, it just doesn't matter very much for their business. Conversely, for a tech company at least, outsourcing engineering, product, marketing or sales is generally bad, since these are the very things that make or break your business. ### What the Box announcement means Until the Box announcement, I was of the belief that if machine learning was in any way important to your business, it should be done in-house. Not that companies should invent their own algorithms - not at all. Your algorithms aren't your competitive edge. [But your data is](https://blog.creandum.com/the-value-isnt-your-algorithm-it-s-your-data-dda4a1bf688b). Having a unique data set that automatically gets expanded as you onboard new customers and they use your product is one of the most defendable moats you can have. Now, Google and Microsoft are unlikely to care about your little business, no matter what you do. They probably don't even care about Box's $500m annual revenue. But they would very much like to be the platform on which others build products on. And by using their API, Box has effectively handed off all the learnings from their data to these cloud giants, who in turn, with no particular effort, can sell those learnings to Box competitors. The downside, in other words, is clear and significant. So why did this well run company make that decision? Looking at the criteria above: clearly machine learning will make a big difference for Box's customers. So the reason must simply be that Box's management came to the conclusion that there was no way whereby they could build better image or speech recognition technology than Google or Microsoft. By outsourcing it, they may not be able to make machine learning a competitive edge, but at least they will know that they will always be at least on par with competitors. Instead, Box will focus on understanding their enterprise customers and their business problems better than anyone else. ### What this means for your business Well, think about it: If box, a publicly listed, $500m San Francisco based tech company reaches the conclusion that they will never be able to build as good machine learning solutions as Google, what does that imply about your business? That's right: you probably shouldn't do it. Actually, let's moderate that a little bit. If: • Your data is **truly** unique • The insights you generate with that data is **the** reason people buy your product • Half your team are top notch machine learning PhDs Then you should build your own machine learning stack. If not then you would be better off outsourcing it. Similar to how you already outsource your servers to AWS, your payments to Stripe and your search functionality to Algolia. The takeaway from this is that in most cases you should absolutely look into whether your product could be augmented with machine learning. And the beauty is that you don't even need to understand it properly to use it, just like you don't need to understand payments infrastructure to use Stripe. From strong abstraction solutions like [Clarifai](https://www.clarifai.com/) and [Google Vision API](https://cloud.google.com/vision/) that you just send images and get structured data back, to more low level offerings like [Azure Machine Learning Studio](https://studio.azureml.net/), that lets you run algorithms on various data types, these are pretty high quality tools that not enough people use. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?type=text%2Fhtml&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&schema=twitter&url=https%3A//twitter.com/creandum/status/923540772334563328&image=https%3A//i.embed.ly/1/image%3Furl%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fpbs.twimg.com%252Fmedia%252FDNETZaOXUAEpRGB.jpg%253Alarge%26key%3Da19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07" title="" height="185" width="500"></iframe> _[Creandum](http://creandum.com) is a venture capital fund powering innovation from Stockholm, San Francisco, and Berlin. We believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. [Creandum backs the companies of tomorrow](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/)._

articles.title: Accelerating the Swedish Music Tech Industry: Creandum welcomes EQT as Partners in Epidemic Sound
articles.author: Staffan Helgesson
articles.text: Simply put, the music tech coming out of Stockholm is phenomenal. Just taking a look at Creandum's existing early-stage investments, [Spotify](http://spotify.com) is the undisputed giant where music hits technology. [Soundtrack your Brand](https://www.soundtrackyourbrand.com/) has totally changed how stores, restaurants, and brands think about music. And today, we're pleased to announce that Creandum's third portfolio company in the music tech space, [Epidemic Sound](http://www.epidemicsound.com/), has announced massive backing to truly transform how organizations soundtrack their stories, and how people soundtrack their lives. Epidemic Sound is a new breed of music company. Epidemic Sound collaborates with musicians all over the world to produce quality music that soundtracks everything from TV and film productions to online videos on YouTube or Facebook. It also reaches directly to consumers, who can also listen to tracks on streaming platforms such as Spotify. We use Epidemic Sound ourselves whenever we cut our own videos, and we're always impressed with how much fun it is to use. Epidemic feels like a collaborative process, where clicking on each track boosts your creativity by helping you envision what the finished product will look, feel, and sound like. It's an amazing product that's testament to the hard work of CEO and co-founder Oscar Höglund and team. The Creandum Fund III initially lead the A-round in Epidemic some three years ago and has now joined forces with EQT Mid Market to accelerate the next big phase at Epidemic Sound. This is an interesting development - that one of Europe's largest Private Equity firms has now joined forces with the venture world to support the company's vision. We've worked with EQT in the past with [itslearning](https://www.itslearning.com/), Hercules with [Linas Matkasse](https://www.linasmatkasse.se/), Nordic Capital with [Cint](https://www.cint.com/), making this the fourth time that we've collaborated with the Private Equity industry during the last couple of years. As Oscar Höglund, CEO at Epidemic Sound, points out in the [press release](http://www.eqtpartners.com/news/Press-Releases/2017/eqt-mid-market-joins-forces-with-epidemic-sound/), "Over the past couple of years two things have happened. We have seen an explosion of online video and a huge increase in demand for quality soundtracks - both activity based music and more mainstream hit music." We look forward to continuing the work with the Epidemic team towards its objective of disrupting the global music industry.

articles.title: Esports — now bigger than the Olympics
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.text: Let's just get the news out of the way: a Counter-Strike tournament just got better TV ratings than the Olympics, the X Games, or the European Song Contest on Danish National TV channel DR3. Ever. The event was streamed live globally on 20 Twitch channels in 16 languages and it was broadcasted on 15 tv channels in 80 countries. A total of 180 million households could tune in to the Copenhagen event on their TV - this is something that has never been seen before, and today there is a bidding contest by major capitals from around the world to host one of the next four [BLAST Pro ](http://www.blastproseries.com/)events in 2018. That's a massive milestone for esports you can put a number on. What's harder to quantify is the atmosphere at the event. I arrived about a half an hour late to the completely full Royal Arena in Copenhagen, hosting 12.000 fans. Stepping inside the stadium was like being hit with a rush of adrenaline - fans were screaming and yelling at the three games running simultaneously, which filled the massive 500 square meter screen above the competitors. At least a third of the fans were decked out with gear from their favorite teams. Being in that stadium you knew the esports revolution is here, but let's look into why. ### First BLAST Pro When [Creandum Fund invested in RFRSH early 2017](https://blog.creandum.com/creandum-invests-in-rfrsh-6d5df134514e), the firm had been looking at the whole pipeline: esports formats, teams, data providers, streaming services, betting, and matchmaking services for some time. Some of us on the advisory team had an affiliation with the competitive gaming scene from when we used to be young, but we never found an investment hypothesis we felt comfortable with. But when [Nikolaj](https://www.linkedin.com/mynetwork/heathrow-redirect/?isSendInvite=true), [Jakob](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jakob-lund-kristensen-3534425a/de), and [Rene](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rene-rechtman-74665/de) pitched us, we saw a huge opportunity in an industry that we thought would inevitably see mass adoption. We believe that the founding team has the ideas and aspiration to bridge a format between the hardcore fans and the mass audience waiting out there. This was the [RFRSH](https://www.rfrsh.net/) team's first event, offering a new format for Counter-Strike:GO. Six of the global top 10 professional Counter-Strike teams played in front of 12,000 ecstatic fans. Compared to tournaments of the past, the games are shorter, where instead a tournament lasting days, the [BLAST Pro](http://www.blastproseries.com/) is shortened significantly. Players love the condensed action, new viewers understand the tournament more intuitively, and overall, the fans get a more compact and predictable experience. Even better, the [[BLAST Pro](http://www.blastproseries.com/)](http://www.blastproseries.com/) is built for media. The game was streamed online worldwide on Twitch, but the action works well on traditional channels. On Saturday, Danish national TV broadcasted live from the event for 6 hours(!). They had their own moderators and cameras moving around the stadium, and their work has clearly paid off. The published ratings show that in the target group of 15 to 39 year old, the first BLAST Pro event got them the best ratings in the history of the TV station, beating out formats we think of as classic ratings machines, like the Olympics and Eurovision. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/nPrOVqfk6SMNlaorKAxcx/fc9af0f58cc66ebd15dabbb41a1ba656/image_281.jpg) ### Big money flows into esports We're not the only ones that have gotten in on the action. In less than a year, we've seen a spike in esports investment like never before: [USD 25m in Dignitas](http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/20853042/cloud9-closes-25-million-investment), [USD 20m in LCS](https://www.sporttechie.com/golden-state-warriors-betting-millions-league-legends-team/) or [USD 33m+ in Optic Gaming](https://esportsobserver.com/report-optic-gaming-lands-investment-deal-aiming-for-owl-and-lcs/) are just some examples of what happened in the last 9 months in esports. Both professional investors ([Hersh Family](http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/20283637/team-envyus-receive-35-million-investment-hersh-family-investments-sources-say), [Disney](https://slingshotesports.com/2017/07/12/disney-invests-team-liquid-axiomatic-accelerator-program/)) and traditional [sports teams](https://www.dexerto.com/news/full-list-of-professional-sports-teams-in-esports/19056) (e.g. [New York Yankees](http://fortune.com/2017/10/19/the-new-york-yankees-are-investing-in-competitive-video-gaming-with-vision-esports/), [Manchester City](http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-36734518), [Boston Celtics](https://www.cnbc.com/video/2016/10/14/boston-celtics-jerebko-on-buying-esports-teams.html), [Golden State Warriors](https://www.sporttechie.com/golden-state-warriors-betting-millions-league-legends-team/)) are making big plays. The [NBA is launching its own esports league](http://www.businessinsider.de/nba-launching-esports-league-2017-2?r=US&IR=T). Juniper estimates [esports revenues to go up to USD 3.5 billion by 2021](https://www.juniperresearch.com/press/press-releases/esports-%E2%80%98let%E2%80%99s-play%E2%80%99-revenues-to-reach-%243-5-bill). Thats billion with a b. Despite the good momentum, it's not proven which model works. What is clear however is that the industry is attracting investments like never before and this will inevitably lead to a further professionalisation of this industry. And as the industry and format becomes more professionalized, we're seeing more and more non-endemic brands joining the club. The numbers from clothing retailer Jack and Jones for example, presented on Saturday behind the scenes, speak for themselves. In Copenhagen, when the new jersey worn by [Astralis](http://astralis.gg/) (one of the teams participating) was announced at a fan event hosted by [RFRSH Entertainment](https://www.rfrsh.net/), a sing

articles.title: Billie — Solving the SME financing gap through technology
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.text: Many SMEs struggle to finance their working capital thanks to harsh payment terms of their bigger customers, or from low payment moral of their smaller ones. Getting paid for your hard work can sometimes take up to 120 days, which is a hardship when everyone needs to pay their employees, rent, and electricity on time. This is a huge issue for so many of the SMEs we speak to. [Billie](http://www.billie.io) is solving this. Most companies try to fight this financing gap through a couple of strategies. One option is using credit facilities with the company's partner bank, which is typically tough to get - or tough to get the amount needed to truly cover the gap. The other option is by factoring contracts with the offline incumbents. In practice, this means inviting a cavalry of suit wearing accountants to ride into your company, who for some months tries to understand ERP systems, accounting processes, and other business matters. Only then you are allowed to join the exclusive cohort of factoring customers. This traditional style of factoring is costly to set up, and hence only makes sense for businesses above a certain turnover. The biggest German factoring company credits €50 billion to only 600 customers per year. Offline processes are slow, inflexible, and expensive. Billie is changing all of the above through technology. **Today we are excited to announce that Creandum Fund III leads the 10m€ Series A financing of Billie.** ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/D5rDY94bAy4M7hy1y3cQl/a0475114faecaf5e5a7d0e20d6de3def/image_280.png) ## "Understanding your customers" as a differentiator What makes Billies product so attractive to its customers comes down to the: 1. Speed of application approval (the process takes 7 minutes to complete) 2. Fair and transparent pricing 3. The flexibility of single invoice factoring 4. The fact that debtors don't know an invoice has been factored - relationships stay untouched Other than with the offline incumbents, Billies customers can choose which of their invoices they want to factorize and which not. Historically, companies needed to pay the agreed fee on all outgoing invoices, and not only on those that matter to them. This flexibility has received great feedback so far. ## Serving SMEs through technology Behind the scenes, Billie is based on a complex array of scoring algorithms developed on hundreds of millions of bank transactions. Adding to this, is extensive experience in regular SME scoring technology, plus a strong base of industry leading partnerships. At the same time, Billie also solves the problem of highly manual KYC checks all traditional financial institutes suffer from. Through a multitude of interconnected databases Billie for example automated tedious "anti money laundering"-checks required by financial regulators. Underwriters are necessary in all credit businesses, but using data to understand your customers and make better decisions for the next one is the classical network effect game we VCs love. Billie is riding this to its advantage par excellence. The founders [Matthias](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthiasknecht/) and [Christian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christian-grobe-91b72584/) have received a BaFin licence (the German financial market regulator) in record time, and have been serving SMEs since June 2017. It is the combination of automated scoring of creditors and debtors that allows SMEs to hand in financing and have money on the bank account within 24 hours after registration. ## Third company, same team In its core, the seven founders of Billie have thought deeply about SME scoring, fraud detection, and credit payments for the last four years. When [Matthias Knecht](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthiasknecht/) and [Christian Grobe](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christian-grobe-91b72584/) left McKinsey in 2013 - where they worked together for five years - they started Zencap, a SME credit platform. They later sold their first startup to Funding Circle. Many of the people that they had hired during that time stayed on after the exit to Funding Circle, and when [Matthias](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthiasknecht/) and [Christian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christian-grobe-91b72584/) decided to start their next company, they quit their jobs at a well funded FinTech to start Billie together. With [Aiga Senftleben](https://www.linkedin.com/in/aiga-senftleben-38762459/), [Julian Koster](https://www.linkedin.com/in/julian-max-koster-905910a4), [Artem Demchenkov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/artem-demchenkov-76b69934/), [Igor Chtivelband](https://www.linkedin.com/in/igorchtivelband/), and [Michael Hartmann](https://www.linkedin.com/in/michael-hartmann-182863a6/) they form the key team of Billie. We love these stories, and it shows the belief in the leadership of [Matthias](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthiasknecht/) and [Christian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christian-grobe-91b72584/). The fact that [Jörg Asmussen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B6rg_Asmussen) (who held various top level positions such as Member of the executive board of the European Central Bank and Deputy Finance Minister of Germany) as well as [Joachim Secker](https://www.linkedin.com/in/joachim-secker-ba49b35/), CEO Targo Commercial Finance (Germany's largest factoring provider) and Chairman of the German Factoring Association, join the company as advisors, shows the respect the two have gained outside their company as well. **We are thrilled to join this group of industry experts.** ## Our Hypothesis The power gap between SMEs and their large corporate debtors is the reason why SMEs have unfavourable payment terms. CFOs of listed companies are not incentivised to decrease de facto cheap credit lines by paying invoices earlier - the opposite is true and will stay true for the foreseeable future.
