articles.title: SME Tech
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.excerpt: Creandum’s view on this broad industry vertical
articles.text: In its fourth fund, Creandum has invested in six companies that exclusively focus on SMEs (Small and Mid-Sized Enterprises) as their customer base, making it nearly 50% of the current fund up to date. In hindsight, we could call this a thesis, but it wasn't on the day the fund closed. However, with Creandum backing [iZettle](https://www.izettle.com/), [Planday](https://www.planday.com) and [Tictail](https://tictail.com) in its last funds, these investments didn't come together by chance. Here are our thoughts on the SME trend - and what we learned over the last months. We call this SME Tech. ### Technology at an inflection point When analysing the SME market and its opportunities, it became clear that we are at an inflection point where technology - often OCR / ML / NLP based -now enables the cost effective processing and operation of products, specifically geared towards SMEs. APIs allow integration of necessary data pools further increasing automation of processing customers. Where one once needed manual, offline, cost intensive, and time consuming on-boarding processes, technology can now take over a majority of this work when dealing with SMEs. Fully automated KYC / AML, risk scoring, account integration and payment connection through APIs, allow new ventures to be built on proven business models, for a so far unserved customer group. **Reflecting on the current Creandum IV portfolio, this is the case for all of our six SME portfolio companies:** **[Comtravo](http://www.comtravo.com)** - Business Travel Booking for SMEs **[Pleo](http://www.pleo.io)** - Expense management for SMEs **[Bokio](http://www.bokio.se)** - SME Accounting **[Tide](http://www.tide.co)** - SME Banking **[Syft](http://www.syftapp.com)** - SME Staffing **[Billie](http://www.billie.io)** - SME Factoring All of these companies have something in common: their fundamental business model is proven, and long established. Often times, massive companies have been built targeting multinationals or at least bigger corporates exclusively - in all of these spaces. When we looked into competitive landscape of all of these industries, we found multi-billion dollar companies in each of the respective spaces, yet often with fewer than 1,000 customers. That would not be possible in the SME space. It was clear that their business processes, on-boarding approach, customer acquisition methods and their product itself does not fit SMEs. ### The market is bigger than you think A phrase you hear religiously repeated by politicians yet often forgotten by investors is that SMEs are the backbone of our economy. **In detail:** To prove my point, look at the travel market. In the US and the EU, four companies dominate the landscape. Each one is doing over $20b USD in GMV. But they're focused heavily on the corporate space. That is despite the fact, that the SME business travel market is 2x the size of the corporate market (USD 870b vs USD 430b) and yet there are no real winners building solutions for SMEs. **To generalise**: In Europe, there are 24m registered businesses. 45.000 (or 0.2%) fall under the large cap category, while the other **99.8%** are SMEs. Yeah, that's the larger fraction. And yes, they have a strong purchasing power as well. Yet most big companies so far have been built in the corporate market. For many industries, you will find subsegments in the SME space that are not served by a champion yet. Our hypothesis is that one can build multiple winners in each subsegment serving SMEs alone. Here's to those entrepreneurs that are onto that. Reflecting on the investments, and from speaking to those entrepreneurs in the space that we did not back, here are the most important things we learned: ### 1. Go to market differs In a good way, SMEs don't require _feature-complete_ before a purchasing department signs a letter of intent. SMEs are more flexible and willing to accept the imperfect, which helps startups go-to-market earlier. On top of that, SMEs themselves are often run by entrepreneurs which in return become both product ambassadors and a great feedback channel. In fact, many of the product improvements for some of our companies come from direct founder to founder interaction. And when things go wrong, SME customers can be much more understanding and forgiving. Furthermore, many SME Techs offer freemium models. These are catered towards the more internet savvy customer base, which then allow for an easier sales process, resulting in shorter sales cycles. Self-onboarding only adds to that. ### 2. Products differ Ultimately, many incumbent products could potentially serve SMEs, but their richness in features can be overkill for smaller customers. Pricing rules are prohibitive for venturing into smaller target segments. And timing requirements for on-boarding, customer service or other vital elements rule out SMEs as a target group from the get go. Furthermore, SME targeted products often follow the less-is-more approach keeping adoption speed up, yet requiring some adaption by the customers. It is clear, that many incumbents struggle to move downstream within their target segment. That allows startups targeting SMEs to operate in a world where they compete against new companies, but are rarely afraid of the established upstream players. The consumerization of the enterprise product has a great impact on SME product landscape, and what these products look like. UX and UI matters. And we are excited about that. The learnings entrepreneurs can draw from their consumer focussed peers are visible in so many of the startups we currently see int he space. ### 3. Customer acquisition differs Customer acquisition for SMEs is tough. Them's the break! And its is far less predictable than enterprise sales. All our SME Tech founders are obsessed with customer acquisition optimisation, and data plays a huge role in most processes. A big part of the success of SME Tech startups lays in mastering the multi channel sales approach of their re

articles.title: Virta Health reverses diabetes with 60% of patients
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.text: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/2vMcHsOCrHXaWL0v59leI5/4a5aa7164f5dac5baeea60efa54f52c5/image_277.jpg) One year into the largest [Virta Health](http://virtahealth.com) [Diabetes Reversal study](https://blog.virtahealth.com/with-sustained-type-2-diabetes-reversal-management-is-becoming-a-thing-of-the-past/) to date, we're pleased to help the company announce phenomenal results in their patient groups. But first, a little background. For those of you who didn't read [our funding announcement last year](https://blog.creandum.com/virta-health-reversing-diabetes-7a8be0c070c), Virta Health is an online clinic offering the first clinically-proven treatment to safely and sustainably reverse type 2 diabetes - and other chronic metabolic diseases - without the risks, costs, or side effects of medication or surgery. It's personalized care from an online clinic in your pocket. Behind Virta health is CEO Sami Inkinen, a Finnish entrepreneur known for co-founding Trulia (IPO in 2012), and a team of top medical professionals who are putting years of research into practice. ### Today Virta is announcing at year 1: - 60% of patients in their clinical trial achieved diabetes reversal. - 94% of insulin users reduced or eliminated usage altogether. - 83% of patients remained active in treatment after one year. This is nothing short of phenomenal. In addition to reversing diabetes for most of the patients, Virta has helped improve their lives by improving blood pressure, inflammation, cardiovascular markers and weight loss - which all leave a massive impact in Virta's patients' lives. Virta has also been busy picking up new enterprise customers (three in the last 60 days alone), such as Nielsen in the last quarter of 2017. Thanks to the quirks of the US healthcare system that puts employers much more on the hook for healthcare costs than e.g. in Europe, Virta is able to save $10k per patient over the first two years - while helping ensure healthy and happy employees at these large firms. Diabetes is a huge issue facing western societies today. With 30 million people in the US with type 2 diabetes and 84 million currently in prediabetes, there's a lot more work to be done. This is one big reason why Creandum couldn't be prouder to be backing Virta Health on their journey. ### Looking at the bigger picture We see chronic diseases as an area where entrepreneurs can make massive changes in customers' lives, and improve efficiency all while reducing healthcare costs. Virta is a great example of what can be achieved in this space. And their position in the value chain is a great representation of what Creandum is looking for in digital health. They've purpose-built a treatment around a custom digital interface, of course learning from each interaction, between patients and a very human health care team. The patient gets a true long-term companion for their customers that will help them get through their hardest times with their chronic disease, or - in the case of Virta help them cure diabetes completely. The one number that characterises this better than any other is the stunning 83% retention of patients after one year. This beats most if not all other digital therapies out there and one we're incredibly proud to be a small part of. PS: If you're working with digitally enhanced treatment of chronic diseases or otherwise have built digital therapies, do reach out. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?type=text%2Fhtml&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&schema=twitter&url=https%3A//twitter.com/_fredrik/status/961343933933596675&image=https%3A//i.embed.ly/1/image%3Furl%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fpbs.twimg.com%252Fprofile_images%252F829966445232676864%252FHDpUSuBI_400x400.jpg%26key%3Da19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07" title="" height="185" width="500"></iframe>

articles.title: Why tech should focus more on Chronic Diseases
articles.text: Since joining Creandum I have spent a lot of time within Digital Health, both with Creandum's portfolio companies, but also looking out for new interesting companies. And by doing so I'm more and more convinced about the opportunities related to tackling chronic diseases, also known as non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Even more so, I'm convinced of the NEED of tackling NCDs - millions of people and their families are impacted and the number is expected to increase. Prevention plays a large role in this, but helping those already affected is also vital. Creandum's Fund's investment in [Virta Health](https://www.virtahealth.com/) is one example within this area - they just announced results of a clinical trial where they've been able to _reverse_ type 2 diabetes in 60% of their patients. But there are likely many more opportunities out there to tackle conditions such as asthma, osteoarthritis, heart conditions, or autoimmune diseases. So, what makes me so convinced? ### 1) The prevalence is huge - and unfortunately growing. Managing chronic diseases is one the main challenges for our society today, and not least for the affected individuals and families. NCDs are by far the most common cause of death worldwide, being the cause for [more than 6 of 10 deaths](http://www.who.int/features/factfiles/noncommunicable_diseases/en/). In the US [almost half of all adults](https://www.cdc.gov/chronicdisease/overview/index.htm#ref17), roughly 120m people, suffer from one or more NCDs. As the population grow older and risk factors such as poor diet and lack of exercise become more common, this number is expected to increase. ### 2) Double cost to society: driving healthcare expenditures and economic loss. As one would expect, long term conditions lead to higher costs. Across the world, an average [10% of GDP](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.XPD.TOTL.ZS) is spent on healthcare, and in most countries the vast majority is due to chronic diseases. American healthcare expenditures equal an [astonishing 17% of GDP](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.XPD.TOTL.ZS?locations=US), of which [+80% is related to NCDs](https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/professionals/prevention-chronic-care/decision/mcc/mccchartbook.pdf), meaning that over 13% of GDP or over 2 TRILLION are spent yearly on NCDs (as a reference [education exp. is ~5% of GDP](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SE.XPD.TOTL.GD.ZS?locations=US)). While being the major driver of healthcare costs, many people don't receive sufficient treatment, especially in developing countries. But the direct expenditure is not the only cost. Only within Europe, roughly 555,000 people die at premature age from chronic disease. The economic loss of these premature deaths is [estimated at around €115bn](https://ec.europa.eu/health/state/glance_en). ### 3) Most importantly - Opportunity to improve outcomes - not only generate cost savings. Treatment today is based on time intervals, or other static intervals - not on personalized individual care. This means that a lot of recourse and visits are put in too early (simply scheduled as a check-up that could be avoided or done using other means than physical visit) OR too late, e.g. as a response to complication. As an example over 30% of patients who undergo chemotherapy [end up at the ER within four weeks](http://www.csqi.on.ca/by_patient_journey/treatment/unplanned_hospital_visits_during_chemotherapy/). In fact, people with chronic conditions are three times more likely to have an unnecessary hospitalization. And those with five or more chronic conditions are [99 times more likely](http://www.oecd.org/health/health-systems/48245231.pdf) to have an unnecessary hospitalization. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5zyEWDT1LWoX4tyiubganV/f512b3b587cc6736e34c8d878e63cce9/image_276.jpg) There is a solution. Leveraging tech to enable e.g. symptom tracking can identify the need for visit or change in treatment before patient needs to go to the ER. Even if there isn't an acute situation to be avoided, self-tracking, remote monitoring, or other continuous intervals lead to better outcomes as it provides both patient and doctor with a better understanding of the condition and a fact based decision support. Additionally, the impact of putting the patient in a situation where they have more transparency and control should not be underestimated. In short, tech (in form of e.g. continuous and remote monitoring, communication between visits, adherence reminders and follow-ups, AI for predicting complications, and a bunch of other stuff people smarter than I will figure out) will not only generate cost savings but also significantly improve the quality. Better quality means people can live longer and healthier lives - that's what makes this area truly interesting! (here's some more on that topic: [https://blog.virtahealth.com/continuous-remote-telemedicine/](https://blog.virtahealth.com/continuous-remote-telemedicine/)) ### 4) UX designed for a long-term relationship. As the name implies, chronic conditions do not vanish and there is a need for people to manage and live with their disease. An interface where the consumer is in charge and benefit continously from a tech-enabled treatment can help form a long lasting, and valuable relationship. While there is of course a lot things to be improved on the medical professional side, I see the major improvements and disruptions coming from innovations which involve the patient - and potentially also the people around them. Tech can help by increasing motivation and understanding of why the patient needs to take certain actions. As an example, medication is not the only way to control asthma. It is also important to avoid triggers, such as cold air, pollution or other things that irritate and inflame the airways. Each patient must learn what triggers to avoid and how to identify them. As external conditions vary over time, these must be monitored and actions or medica

articles.title: The beginner’s guide to the not-so-French tech ecosystem
articles.text: France has become increasingly interesting as a VC, so I recently set out for 36 hours in Paris, giving myself a crash course in the French tech ecosystem. This leaves me nowhere close to being an expert, but luckily this isn't our team's first foray into France; [Carl Fritjofsson](https://medium.com/@fritjofsson) has led our work there and Creandum's Funds first investment, [Clustree](https://www.clustree.com/), was made roughly a year ago. In this guide, I'd thought I'd share the basics for those who, just like me, are curious on what the French tech scene has to offer. ### It's on fire! First of all, the number one thing this trip showed is that there is a lot of momentum and the french tech scene is growing. **A lot**. Every single person I spoke to was mentioned this as one of the main characteristics of the French ecosystem. A quick look into [CB Insight](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/report/french-tech-q4-2017/) confirms this; funding reached nearly $3.2 bn in 2017 and grew 49% vs. 2016. Meanwhile the number of deals grew by 45%. And that says a lot considering 2016 was already a [strong year for the French tech scene](https://www.economist.com/news/business/21717411-capital-now-leads-europe-number-venture-capital-funding-rounds-rise). ### Skills are there Talent is available and not (yet) as costly as elsewhere. There are a number of highly regarded- and state funded - universities and technical educations producing good engineers who are in turn are fuelling the development within AI and data science. This is not only fuelling the local companies but also attracting foreign ones, for example, Google is expanding their [AI research center in Paris](https://techcrunch.com/2018/01/22/google-is-launching-an-ai-research-center-in-france-and-expanding-its-office/) and Facebook has gotten closer to the talent pool. ### Success cases has contributed to shift in mindset - and is enabling a new generation The success of companies such as [BlaBla Car](https://www.blablacar.com/), [Criteo](https://www.criteo.com/) and [Vente Privee](https://secure.uk.vente-privee.com/registration/AboutUs?CountryCode=EN) has contributed to the the development; more companies are founded by alumni of the big names. There is also shift in mindset; earlier high performing students went into consulting, banking or large corporates - now both the appetite and acceptance for pursuing entrepreneurship is a lot greater. When speaking to the people I met, I noticed it was hard to talk about French tech without mentioning [Xavier Neil](https://twitter.com/xavier75?lang=en), who among many other things changed the game for French telecom by the launch of low cost operator Free, and have come to play a large role in creating infrastructure to support a new generation of entrepreneurs. In 2013 he founded [42](http://www.42.fr/), a non-profit computer programming school in Paris, he has invested in over 600 start-ups via [Kima Ventures](https://www.kimaventures.com/) and the latest flagship of the French tech scene, [Station F](https://stationf.co/). ![Station F: _Did I mention that the interior is pretty freaking awesome as well?_](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6qtlzNSUyMXb2Ylk3aiLrc/65d0b4c1b5813f0eaf978b3219e0940d/image_275.jpg) Station F is one the largest start-up campuses in the world. The old station that opened in June 2017, hosts people and organizations for all the parts needed in an eco-system: start-ups, incubators, service providers like Facebook and Amazon, as well as investors. Access to start-ups is given via different programs, one which I personally liked the most is what is called ["Fighters"](https://stationf.co/apply/fighters/) where people with the right mindset but who do not have the financials means are accepted into a 1 one year program free of charge, with the guiding thought that diverse backgrounds drives innovation. During this year the plan is also to provide housing adjacent to the campus. ### International interest is growing An increasing number of international VCs - Creandum and myself included - are turning their eyes to France. Having people on the ground or full focus on covering France was unlikely a couple of years ago due to a lack of interesting deals, but now a majority of large European VC funds have presence in some form - [here's](https://blog.serenacapital.com/the-ultimate-vc-list-updated-e5166156f515) a pretty impressive list compiled by Serena Capital covering VCs active in the region. ### And the president finds it pretty important too At his first speech after being elected president Macron stated ["I want this country to become a country of unicorns"](https://www.ft.com/content/61c5f20a-81a8-11e7-a4ce-15b2513cb3ff) at the [Vivatech](https://vivatechnology.com/) festival in June 2017. The government has also made it easier for foreign tech talent move to France via the [French Tech VISA](https://visa.lafrenchtech.com/), enabling further internationalisation and likely competitiveness of the french tech scene. As in my native Sweden, there has been a lot of discussion related to taxation and incentives but the impression I got was that also the political agenda strongly supports a continued growth of the French Ecosystem. ### Ok, there's still a distinct French view of the world. In my research before the trip, and during my 36 hours in Paris, I noticed many startups seemed to be building products with a distinct "France first" attitude compared to the "global from day one" attitude I've gotten so used to in the Nordics. While France is a fairly large market - and maybe even an underserved market linguistically - I still have a gut feeling that the most successful French startups will be the ones thinking about offices in Shanghai, not offices in Nice. But this French view of the world plays out in cool ways too! One thing I found most interesting is that a few French VCs had their eyes on French-speaking Africa. Partec just launched an Africa focused fund and

articles.title: Inside the dusty brains of the first backer of Spotify
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.excerpt: Looking at how we were right and wrong…
articles.text: At the Stockholm Arlanda airport, getting ready to fly to New York for Spotify's [Capital Markets Day](https://investors.spotify.com/home/default.aspx), I dug through the deepest corners of Dropbox to look for an old slide. On Thursday Spotify will present their fundamentals and vision to investors, and it's hard not to be reminded how eleven years ago we gave the same thing a shot on that slide, before the fund led Spotify's first institutional round of funding. So rather than hosting an event in NYC, we added Spotify to our humble "Hot List", the early stage of our screening process where we pitch the company to the rest of the team. Our Hot List is typically a short list of companies that merit special attention, and to inform the group we put too many words on one slide (a practice that continues to today). Looking back at this slide really is a time capsule from 2007 of what we thought about Spotify, technology, and the music industry. Some of our views were right and some were wrong, but luckily a few ideas were wrong for the right reasons. We attached the slide above with numbers redacted, because things may have changed before the actual deal was on the table and we would hate to confuse the record. But we left all our factual errors for the world to see. ## What we were right about: ### "Better than piracy" was key I remember in 2007 all the headlines about music were about the death of the industry. How piracy was killing its revenue and how there was no way back. I personally felt part of that demise- as someone who considered themselves active music consumer I found myself going where the _almost-instant_ and _almost-endless_ supply of music was: Limewire, uTorrent – you know most of them. ![Classic branding.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/72T8xG762zz1TpgMHw2rUT/741952195bd3fc15c2bbadfac17a1191/image_271.png) So one thing we really bought into was one of Spotify's fundamental beliefs at the time: in order to win against piracy, you need to provide a service that was ... "Better than Piracy". That meant truly instant access to every song you could think of... and preferably free to use. We really wanted to believe that by doing so, Spotify would open up a massive audience. And that that audience would be valuable. But there was a lot more behind that phrase. In order to succeed, Spotify's small team had to deliver the world's music catalogue instantly and reliably. If there was even a couple of seconds delay after clicking on a song, it wouldn't feel like you had access to the world's music! I remember the team obsessing about this and not compromising. "Better than piracy" was where the bar was. At the onset Spotify relied on P2P technology which was proprietary and which they had tuned to work in a brilliant way. This structure kept costs down but, most importantly, provided a hands-down better experience than any other legal (or illegal) music solution. ### Playing fair with rights holders was key At the time of this Hot List slide, Spotify was still negotiating with rights holders on how to license its music at scale. As you can see, after the first few meetings with the team, we were a bit hesitant to have Creandum back them before understanding how the rights situation would play out. According to the slide there was even consideration about splitting the deal up (which I had forgotten - this otherwise stupid idea must have been scrapped shortly thereafter). This rights holder topic, and the discussions that followed over the many months until Creandum backed them taught us about the strengths of the founders. They were playing hardball to increasingly keen investors, while at the same time being sufficiently patient to get truly viable deals with rights holders. Allowing for a free, truly interactive part of the service was key – otherwise the ‘better than piracy' promise would just not hold. They knew what they wanted, and they went out and got it. Looking at the bigger picture, we felt very comfortable with the founders' approach to always play fair with rights holders with no grey zones. Our late-night discussions about Spotify and rights would ultimately build the mental model that led Creandum to pursue companies like Epidemic Sound and Soundtrack Your Brand, and not some of the other opportunities in the music space. ### Team was key One thing that shone through was that Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon were world-class entrepreneurs that had the skills, network, and passion to build something as massive as Spotify. We wrote about this on our [website profile](https://www.creandum.com/stories/spotify). ![Daniel and Martin, soon 10 years ago](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6IwHaybyLz2UdkZBAOmLAs/171830b559a0c891d508bfa16f762d3a/image_272.png) You would look at the quality of discussions and arguments that Daniel, Martin and other team members – senior and less senior, had and you would ask yourself, "are the other companies I'm looking at pushing themselves to that level?" Are there even ones in Europe with the same ambitions and high standards for themselves and their recruitments? At that time there really wasn't and I'm even hard pressed to point one out in the 11 years that have passed. And it's not like I haven't looked... We all know now how crucial recruitment is for any early-stage company, but was even more so for a consumer tech startup in Stockholm in 2007, where the tech entrepreneurship scene looked nothing like today. The team succeeded by building a world-class talent pool in Stockholm when the startup scene was only starting to take off in Europe. We can easily give Spotify thanks as to why Stockholm is now leading lists of European startup capitals. And of course on a personal note an even bigger thanks for helping to propel Creandum's brand to where it is today. ## What we were wrong about ### Mobile (we had no idea of how important it would become) ![The best way to play Zara Larsson in the old days](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4

articles.title: The most important decision you make as an entrepreneur is who you partner with
articles.text: ### Guest post by Careship Founder Antonia Albert _**Creandum note:** Today we're excited to announce that Creandum has invested in [Careship](http://careship.de), a Berlin-based company which is solving how we care for our elderly so they can age at home, one of societies largest challenges. Careship offers a platform that can deliver a significantly better care experience for families - not settling with just finding a caregiver, but providing transparency and contact with their loved ones' home life through the lens of the caregiver._ _Typically we write our own retrospective about what stands out about each company, but we also know that the best founders can choose their own investors. So, we decided to instead give the microphone to Careship founder Antonia Albert, who provided us with the blog below. For more information on the funding round, read the coverage in [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2018/04/05/careship/) or [Handelsblatt](http://www.handelsblatt.com/my/unternehmen/it-medien/careship-deutsches-pflege-start-up-streicht-millionen-ein-/21138412.html?ticket=ST-585848-MLxtpCqwCi4ud6dksFse-ap3) here._ From a young age our grandmother has always told us: "Choose someone who cares". This advice still guides us to this day, so much so that our family even has specific word for it: _Kümmerer_. As an entrepreneur, starting your own company is similar to embarking on an epic journey: you set sail and leave safe harbour, and your vision guides you like the North Star. However, it's not enough to simply have a clear vision. In order to successfully reach your destination, you need a strong crew to accompany you along the way and help you navigate the rocky shores of entrepreneurship. Who you decide to take onboard will define whether you succeed, and for us it is critical to choose people who care. With **Careship, we are not creating a new market, but we are solving one of Europe's largest and most relevant social problems**. In order to make a real difference, we need the most committed crew onboard. Our crew consists of our teammates, our investors and our mentors. We have always been very careful with choosing who we partner with and whose advice we take. At Careship we use three guiding principle to select our crew: **a shared vision**, **shared values** and boatloads of **passion**. 1. **Shared Vision**, to us, means that everyone understands the underlying purpose of why we are doing what we're doing, and why we set sail in the first place. Everyone onboard needs to identify with our vision, and stand behind it 100%. Having this shared vision gives purpose, purpose creates commitment, and we need people who fully commit to making social difference. 2. Secondly, it is essential that we share the **same set of values**. At Careship we carefully nourish our culture because we believe that a shared value system is the foundation for long-term success. Roy Disney said: ‘When you're values are clear, making decisions becomes easier' - and there is a lot of truth in that. 3. Finally, we want to be surrounded by **passionate people**. The average life expectancy in Germany is 81 years. This is 29.565 days, and every day is precious. We strive to make every day inspiring, fulfilling and exciting, because we believe life is too short for meaningless work. By creating a passionate environment where people feel motivated, our crew can bring their best ideas and learn something new every day. Our crew also consists of our investors. Investors, to us, are long-term partners, that not only provide a source of funding, but also stand behind our vision, share our values and passionately jump onboard to join us on our ambitious journey. When investors choose who to invest in, they have an investment codex as well as a framework to help evaluate an investment decision. Creandum applies a so-called ‘hot list' for startups, as seen [in the example of Spotify](https://blog.creandum.com/inside-the-dusty-brains-of-an-early-spotify-investor-looking-at-how-we-were-right-and-wrong-7938abcd36e1). At Careship, we also have a codex when we choose a potential investor. We call this our ‘Careship Caring Codex', and we apply the following checklist to evaluate a potential investor: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/56xfCqOTUan0nKyxMIR1E2/a800943826fcc645837342ca361d7492/image_270.png) Looking back, we can say that our checklist has served us well so far. **We consider ourselves very fortunate that we have always been able to choose our partners**. We are very lucky to be working with a truly amazing crew including [Spark Capital](http://sparkcapital.com/), [Atlantic Labs](http://www.atlanticlabs.de/), [Ananda Ventures](http://www.anandaventures.com/en/), and [Johannes Reck](https://www.crunchbase.com/person/johannes-reck) from GetYourGuide, amongst others. Investors don't just invest in companies, they invest in people, they invest in us. They trust us to do our best possible job, we trust them to support us along our journey in the best possible way, and our team trusts us to choose the best ones. When we set sail with Careship, we aimed to work together with the best crew. We are very grateful that Creandum jumped onboard and is part of our crew now. Our grandmother would approve, and we are looking forward to a great journey together. _**Creandum note:** Thanks Antonia for this guest post! For Careship coverage, you can find articles in [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2018/04/05/careship/) and [Handelsblatt](http://www.handelsblatt.com/my/unternehmen/it-medien/careship-deutsches-pflege-start-up-streicht-millionen-ein-/21138412.html?ticket=ST-585848-MLxtpCqwCi4ud6dksFse-ap3). And now that you know Careship's core framework, they're [hiring great people in Berlin!](https://careship-jobs.personio.de/)_

articles.title: Spotify — Europe’s first real Aircraft Carrier
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.text: # Spotify - Europe's first real Aircraft Carrier Spotify just released their [first quarter report last week](https://investors.spotify.com/financials/press-release-details/2018/Spotify-Technology-SA-Announces-Financial-Results-for-First-Quarter-2018/default.aspx), showing performance at the high end of earlier guidance. We thought it was important to once again reflect on the huge importance of Spotify's contribution to the European tech scene. The Spotify direct listing is probably the most significant event in the European VC and Tech industry in the past 20 years, and for Sweden, perhaps in the last 100 years. It was the third largest Tech listing in the US, which has shown Europe can not only create BUSD "unicorns", but now a multi-billion publicly listed consumer brand that engages hundreds of millions of users daily. Spotify sits firmly beside Facebook, Instagram and Netflix on the front page of consumers' phones. It's a milestone for European tech. It's proof we can now truly compete with Silicon Valley. It's Europe's first "Aircraft Carrier." ### A boon to the ecosystem. Exits do more than create cash returns to founders and investors, they also drive the tempo of the startup scene. Historically European companies have sold out too early to US companies, but with Spotify remaining independent in Europe, you can expect a massive impact on the region. We've seen this already; over the years Spotify has acquired dozens of companies - like Tunigo and [Soundtrap](https://www.soundtrap.com/). And perhaps the most important one was the [early acquisition of The Echo Nest](https://techcrunch.com/2014/03/06/spotify-acquires-the-echo-nest/), a Massachusetts-based music intelligence platform whose technology has led to Spotify's smart playlists and enhanced discovery. European companies acquiring in America is more common today, but just four years ago it was unique that Spotify was acquiring American tech and talent, and not the other way around. Outside of acquisitions, Spotify's listing will boost entrepreneurship in many ways. Now that Spotify is public, many current and ex-employees can more easily cash in on options and shares. A significant part of this will come back as investments in new startups and teams. Many current employees will be able to think about trying their own wings outside Spotify, as we have seen over the years backing teams with roots within for instance Spotify. And others will become angel investors or even start their own VC Fund. Soon, the tech press will be talking about the "Spotify Mafia" just like the narrative PayPal and Skype. And Spotify, like [Klarna](http://klarna.com) and [iZettle](http://izettle.com), has become a huge magnet that is attracting international talent to work in Stockholm. At Klarna more than 60% of their employees come from 52 different countries. Spotify has similar numbers. This is of huge importance to create a flowerbed for new startups and innovation based in Sweden. ### A major impact on European VC fundraising It's only in the last 5 years that investors have been rewarded for investing in European VC when compared to US counterparts. The European VC ecosystem is much younger than the US, perhaps 25 years (vs 50 years in the US), and suffered from poor timing. Many of the early European VC funds were created in the late 90s and failed miserably with the dot com bust where over 50% of the funds disappeared. There were only a few pension funds and institutional investors who were brave enough to continue to invest in VC, and for Creandum these included the 6th AP fund and Skandia, who have been backers ever since Creandum was funded in 2003. This is including Fund III raised in 2012 when none of the Creandum funds had seen an exit (although Fund II did have some interesting companies like, for example, iZettle and Spotify). With Spotify now public these investors are well rewarded for taking this risk and supporting us and other VCs. The Creandum Fund II includes not only Spotify, but also [iZettle](http://izettle.com), [Linas Matkasse](http://linasmatkasse.com), [Cint](http://cint.com), [Videoplaza](http://videoplaza.com) and several others. It will probably be one of Europe's best performing funds ever. It will be a huge payback that hopefully will go back to the ecosystem, backing VC funds but more importantly contribute to the Swedish society through pensions and new start ups etc. The importance of a thriving stable entrepreneurial ecosystem for the benefit of our society cannot be shown in a better way. ![Photo by [U.S. Pacific Fleet](https://www.flickr.com/photos/compacflt/) on Flickr](https://miro.medium.com/0*wTCUgNdbX14fd3Xr.) ### The Aircraft Carrier So why is Spotify Europe's first real "aircraft carrier"? It's a [term we've used](https://blog.creandum.com/the-importance-of-aircraft-carriers-abf6c721c4b9) to describe tech giants that have a huge impact on the local startup scene. We call them Aircraft Carriers because these tech giants are indestructibly large platforms with strong moats and drive forward in the ecosystem. They attract talent, acquire companies and launch partnerships. It is also a platform for new innovation, new ideas and startups. We know for sure that Spotify will not be the only Swedish Aircraft Carrier - later this year iZettle may go public, and we would not be surprised if Klarna did as well. Which of the others in Creandum's portfolio will be the next one? _Johan Brenner is a General Partner at Creandum. We believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. Check out our [website](http://creandum.com) or follow [Creandum Family](http://medium.com/creandum-family) on Medium to learn more._

articles.title: What is needed to get from Seed to A round — learnings from Pleo
articles.text: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/2t3rxro9rzdvjyRyTTSjr5/ffd06773f4e6ec9c1eb081700166d694/image_265.jpg) We are incredibly excited to announce that [Pleo](http://pleo.io), a company that [Creandum](http://creandum.com) backed in February 2017, has now raised a $16m A round led by [Kinnevik](http://kinnevik.com), with participation by Creandum, [Founders](http://founders.as), [Seedcamp](http://seedcamp.com) and [Vækstfonden](http://vf.dk). All credit goes to the amazing Pleo team, led by CEO [Jeppe Rindom](https://twitter.com/jepperindom), for having executed so well. Pleo is a simple business spending solution. It combines a Pleo payment card (that can be easily assigned to employees with individually set limits) with software and mobile apps that automates expense reports and bookkeeping. On top of giving your employees and CFO more power, it tracks all company spending in real-time with advanced analytics. Already when [Creandum backed Pleo in the seed round](https://blog.creandum.com/why-we-think-pleo-is-the-perfect-fintech-company-23ada9223270) we were incredibly impressed by the super smart and experienced Pleo founders, by Pleo's powerful business model, the obvious market need (who doesn't hate expense reports?), and by the sophisticated yet beautifully simple product that they had built. At the same time, we knew that it was still early: At the time, Pleo had few customers, most of which were small, we were not yet sure how well go-to-market channels would work. The team was still only the two founders plus a handful of people. Pleo today is a completely different company: thousands of customers who are exceptionally happy, a team of 50, and real revenue that's growing extremely fast. How did they get there? Here are the key learnings from working with the Pleo team these past 15 months on what to focus on when going from seed to A round stage. ### Hire exceptional people ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5w3CKibjOhRYM5GCF2Xto0/af5acabb13090bc0df96ddfc9bc043ec/image_266.jpg) The quality of the early people you hire sets the bar for the rest of the life of your company, which means you need to balance scaling the organisation quickly with only hiring the best. This applies across roles. There are three key challenges: - You need to attract the best people - those that could get a job anywhere - to work at your little company. This is ultimately a sales job, and the Pleo founders are exceptional at laying out the vision for what they're building. - You need to be able to assess whether people are really great. This is especially hard for roles that are different from yours. Jeppe and Nicco have been really good at using their network here: for instance, since neither of them are online marketing experts, they've been great at talking to CMOs and online marketers at more advanced companies, to learn what to look for in the right candidate. - No matter how well you do, some hires will not work out. These situations are some of the hardest ones as a founder. Nonetheless, there's only one solution: assess people as quickly as possible, and if you believe that they are not the right fit, let them go immediately. ### Become feature complete Startup common wisdom tells us that you should launch so quickly that you should be embarrassed about your MVP. The time between the seed and A round is when you need to build out your product so that not only the most enthusiastic customers will want to use it. In Pleo's case, a lot of this had to do with onboarding. Fintech companies, especially in the B2B space, have much higher requirements on knowing their customers than other companies, and while Pleo has always adhered to all the rules, in the beginning that process was still largely manual. Which, we know, doesn't scale. In other words, a lot of Pleo's product development efforts these past 15 months have been on making onboarding automated and super smooth. ### Delight your customers Your happy customers are your best salespeople. And something that Pleo has been remarkable at has been to delight their customers. They have a close-to-unheard-of NPS of around 80, tons of new customers come from word of mouth, and within each customer, we see Pleo being used more heavily. Put simply, this customer love helps Pleo grow faster. It is driven by product development, particularly Pleo's exceptionally smooth onboarding, but very much also by investing in an exceptional customer success team. And it is ultimately driven by spending time with the customers, to make sure that they succeed. ### Nail scalable go-to-market channels This was definitely a risk when Creandum backed Pleo in the seed round. The team had done some promising experiments with online ads, and we had a strong hypothesis that the simple and beautiful product would be easy for customers to love. But we didn't know. This is almost always the case in seed rounds. When raising the A round, you need to have a strong hypothesis, backed by data, about what works and what doesn't. Key here is to run continuous experiments, both testing new channels and iterating on existing ones, combined with rigorous measurement of what works and what doesn't. The Pleo team has tested Adwords, partnerships with accounting firms, Facebook ads, outbound sales and several other channels. Some of these work, some don't, and the team is still iterating across all of them. ### Get traction This should be a result of the initiatives above: Unless you're building something extremely hard, like a rocket or an autonomous car, then you need to have real traction to raise an A round. Most of the time, this means revenue, although for some businesses, a large, fast growing and very engaged free user base is just as attractive. We are incredibly excited to start working with Kinnevik, which is one of Europe's leading investors in fast growing technology businesses with experience from companies like Zalando and Betterment. We're also excited to welcome Andre

articles.title: Creandum backs FirstVet (+ puppy gifs)
articles.text: As proud backers of [KRY](https://www.kry.se/en/) we've seen the benefits of telemedicine firsthand. But when we first heard of [FirstVet](http://firstvet.com), the digital veterinary clinic for animals, our first reaction was slightly skeptical. I mean, dogs can't talk, how would that work? (spoil alert: turns out it works ) All jokes aside, we're strong believers in how technology is changing how we act with medical care, both for people and now with pets. And today we're proud to announce that Creandum Fund IV has led a €5.1 million round in FirstVet, the leader in veterinary services via video for a wide range of animals, from cats and dogs to horses and even more exotic animals such as mini pigs, ferrets or spiders. The digitalization of veterinary clinics is coming fast, and FirstVet is paving the way in Europe. The company saves pets and pet owners from unnecessary and stressful trips to the vet by offering video meetings with veterinarians directly from your smartphone, tablet, or computer. Just like your local animal clinic, FirstVet's veterinarians assist animal owners with advice, diagnosis, referral, and even prescriptions. If in-person care is needed, FirstVet promptly refers sick and injured animals to the nearest and most suitable specialist. ## Animal care becoming more human = large and expanding market We saw a few trends that made FirstVet super interesting: **Pets are family members and demand for their care is becoming the same as for any family member + =** My (Sannas) grandfather was a vet and as a child I loved the room in the basement where he had his clinic; it had a bright light with a huge magnifying glass and the shelves were full of glass jars with different types of parasites in them. I also remember a very common part of his job; putting sick pets down. This is still common for vets, of course, but there has been a shift in how much care and efforts are made to cure an animal compared to then. Maybe it's all the pet-friendly movies we watched growing up, like 101 Dalmations and Beethoven but for whatever reason, today we don't treat our dogs like dogs, we treat them like part of our family. This comes with many rewards, but it also means we are much more likely to demand the highest quality care and request professional help at earlier stages then before. **People spend more on their pets ** Today people have grown closer and closer to their pets, spending money on everything from organic food, baskets full of toys (According to American Pet Products Association close [70bm USD](http://www.americanpetproducts.org/press_industrytrends.asp) was spent on pet related products and services in US alone) and in growing numbers, pet insurance. This last point is one of the key factors why FirstVet plays an important role today. In the past when your dog or cat got sick, you took it to the vet and you left with a bill. While those were simpler times, it also meant you typically had less options and opportunities to foot a large bill. Today pet owners get their insurance company involved when they go to the vet, which allows for you to hedge risk against your pet getting sick, and allows your insurance company to find FirstVet a perfect fit to lower costs by serving more patients or provide a higher level of care at lower cost by referring the animal to the most suitable specialist when needed. **Win for everyone involved ** The consolidation of vet clinics, increased prices, and increasing insurance premiums drives need for this type of service. It's a win-win-win for everyone involved; pets and pet owners get help directly at low cost, insurance companies can save money by getting the right care for the animal in right time (avoid unnecessary visits and/or refer them to the partner appropriate clinic) and vets can an additional source of income and an option for more flexible work. ## This is the team to transform veterinary care. Since launching in 2016, the company has shown an impressive growth month over month, driven in part by building key partnerships with insurance companies who offer FirstVet to their customers for more immediate and cost-effective care. The company has a long history of building partnerships in the pet industry; behind FirstVet are the former founders of VetZoo, Sweden's leading online store for pet owners. With his team, CEO David Prien has built up an impressive business with limited resources and they are a key partner for a large number of insurance companies. We looked at similar players across Europe but no one is even close to offering what FirstVet do. They today have agreements with close to 100% of pet insurancers in Sweden, Finland was recently launched and the company has it's sight on Europe. (Yes, they are hiring, get in touch [here](https://firstvet.com/sv/career)) We're big believers in telemedicine and knew that a great team like FirstVet would do for veterinary care what KRY did for telemedicine. There are a lot of similarities between the two, but one advantage is that animal care is a lot less regulated than human care, which allows FirstVet to expand into new geographies quicker. Also the fact that payments are settled either out-of-pocket or via insurance companies makes scaling less complicated. As a bonus, this investment has allowed us to use more puppy GIFs than ever before. And seriously, who doesn't like a cute puppy? <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2FPkVHsFmmLeBfa%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&display_name=Giphy&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FPkVHsFmmLeBfa%2Fgiphy.gif&image=https%3A%2F%2Fi.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FPkVHsFmmLeBfa%2Fgiphy.gif&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="" height="244" width="435"></iframe> _More about the company and the investment in [DI Digital](https://digital.di.se/artikel/tar-in-53-miljoner-till-sitt-kry-for-veterinarer) (Swedish) and [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2018/06/26/firstve

articles.title: Automating your HR & payroll — why Creandum backed Factorial
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Today we're proud to share that [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/) Fund IV has led a seed round in Barcelona-based [Factorial](https://factorialhr.com/), the best HR solution for SMEs. Additionally, our friends from [Kfund](https://kfund.co/) and [Point Nine Capital](http://www.pointninecap.com/) have joined the round as co-investor, in what we feel is one of the most exciting companies coming out of Spain. In this post, we wanted to share what our thought process was in this funding round, and how we fell in love with the team. HR has been an area Creandum followed closely and has been active in; the Creandum funds have invested in companies including Planday and Clustree, but this market has many challenges to solve. ## But first, Vamos España This is a special one as it is the Creandum's funds' first investment in Spain - a geography that we've been following closely for the past year now, and one I have been visiting every few weeks. Every time I go there it's a pleasure to meet with impressive teams in the vibrant cities Madrid and Barcelona. I started following the local tech scene in Barcelona during my studies at ESADE, and am truly impressed how the tech ecosystem has evolved since then - we're excited to focus much more attention on the region going forward. Thus, if you're a Spanish founder looking for a European VC with a bridge to Silicon Valley (we run a SF office), [be in touch](https://www.creandum.com/team/peter-specht)! ## What makes Factorial so interesting for us ### Market and addressable need: Talk to any small business owner and you'll quickly find out how SMEs hate wasting time and money on HR. The fact is that SMEs are still using spreadsheets, Word, paper folders and a mix of single tools to manage their core HR needs like vacation, contracts, benefits, organization design, and payroll (Creandum is bullish on the SME sector - read more [[here](https://blog.creandum.com/sme-tech-creandums-view-on-this-broad-industry-vertical-7cb26289fc14)](https://medium.com/@specht.p/lessons-learned-from-creandum-sme-day-2018-74eb59ed0e56) & here). In the tech world it's easy to forget how incredibly manual this still is for the majority of companies out there. So much manual processes that are repeated by people over and over. The need is clear, and a decent HR software market has already developed over the past years. However one of the biggest pain points - payroll - has not been properly addressed yet, and HR solutions haven't cracked the productization and automatization that make this easier. Looking at European market there are 22 million SMEs, a significant portion of these with need for HR solutions. That said HR solutions make most sense if organizations have a reached a certain size in employees and we saw companies starting using such software mostly from 10 employees upwards. Doing the math bottom up and top down gives you a huge multi billion $ TAM in Europe and the large opportunity to build a bn$+ company, which is the potential that Creandum looks for. This is a complicated problem but the solution is Factorial: a free, easy to use all-in-one HR platform integrating benefits, payroll and core HR features (employee database, time off tracking, document management etc.). The team developed its own payroll engine and a platform that brings together employees, HR and legal advisors enabling real-time management of payroll. ### Product I rarely came out so enthusiastic from a product demo. You can sense the team's love for detail with a super slick UI and great ease of use. The right core HR functions in place with easy time off management, managing of key employee documents, dashboards for HR managers, reports etc. and employee benefits, which employees can select within minutes. The relevant functions are smoothly integrated with the payroll functionality - with instant calculation. When you adapt e.g. a one time bonus of an employee or general working hours in the contract, you can instantly see the effect calculated for the payslip (no, you don't have to call your tax advisor anymore or wait until the end of the month to see the effects of any payroll related changes). Our impression was reflected by happy customer interviews and a very high NPS score. If you are an SME it's best if you try it out yourselves at[ www.factorialhr.com](http://www.factorialhr.com/). ### Business model Factorial is offering a free core HR product (yes it's free and it's awesome) + additional features for a paid plan (including payroll). The SME market has its own challenges, but this model fits well to our experience with Creandum's portfolio company Bokio (free accounting) - offering a valuable free product and having adjacent services/functionalities that you can monetise. A good base for virality and happy users. ### Traction With limited sales and marketing resources the company has been able to establish a broad and fast growing user base for its core HR solution, not only in Spain but also internationally (mostly driven by organic growth). Over 20 thousand companies signed up already. On top of that, the company figured out monetisation for their free product at an early stage. ### Team Probably the most important criteria for an early stage company (or any company) is the right people. Meeting many times with Jordi, Bernat, Pau and team in person and via video we were really impressed how product driven they were (also all founders with tech background), loved the energy and the dynamics in the team, including a remarkable curiosity level, bombarding us with as many questions as we asked them. This combined with their extensive experience in the startup world building up companies in C-level positions before in Spain and San Francisco are a fantastic setup for a SaaS success story "made in Spain". ### Concluding Factorial is solving key needs with a high pain point for SMEs. It fits well into our hypothesis that the most valuable SaaS companies are the ones where the softwar

articles.title: Amplified Intelligence for Troubleshooting
articles.text: ### Creandum backs Mavenoid in a $1.9m seed round Co-authored by [Staffan Helgesson](http://twitter.com/shelgesson) & [Lauri Lehtmaa](https://twitter.com/laurilehtmaa) We are proud to announce Creandum Fund's latest invest in [Mavenoid](http://mavenoid.com) - a virtual agent for troubleshooting. The $1.9m round was co-led with our friends at Point Nine Capital, as well as angel investors Erik Byrenius, Andreas Ehn, Leo Giertz, Alfred Ruth, and Jeremy Yap. ### Amplified Intelligence for Troubleshooting Technical support is the cornerstone of great customer experience–a necessary offering for every technology company out there. Technical support today is provisioned by and large by support engineers - the more complex the problem, the more skilled engineers are needed to troubleshoot issues. Skilled staff is, however, expensive and in short supply, so oftentimes compromises need to be made. In order to help companies overcome these limitations, Mavenoid has developed a state-of-the-art virtual agent to open up knowledge sharing within organisations. Mavenoid's proprietary troubleshooting algorithm puts the knowledge of the most experienced engineers in the hands of the most junior ones, or even directly in the hands of regular consumers. Headquartered in Stockholm, Mavenoid is founded by two former Palantir engineers. The technology is built on top of years of research conducted by RISE SICS in close collaboration with the Swedish Armed Forces to help mechanics repair tanks and terrain vehicles. Traditional approaches to share knowledge internally are most often either centrally authored PDF documents or decision trees that try to connect symptoms to causes. Both of these approaches are difficult to edit, are not collaborative, and lack any kind of feedback loops. Decision trees in particular are very difficult and costly to set up, and equally costly to maintain and edit. More so, decision trees are inflexible and prone to errors, as one wrong answer puts the user on a wrong path. Mavenoid combines human knowledge with machine learning & human observations with machine readings to amplify the work of support engineers. ### A billion dollar market opportunity Mavenoid's approach, in contrast, offers value from day one - it takes hours instead of weeks to set up, has a collaborative layer, and includes feedback loops that make the troubleshooting process smarter over time. Furthermore, Mavenoid's probabilistic approach to troubleshooting overcomes the limitations of decision trees, and accepts the fact that humans are prone to errors. We see technical support as a growing issue - think of your car as an example. That '92 Honda Civic you started with was a breeze to fix, but today your Tesla involves much more complicated and interconnected systems that require detailed knowledge to fix. Today's tanks, factory components, and computer systems are no different. We see diagnostics increasing in priority to become as important of a business unit as analytics or logistics, and there is clearly a billion-dollar opportunity in freeing the time of expert support engineers by presenting troubleshooting knowledge in a 21st century way. We see them on this path already. Since launching less than a year ago, Mavenoid has signed deals with seven of the largest enterprises in the Nordics, including Alfa Laval and Scania. Mavenoid is used to help businesses and consumers repair everything from trucks and cranes to home alarms and robotic lawn mowers. ### Strong Complementary Team It's a cliché, but early stage investments revolve a lot around the team, and Mavenoid's founding team ticks all the boxes for us when it comes to building a global enterprise software company - a perfect combination sales as well as deep technical expertise to tackle an underlying global BUSD market opportunity. We are extremely humbled to be able to work with such entrepreneurs, and equally excited for the future of troubleshooting. CEO, Shahan Lilja, was the first deployment strategist at Palantir in the Nordics, and was previously a research intern at Microsoft Live Labs. Shahan has dual degrees in Engineering Physics from the Royal Institute of Technology and Business & Economics from the Stockholm School of Economics. CTO, Gintautas Miliauskas, was a forward-deployed engineer at Palantir and, prior to that, a senior software engineer at Google. Gintautas has a BSc in Software Systems and an MSc in Philosophy from Vilnius University. With the funding secured, Mavenoid is hiring technical and non-technical roles to make its platform self-serve, and expand outside of the Nordics - _**[more info on their website](http://www.mavenoid.com/careers/)**_. _At Creandum, we believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. Check out our **[website](http://creandum.com)** or follow **[Creandum Family](http://medium.com/creandum-family)** on Medium to learn more._

articles.excerpt: Job creation inside venture
articles.text: Software is eating the world and robots will take all our jobs. We've heard about these things many times, and considering the impact it will have on society they are important topics for us all to contemplate and act upon. But technology startups also represent something amazingly important. They are the part of the lifeblood of [job creation in society](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2015/aug/17/technology-created-more-jobs-than-destroyed-140-years-data-census). As the [Creandum](http://creandum.com) Funds celebrate 15 years of investing in early-stage technology companies, we decided to do some number crunching on our end to understand job creation within the portfolio. Thanks to some sleuthing by our friends at corporate data powerhouse [Craft](https://craft.co/) (thanks [Ilya](None)), we found that 64 Creandum portfolio companies today employ... **...10,000 people! ** (9,731 to be exact, but seeing how some Creandum companies that have been acquired aren't counted we think it's fair to round it up to a nice even figure). These startups give purpose and meaning to 10k engineers, designers, customer success managers, sales professionals, marketers, HR managers, and many more. These people are the collective creators and champions of change, and are a true testament to how Creandum portfolio founders play a substantial part in shaping society. We couldn't be more humbled and proud to be associated with such an impact. To everyone working hard within the Creandum portfolio - thank you! Looking into these numbers a bit, since 2003 the Creandum Funds have invested into around 80 companies. If we were to average out the investments across total employee base, we would have 125 employees per company. When the Creandum Funds typically invests the average team would be around 10 employees, meaning our _VC job creation index_ (new jargon we just invented ) of 12.5x; for every 1 team member Creandum Funds fund, 11.5 additional jobs are created. Although logically partially correct, the above calculation is not a reflection of reality. ![Job distribution across the Creandum portfolio.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5TqTClMRO5O81neKMogBaG/ff110b69d315ce2c8a1cc021ec1488d0/image_263.jpg) This chart shows the distribution of jobs across the Creandum portfolio. It's not a huge surprise, but job creation follows the same [power law dynamics as venture returns](http://reactionwheel.net/2015/06/power-laws-in-venture.html), where the vast majority of jobs and returns are generated by a small number of companies who hit it big - [Spotify](http://spotify.com), [Klarna](http://klarna.com) and [iZettle](http://izettle.com). Adding some granularity to the tail of the chart, if we were to remove the top 3 outliers from above, the remaining distribution becomes a bit clearer. Many of these companies were founded only a few years ago and are recent investments of the Creandum Funds, and we have many reasons to believe we will see similar trends of massive organizational growth to small few of these if we extrapolate 5–10 years from today. ![Job distribution across the Creandum portfolio excluding top 3 largest companies.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6RVHLgrLETPzoLz6DigRiG/96e4f3a0c46e01c24c32e47d90a38acf/image_264.jpg) We often refer to the _Creandum Family_ as the formal and informal network of founders and management within Creandum portfolio companies. But in reality, this family extends far beyond those individuals, and is in fact 10,000 strong. We are ever so proud of everyone's contribution to this family, and our commitment is to work hard every day to keep developing this network further. If you are part of the Creandum Family always know you are free to reach out to any of us at any point in time. We are here to serve you. Until the next 10,000! <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2Fxv99RkOqxiAnu%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&url=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fgifs%2Ffollowers-10000-xv99RkOqxiAnu&image=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2Fxv99RkOqxiAnu%2Fgiphy.gif&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="" height="244" width="435"></iframe>

articles.title: Creandum’s Perspective on Co-Living
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.excerpt: Hypotheses On a New Business Model 1/2
articles.text: Recently, real estate prices in many European regions have been reaching all-time highs. One answer to this is Co-Living. We are excited about this concept. Last year Berlin, one of Creandum's home cities, had the [fastest rising property prices](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/apr/10/berlin-world-fastest-rising-property-prices) in the world. Consequently, it is becoming harder and harder for young urban professionals to buy property in the city or to find affordable living space to rent. Simultaneously, the housing needs of millennials are changing. The mantra ‘my home is my castle' is no longer valid for everyone - certain groups of predominantly young people prefer flexibility and service over ownership. ‘Co-living' is hot, and it rides on the wave of the successful co-working movement. Inspired by a crowdsourced definition of [Co-Liv](https://medium.com/@purehouselab), we understand co-living as: ‘a way of living in an (at least partially) shared living space with the purpose to improve the quality of life of its residents, through the enhancement of social networks and/or a higher/more flexible standard of living.' Although of course not suitable for everyone, we believe that co-living is a phenomenon that is here to stay. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/ZDIXkbxSH8ja3TO1Cv55r/00d2de11b5327a1c7da4787273f8f864/image_261.jpg) ## A set of hypotheses underline this belief: ### 1. Big cities will continue to draw people - and will become even more popular over time _Big cities are booming. The [UN estimates](ttps://population.un.org/wup/Publications/Files/WUP2018-KeyFacts.pdf) that in 2050, 68% of the world's population will be urban, up from 30% a century earlier. Although urbanisation and population growth are happening at a different pace across regions (strongest in the developing world; even slowing down in certain areas in Northern Europe and in the US), the global trend is towards urbanisation. A [McKinsey Global Institute study](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/urbanization/urban-world-meeting-the-demographic-challenge-in-cities) estimates that over 86% of the world's GDP growth in the next 15 years will be generated in cities._ _All in all, our expectation is that cities will globally gain importance as both economic and creative hubs. I guess that is not a surprise, right?_ ### 2. Real estate prices in metropolitan areas will continue to soar, making it increasingly difficult for young urban professionals to afford buying a house on their own _Already, it is becoming close to impossible for young people to afford buying a house on their own in an urban area. Overall, for [7% of people in the EU](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Urban_Europe_%E2%80%94_statistics_on_cities%2C_towns_and_suburbs_%E2%80%94_housing_in_cities#Housing_in_cities), housing costs (either rent or mortgage) exceed half of their disposable income. It is debatable whether housing prices in real terms will increase, partially because tax subsidies for mortgages payments are being reduced in certain countries (e.g. in the Netherlands)._ _However, our expectation is that with growing urban population real estate prices will - at least in nominal terms and as a trend - continue to rise over time. You have to ask yourself, do you really believe the inner cities of the most popular capitals will become less popular going forward? We don't._ ### 3. The desire for flexibility is crucial for millennials - freedom of geographical location and corresponding living situation form a major part of this flexibility _For millennials, jobs are no longer a lifetime decision. Neither is location. Even though the intention might be there to make a marriage everlasting, the majority of the marriages carried out today in the Western world will end up in a divorce. All in all, the increased number of changes in one's personal situation are drivers for a higher degree of flexibility, also in terms of housing. In 2016, over [11.8 million EU citizens of working age (20–64) moved countries inside the EU](http://ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=738&langId=en&pubId=8066&furtherPubs=yes) either for their current job or to seek employment. This number has been increasing steadily in the past decade, and even with pressure on the EU as an institute, we do not foresee that this number will stop growing soon._ ### 4. The experience economy makes that young people in Europe (following the example of US young professionals) are willing to pay for services that increase their quality of life _With the rise of the sharing economy, freedom of use has - at least for some people - become more important than possession. This phenomenon has its impact on the desire of young urban professionals to own property. In addition, the concept of the experience economy (experiences are more valuable than goods) results in the fact that time off is more and more valuable. Consequently, young people are willing to spend significant part of their income in order to free up time for other experience-related activities. Not only can cleaning be outsourced, saving time by for example having a gym inside your apartment building is worth paying for._ _This willingness to pay for services is something which has existed in the US for a longer period of time, but which is now emerging in Europe as well._ ### 5. Social capital will be ever more crucial in the future - housing will play a role in forming productive networks _Co-working has proven that people value each other's company, and that they are willing to pay a premium for being surrounded with like-minded entrepreneurs and starting businesses - at least that is most successful co-working spaces are marketing._ _With automation being able to take over many manual and straightforward tasks in the future, adding value through connections and networks will gain territory among a broad group of people.
