articles.title: Backing Klaus — because customers deserve quality support
articles.text: I'm excited to announce that Creandum V is leading a $1.9m Seed round in **[Klaus](https://klausapp.com)** (formerly Qualitista)— the conversation review and QA platform for customer service teams. This marks the first investment into the Baltics and Estonia in particular by the Creandum Funds. ### Customer service is no longer a cost centre Customer service has often in the past been perceived as a cost centre, especially in traditional industries, driven by transactional revenue streams, in which the link between post-purchase support & profit has been seen as weak at best. Today, however, when most everything and anything is being offered as a service, the importance of customer service is impossible to ignore. Customer service is a driving force behind customer happiness. Great customer service defines brands, helps companies retain customers & ultimately sell more services. Customer service is clearly a revenue centre, and a competitive differentiator - it is, after all, much more expensive to acquire new customers than it is to retain existing ones. "89% of companies will compete predominantly on customer experience by 2020" Gartner ### **Increased customer expectations** Customer service is a core part of any product, and customers, with ever decreasing attention spans, expect timely & personalised service. There's no surprise then that real-time communication tools such as Intercom & Drift among many others are thriving. These platforms bring customers closer to companies, and fulfil the preferences of customers - better approachability, with more frequent and personalised customer service. ### ...lead to a lack of insights internally This shift creates a myriad of issues for internal management. How do we know what we as a company are doing our best? The golden standard is to measure customer satisfaction (CSAT) or net promoter score (NPS). While useful for many reasons, these indicators are inherently lagging and aggregate in nature, and offer little actionable insights to support agents and managers alike. Drawing parallels with software development, if companies were to measure the quality of their software through end-user satisfactions, then they will have already dropped the ball once they start seeing symptoms in those indicators. The root cause may no longer be a particular bug in the source code, but the issue may be cultural, which is much more difficult to change down the line. That's the very reason why modern software companies embrace code review - the act of systematically peer reviewing source code for mistakes in order to ship code of uniform quality. ### Klaus & conversation review to the rescue! Martin & Kair, the co-founders of **[Klaus](https://klausapp.com)** _(formerly Qualitista)_, witnessed just that at their time at **Pipedrive** when building out the support function. As a Global Head of Customer Support, Martin lacked sufficient and actionable insight to his team's his team's performance, and the quality and consistency of service that their customers received. To make matters worse, customer service roles have some of the highest employee turnover rates of any industry, which makes it difficult to scale the onboarding of new agents, and to keep a uniform service quality. After hiring over 100 customer facing support specialists, it became clear that the best way to ensure consistent quality is to have a system for giving feedback to agents on their work - bringing the equivalent of code review to customer service teams. While establishing a process for conversation review bore fruit initially, it also became apparent that spreadsheets won't scale across a large support organisation, and for better adoption & insights companies need purpose-built tooling. As a result, Martin & Kair decided to team up in 2018 to partake on a journey to build Klaus, and bring the best practices behind building world class customer service teams to the market. They launched the product 6 months ago, and have sine witnessed rapid growth and adoption by many leading tech companies such as Automattic (WordPress), Trivago, Soundcloud, Figma, Wistia, and many others, who have already carried out over 200,000 conversation reviews. We are excited to be partnering up with Martin & Kair in their mission to help companies build better customer service teams & culture. From day one, we were impressed by the unique insight & the first hand experience that the founding team had, complemented by the speed at which they had built a beautiful product that gets a lot of customer love. The founder-market fit was unquestionable. We believe that in the world driven by conversational & real-time customer support, quality management is ever more difficult & crucial at the same time, and every company will want to use it. Klaus is in a pole position to define the category, and is only scratching the surface of what's yet to come. Are you looking to up your customer service? [Check out Klaus to learn more](https://klausapp.com/). Want to join the mission? Klaus is hiring (the team is semi-remote).

articles.title: Backing Trade Republic
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.excerpt: Commission free trading for everyone
articles.text: My deep interest in fintech started about 20 years ago when I co-founded eTrade Nordic, one of the first online brokers in the Nordics. It opened up new opportunities to the stock trading market by offering customers direct access to their trading accounts, which at the time was a new idea. It made trading easier and cheaper than ever before. One thing that's a little shocking today, is that in some countries opening up a brokerage account in 2019 looks about the same as 20 years ago. While back then you would happy wait up to 5 days to fully set up an account, and show your friends you can buy a stock in 12 clicks and 5–20€ per trade, today you would expect better. If nothing else, a sleek mobile app, but in many cases trading platforms are too similar to what was developed decades ago. This was reality until we met Marco, Christian and Thomas from[ Trade Republic](https://traderepublic.com/). Trade Republic is the first mobile-only and commission-free broker in Germany - making trading stocks dead simple and intuitive with a mobile-only approach. Over the last three years the founders focused on building a digital and secure infrastructure, managed to acquire a banking license, and secured some key partnerships to set up one of the leanest online brokers in the business. Trade Republic, like most online brokers, secures revenues through payment of order flow from trading partners. The major difference is that Trade Republic is willing to share these revenues directly with their customers, enabled through their lean and mostly automated backend/cost structure, and therefore allowing customers to trade commission free. ## Our hypothesis: €1 trades are great. A fantastic service is even better. Even though Trade Republic is [the cheapest online broker in the german market](https://www.faz.net/aktuell/finanzen/meine-finanzen/aktienhandel-in-deutschland-der-guenstigste-broker-im-land-15990462.html) with only a fixed settlement fee of 1€ per trade, we don't think being the cheapest is the way to build the best trading tool in Europe. The service you can provide is _the_ defining factor. Even though Trade Republic only opened up their brokerage services a couple of months ago, their mobile-first app is incredibly polished and their service offering can already keep up with the biggest and most established players in the market, which is probably why their customers already number in the five digits. Trade Republic's offering includes: - the longest trading hours available in Germany (7:30 to 23:00) - easy online onboarding that will get you trading within 10 minutes - access to more than 6,500 German and international stocks - access to more than 500 ETFs - advanced stock searching, news feeds, and a range of features to make trading easier. Most importantly, they are building their free offering even further, which is why we are proud to help announce that together with the new financing round, Trade Republic's services now also include free derivative trading. Stay tuned in the coming months for even more features. This market was poised for disruption for some time, and we've seen that this is the team to do it. It goes without saying that we are very excited to work together with [Christian](https://www.linkedin.com/in/christianhe/),[ Thomas](https://www.linkedin.com/mynetwork/invite-sent/tpischke/?isSendInvite=true),[ Marco](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marco-cancellieri-5a48b2a2/) and their team, to make trading cheaper, faster and more intuitive than ever before. Read more in [Handelsblatt](https://www.handelsblatt.com/finanzen/banken-versicherungen/digitaler-broker-start-up-trade-republic-per-smartphone-an-den-aktienmarkt/23895122.html?ticket=ST-1350574-weIMhHgBTW6XBk5kHgiY-ap1) (German). _We believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur. Check out our **[website](http://creandum.com/)** or follow **[Creandum Family](http://medium.com/creandum-family)** on Medium to learn more._

articles.title: Diversity inside European VC 2.0
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Limited progress made
articles.text: [Last year](https://hackernoon.com/diversity-inside-european-vc-more-work-needed-c545353b7e4c) [Creandum](http://creandum.com) launched its annual _Diversity Index_ - a look inside the five funds' portfolio companies to measure the role of women across each organization. This is one attempt out of several Creandum is doing to push for better gender balance within the tech industry, on the premise that what gets measured gets done. ### The why. Just to repeat the rationale of why diversity is important I quote our post from last year: First, it makes business sense to do so. It's not subjective liberalism. It's facts! This [2016 working paper by the Peterson Institute for International Economics](https://piie.com/publications/wp/wp16-3.pdf) surveyed 21,980 firms from 91 countries and found a correlation between women in leadership roles firm performance. The paper concludes, "The estimated magnitudes of these correlations are not small: For profitable firms, a move from no female leaders to 30 percent representation is associated with a 15 percent increase in the net revenue margin." Secondly, we value diversity of thought to build the most disruptive companies. [The strongest companies we see have founders that challenge each other greatly](https://blog.creandum.com/10-years-later-getting-to-know-spotify-before-series-a-2279e7e54be0), but to do so requires founders from different perspectives and convictions. If you were to start from scratch to build an industry with high diversity of thought to solve new challenges, you wouldn't staff it exclusively with 27-year-old white men from the same schooling.We've now completed our second diversity index and the big question is, how are we doing? The short answer is that things are moving slowly, if positively. This blog post is published to give an update, air our dirty laundry, and continue the important conversation about women in tech. Furthermore, last year we saw a very tangible commercial impact related to gender diversity. One of Creandum's medium-size portfolio companies had the opportunity to acquire another firm, but eventually pulled away from the deal because the company being acquired had a 100% male team. The reasoning was that there was a big cost of bringing on board an all-male team, which didn't outweigh the benefits of the acquisition. We expect to see many more examples of poorly managed organizational diversity having a negative impact on shareholder value. ### The how. There are many ways to measure diversity, and we're focusing specifically on gender. We send a poll to the portfolio company CEOs measuring the number of women across 3 dimensions in their respective organizations; the number of women across the whole organization, women on the management team, and women in board positions. This year we surveyed 44 portfolio companies and 41 responded. ### Whole organization: 36% women (+1%) This year Creandum's active portfolio counted 3623 employees of which 1317 are women, nudging the percentage up one point compared to last year when the number was 35%. Is this what progress looks like? We'd prefer to move fast and break stuff, but in reality, very little has budged. This number is somewhat remarkable because there's been a lot of movement in the funds' portfolio companies. Later-stage companies with giant headcounts like Spotify and iZettle have exited, and 9 early-stage firms have joined us. Despite it all, the number is still hovering there in the mid 30's. ![2018 to 2019 year-over-year change in female-to-male ratio, arranged by headcount](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/EnF5NPyaR9yEEq0ZMoN1) Looking deeper at the firms measured in 2018, 17 increased their female/male ratio while 13 dropped it. It's difficult to tell a clean story out of these numbers. Some companies who were close to 50% male-to-female actually dropped to 40%, which is still bringing up the funds' average but is a concerning sight. And frustratingly, there are the companies who were already doing bad with hiring and retaining female employees and are now doing worse. On the positive side, there are companies making 10% positive changes in their workforce, even with headcounts in the 80's. That's a decent change in one year that took intentional effort to accomplish. The new companies measured in Creandum's portfolio aren't unique. Three are bringing up the average while six are below it. In total, the new companies added in the past year average out to 31% female. ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/dOE8SpQTqqbD6XTYZryO) ### Women in management: 23% (+2%) This number has moved slightly and we see signs of progress; a growing number of companies have at least one female manager. Roughly 33% of the fund's portfolio companies have at least a quarter of their management team made up of women. 15% have at least a third. And only 3% of the fund's portfolio have more than half women in management. ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/pBPg8lXpSFa4PydCrwAG) We see **women in management as the most important metric to balance** because where we see women at the top, we see more women overall. In our numbers, if the management team has at least 25% of women, we see an average of 42% total female headcount (!). If there's at least one woman in the management team, we see 34% female employment -roughly the average. When there are no women in the management team, the number of women in the total organization is averaged in the low 20's. ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/46q9wzhKSXqul17zJOQN) If there is one thing we push Creandum portfolio founders to think about when it comes to gender diversity it's to ensure they hire women into management roles. ### Board Members: 10.3% (-0.2%) At the other end of the funnel are female board members. At early-stage companies, these are typically venture capitalists, angel investors, and trusted advisors. A little over 40% of Creandum's portfolio companies have at least 1 female board member, but that leaves about 60% (!

articles.title: Creandum Promotes Peter Specht
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.text: Peter joined the Creandum Investment Advisory Team in Berlin in June 2017, and quickly became crucial contributor to our growing activities in Germany and in Spain. **Today, we are excited to announce the promotion of Peter Specht to Principal.** Peter previously worked at Bain, after time spent at Google and Rocket Internet. During his time at Creandum, he demonstrated a relentless work ethic, analytical practice and his networking capabilities. He played a vital role in the due diligence of countless unclosed deals, but helped put the deals of Billie, Argent, Voi and several not yet public portfolio companies into place. In Germany, Peter lead the deals in Cargo.One and an additional undisclosed deal. Furthermore, he built out Creandum's footprint in Spain, which ultimately lead to the backing of Factorial HR. When we hire new members to the Creandum Investment Advisory Team, we do so selectively, deliberately and with a good amount of effort. We never fill roles, we try to find the perfect addition to the team. The candidates go through a multi stage, several week long process, which we hope allows us to select the perfect team member. We always try to find an individual who hopefully stays with us for a very long time. It fills us with great joy, when after two years already, Peter is ready to take the next step and become a senior member of the investment team. With the promotion to Principal, Peter will continue his work in the ecosystems, and lead deals of all sizes across Europe and the US.

articles.title: Perspective on Mobility Tech
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.excerpt: What’s next?
articles.text: Our whole lives we've been living in the transportation paradigm created in 1908 when Henry Ford rolled off the first car available to the masses, a world where we buy, drive, and park privately-owned cars running on gasoline. In the coming years it's clear we're due for another huge paradigm shift in transportation. It may be more subtle than the first car showing up in your village, but no less revolutionary. The groundwork for this massive change has been laid in the past years, with mobility companies like Uber, Lyft, Voi and AV players such as Waymo, Zoox, Tesla and others as the first harbingers. Beyond building platforms these companies are leveraging technological advancements in machine learning, computer vision and battery tech and are not only creating technology that makes life easier for drivers, but are also providing new platforms for service companies to operate. Cities are following suite (or will) with infrastructure for electric car charging, specialized lanes for electric vehicles & carpooling, and connectivity services like 5G. And playing into it is a huge change in behavior in cities, where consumers are getting used to owning fewer cars and relying on on-demand and pay-per-use models for getting around. This change is resulting in an abundance of new opportunities, which has also been reflected in VC funding in mobility tech in the past years. Funding in the space increased 20x over the past 5 years, reaching its peak in 2018 with $33bn. Shared mobility services have been the largest area of funding, representing over 50%, followed by transport & logistics (which I will exclude when looking at mobility in the following) and then autonomous vehicles, car connectivity and fleet management. Beyond that we've seen first mega IPOs this year with Uber and Lyft ringing the bell. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/ZJUgvj9WRnyq6FS0OAlrn/b2c0cb205179fef573d41fc828b00629/image_225.jpg) ## So what will be next? We believe: **Vehicles will...** - become smaller to maximise utilisation of space in cities, reduce congestion, be more efficient, and increase throughput - be electric and more sustainable - be autonomous - And they will be actually entertaining - think about the free time you'll have once someone else is driving **Consumers will...** - opt for more on demand and shared services - use multiple modes of transportation in general and also combine them in their trips, like combining scooters with public transport etc. rather than relying on a central vehicle ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7Caizuxv0bIuLz1PkrMg8i/ebea2a13242818d277b4667a7a69efb5/image_226.png) **Infrastructure will...** - be more connected. We'll see integration of real time information and infrastructure with e.g. full visibility on traffic flows, parking spots, assisting autonomous driving. As powerful as it is, it will take considerable time until we see this at scale **Regulation will...** - be a key driver determining adoption and timing - be driven by sustainability, safety and efficiency ambitions. Regulators and mobility companies will have to work even more side by side - mobility services in cities will become more regulated e.g. limiting amount of players through licenses. We already see it happening in the scooter and ride hailing market ## When will we see adoption happening? ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/N1V8ZfFCRQCkKhttsy99) There are many different forecasts. The BCG analysis above gives a good overview for possible timelines. The most ambitious view in the market is probably [Elon Musk claiming](https://www.businessinsider.com/tesla-robo-taxis-elon-musk-pt-barnum-circus-2019-4) 1 million autonomous Tesla robo taxis on the streets in 2020 (I doubt that ;-)). But looking at more stats and speaking to the industry one takeaway is that it will take more time to see autonomous vehicles at scale than most people think, primarily due to regulation, safety requirements and costs. ## Creandum's areas of interest as a VC: ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/qx8InDKPTgOfBawo6vFh) Creandum is interested and looking at most of the areas, but digesting these a little, here's what I'm in particular bullish on: ### 1) Smart mobility services in combination with adjacent technical innovation Mobility services are the largest market segment, making this a naturally attractive segment from a venture perspective. If we look at the _"distance value chain"_ many very significant companies have been built along it already. ![](https://cdn.filestackcontent.com/rKJCA0E6QZOTmALgcoRf) We are bullish on the general opportunity in this space and the Creandum funds have invested into e.g. [Voi](https://www.voiscooters.com/) and [Bolt](https://bolt.eu). Yet digesting the logos above, the mobility services are already heavily funded and consumers' needs for travelling the different distances are well covered. However we believe that **adjacent technical innovation entails** **new opportunities**. So we continue to look closely at this area in particular with technical innovation involved, be it on the hardware, platform or service side. Startups going forward need to (even more than in the past) have a unique angle or advantage to overcome the already prominent competition to win over consumers' minds and wallets. ### 2) Data & cybersecurity As we become more reliant of smart technology to get around, we'll need to be more reliant on data and communication security to get us there safely. These sort of companies could include data platforms, connected vehicle technology (V2X) or cybersecurity solutions for cars. We see an exponential need for these technologies and consider them core for increasing efficiency and safety of new vehicles. ### 3) Battery tech The demand for batteries is exploding. The Li-ion battery market worldwide is [forecasted](https://www.reportsanddata.com/report-detail/lithium-ion-battery-market) to increase from $36bn in 2018 to $109bn in 2026. articles.title: Creandum backs e-motorcycle company Cake
articles.author: Staffan Helgesson
articles.excerpt: Creating a new category in the urban commuter market
articles.text: When I'm thinking of motorcycles, big, noisy Harley Davidson machines come to my mind, with Jax Teller riding down Route 66. I barely see them in the city centres, in fact I don't see any younger fellows riding a motorcycle. It seems the major players in this segment are focusing solely on the Baby Boomers, lagging behind in innovation to attract a younger generation with a different mindset towards sustainable mobility and personal vehicles. In the wake of constraining regulations for combustion engines and a massive increase in environmental awareness, we are seeing a rapid movement towards electric solutions. Tesla has disrupted the entire auto industry forcing legacy carmakers to develop competitive electric vehicles (well, sooner or later - it took Porsche 11 years to [unveil their first e-vehicle](https://www.theverge.com/2019/9/4/20849437/porsche-taycan-turbo-ev-photos-mission-e-car-hands-on) to combat Tesla). The change to e-solutions continues in the two-wheel market: Electric scooters and bikes are taking over city centers, becoming the major means of transportation for urban city dwellers. **Electric vehicle adoption isn't a short-term trend.** It is a transformational change that is here to stay and will fundamentally change the transportation industries that for decades relied on the combustion engine. We are now amidst the Electric vehicle revolution and we are happy to announce that Creandum is fueling the e-revolution of the so far slow-moving motorcycle segment. Together with our friends from e.ventures, Creandum's fund has led a $13 million series A round in [Cake](https://ridecake.com/), a Swedish headquartered company developing high performance electric motorbikes aiming to create a new category in the urban commuter market. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3PwqdfaZ420XSj0oQGx8bR/0c4c27d85ba4903e62f209af0194559c/image_222.jpg) Cake was founded in 2016 and recently launched its first zero-emission model, the Kalk. Despite being very quiet, light and clean, it doesn't compromise on design or performance: Powered by a 15-kW electric motor the Kalk weighs under 70 kg, allowing it to accelerate up to a top speed of 80 km/h. A 52-volt lithium-ion battery runs the bike for competitive torque and range (up to 100km). The bike's design is maximized for trails and gravel roads. But it also comes in a street-legal version, making it perfect for carbon-free city commutes (Not convinced? Watch this [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9xVKRvlMzos)). It is easy to ride, perfectly made for young drivers with little experience since the electrical drive-train means no clutching or shifting gears. Going forward, Cake is planning a range of motorcycles targeting different customers, the pure off-roaders as well as their urban siblings. Similar to Landrover and Volvo Cross Country, who came down from the mountain targeting the mass-market of city dwellers, Cake is aiming for serving urban commuting needs with their vehicles, doubling up as excursion tools in the countryside for weekends and vacations. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/48623r6PFLRMiIZvyt86Jr/0fa665a02d71ef728662c41f23ee9724/image_223.jpg) The engine behind Cakes innovative products is Stefan Ytterborn, a serial founder with a proven track-record of building successful global brands: He played a key role in IKEA's explosive brand growth in the 90's and also founded the iconic ski helmet company [POC](https://www.pocsports.com/us/home/) (believe it or not, it stands for "Piece of Cake"...). Like many Swedes, he is an essentialist in style - no wonder the design of his first e-motorcycle Kalk has won several design awards and has recently been selected by the Swedish National Museum for its permanent collection. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3JT2YcixguxFC4v1qHeLWg/2fb29ab3d47f33e4e3c52d2e0adf0397/image_224.jpg) **Creandum's hypothesis is that mobility is facing a major paradigm shift**. Supporting Stefan and his team on their mission to speed up the journey towards a zero emission society fits in perfectly with our hypothesis. The clean and quiet characteristics of the bike hits the sweet spot where transportation in urban areas is heading and the lightness and simplicity invite new target groups with less experience to use it. Multiple industries have experienced the "urban outdoor"-hype, ranging from automotive (Land Rover, Jeep), to clothing (North Face, Canada Goose) and we expect a similar trend for electric motorcycles. It is a growing market segment with no category winner yet. Seeing Cakes' promising initial traction and being the first to attempt to crack the mass-market in this segment, it's a big opportunity for Cake to become the category leader. It's not every motorbike that can boast an appeal to both professional adrenaline junkies (e.g., veteran Paris-Dakar desert racer Olle Ohlsson, two-time enduro champ Robert Kvarnstrom) and everyday metropolitans alike. The combination of a stellar team, award-winning design paired with a very well functioning supply chain and a solid manufacturing setup, makes the company a strong candidate to become the Patagonia of motorcycles. A fresh new take that can speed up the slow-moving e-motorcycle market. At Creandum, we believe Cake has all it takes to win and we are beyond excited to support Cake's mission to inspire people to speed towards a greener society by combining excitement with responsibility. _The Creandum funds have backed several mobility startups in the past such as Voi, Bolt, Distribusion (& further still undisclosed ones). If you want to learn more, check out [creandum.com](http://creandum.com)._

articles.title: How to do due diligence on investors
articles.text: Before starting to work in Venture Capital I thought investors were the ones choosing what teams to back. A quick learning however was that great teams choose their investors. But how do successful teams go about that? Terms, resources and personal chemistry of course play a large role in this. Yet, one of the least talked about, but oh so important, aspect is to do a due diligence and reference check the people you are considering to work with for a looong period of time. You wouldn't hire someone into a key role without properly reference checking them - be as diligent when choosing investors. Let's get practical, how can you go about this? **Have a look at the team.** What does the investment team look like? Are they diverse in terms of background and experience? Ideally you would see experience from running start-ups, finance, engineering etc. Can they bring new and relevant thinking into the room? Will they complement existing investors or angels, or people you plan to bring onboard for the round? Take a look at the whole **Ask for an anti-reference.** Ask for a reference where the person(s) was involved but things went south. You will hear how they act at their worst, and it will most likely not be sugar coated. A serious investor should both be conscious about this, and willing to share. If they cannot think of such a person or occasion that's a telltale too... **Ask to be introduced to founders they have worked with before.** Ideally you would talk to people who where at a similar stage (seed, A-round etc) as you but where outcome differed e.g. - A portfolio company, where they followed up in later round - A portfolio company that raised further capital, but where they decided not to follow up - A portfolio company that failed **Dig out your own references.** Even with the holistic approach above, there might be some selection bias in what references the potential investor chooses to introduce you to. Make sure to dig out some of your own to validate the information. While doing this, be careful in not only looking for confirmation of what you heard before but rather dig deep and ask for concrete examples **Good things to ask.** If answers are generic, ask again and make sure you get concrete examples - Give an example of how xx has helped you? - When is XX at their best? How did that show? - How have you best utilized this person as an advisor? - How do they deal with conflict of interest? - How does xx act in good times? How do xx act in bad times? - What is xx level of involvement? - How much do you trust xx? - If you were to raise a similar round again, how hard would you fight to include XX over other investors? **Know what you are looking for, and make a holistic judgement.** Of course it's not black or white, there are no right or wrong answers, all investors have their strengths and weaknesses. But if you follow this you will be able to make a more informed decision and likely get more than a bag of money to run with.

articles.title: Creandum backs Shapr3D
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.text: # Creandum Shapr3D We are constantly on the lookout for products and services that delight users. _**As a first principle, it is a useful simplification to consider user love as a proxy for the adaptation of the product market.**_ In the market for CAD software, this isn't always so simple. When we met [István Csanády](https://www.linkedin.com/in/icsanady/) for the first time and got introduced to [Shapr3D ](https://www.shapr3d.com/)I really felt I'd seen something unique. Here was the most intuitive, mobile (!) 3D modelling user interface I have ever seen. So very different from another well known CAD software I fought with for seven long weeks with as an engineering intern at Sandvik in Orléans, 20 years ago. Shapr3D is intuitive, yet very versatile. Perfect for those first steps in the design process, yet powerful enough and with perfect Solidworks portability to align nicely with the downstream process. I wasn't alone. The super intuitive interface wows not only professional users such as industrial designers and architects, but also semi-professional graphic designers, game designers, and hobbyists. Today, even professors at universities are starting to teach courses based on Shapr3D. The tablet interface isn't just a better way to interact with CAD drawings, it also lends itself so well to screen capture; it's simply beautiful to watch designs come to life with the tool. And since so much of a company's value and competitiveness today is defined by how efficiently it can go to market, this made me even more intrigued and interested. As an example, the company grew their [Instagram following](https://www.instagram.com/shapr3dapp/?hl=en) to 157.000 in just a few weeks from launch. [Design influencers](https://www.shapr3d.com/story/patrick-jouin) feature the software and product videos are going viral. But there's more: the tablet-first touch interface lends itself so well to screen capture. It's simply beautiful to watch designs come to life with the tool. And since so much of a company's value and competitiveness today is defined by how efficiently they can go to market, this made me even more intrigued and interested. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.youtube.com%2Fembed%2FxmAjvfNL9mA%3Ffeature%3Doembed&url=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.youtube.com%2Fwatch%3Fv%3DxmAjvfNL9mA&image=https%3A%2F%2Fi.ytimg.com%2Fvi%2FxmAjvfNL9mA%2Fhqdefault.jpg&key=d04bfffea46d4aeda930ec88cc64b87c&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=youtube" title="" height="480" width="854"></iframe> Thus, István and his super efficient team in Budapest _**master the most desired (and least expensive) marketing channel: Word-of-mouth.**_ Of course they benefit from endorsements of the influencers of the close creative design community, but the most important factor for turning customers into evangelists is - again - the product. ![István's appearance on the #creandum-family Slack says it all](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7s2aj2VtvEklaTz6nSWUtm/f27853287c0b04c24f3197333fa7d679/image_221.png) So, in short - the reasons I am so excited to be working with István and for the Creandum funds to co-lead the Series A funding round together with Point Nine Capital are: - A product users love, by making hard things easy thanks to a drastic innovation in the user interface. - A new way to reach the market never seen before in the stale segment of CAD software, with consumer-like marketing and self-onboarding. We are beyond excited to see the Creandum funds add its first Hungarian startup to its portfolio, giving us an excuse to spend more time in this beautiful city full of startup talent. And furthermore, I'm grateful to be working together with the Shapr3D team to make 3D designing easier, cheaper, and more fun than ever before Wanna [join the ride](https://www.linkedin.com/jobs/search/?keywords=Shapr3D&location=Hungary)?

articles.title: Consumer Internet 3.0
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Privacy and Digital Consciousness
articles.text: Almost 30 years ago the Internet revolution started and the first wave of digital products and services for consumers emerged. The main innovation of the world wide web was that it allowed close to zero marginal costs to serve new users. Instead of charging consumers upfront for access, companies saw digital advertising as the holy grail and default mechanism of monetization. This was _Consumer Internet 1.0._ Things have changed. _**Consumer Internet 1.0**_ taught us to get most online products "for free". Initially, companies served relative harmless contextual ads based on the website you visited. But soon the cookie was invented to track a user across multiple websites with the purpose of better understanding the customer and serve more efficient advertising. The second phase, _**Consumer Internet 2.0**_, started roughly 15 years ago which predominantly was manifested by large social platforms like Facebook. The main difference to its predecessor was that this time, it was all about bringing the consumers' IRL identities to the online world. Over time, subsequently more information about our real lives started to emerge online, and smartphones added a critical data layer around location proximity to the mix, combined with constant online availability. These services were designed to be addictive with the purpose of collecting more data and generating more opportunities to serve ads. As consumers began to devote themselves more and more to these platforms, the power of corporates tracking this data grew increasingly stronger. Most people didn't care about sharing their data or weren't aware of any downsides to such, as the services these digital platforms provided were so alluring. So corporates over-invested in extracting more data from their users and reselling that to anyone who wanted access to it. At least until recently... ### A changing tide. During the past couple of years, a few things related to consumer data happened. 1. Regulators opened their eyes to the issues that come along with tracking individuals at scale and decided to push for better data transparency and management. GDPR, with all its flaws of actually making the large internet giants even more powerful, was the first of its kind. And we'll see more and more of these coming, with for example California's Privacy Act. 2. Consumers started to see real examples of data breaches, e.g. Equifax, Marriott, Cambridge Analytica, and many more. These events have helped the average internet user not only to understand what type of personal data companies are tracking but also to see the dangers if their data is being used unlawfully. 3. Individuals, as well as authorities, came to realize that public opinion can and is manipulated through digital platforms, which can have dramatic impacts on the world. The stakes are suddenly as large as they come! Consumer internet giants are more powerful than governments and they can and will abuse consumer data to generate more revenue. What we thought was "free" has come at a huge cost. Consumers started to realize that if they don't have to pay for an online service, they are the product! This sparks the beginning of... ## Consumer Internet 3.0. We are now entering a new era of consumer internet which is centered around 2 new dimensions: _privacy_ and _digital consciousness_. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2FFHUP0pKKDPAqc%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&url=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fgifs%2Fcat-privacy-FHUP0pKKDPAqc&image=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FFHUP0pKKDPAqc%2Fgiphy.gif&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="" height="244" width="435"></iframe> Consumers have acquired digital literacy which prevents them from accepting that all their entire online behavior is being tracked. They will opt-in and out of tracking based on the needs and value gained from specific services at the time. They will question and scrutinize the commercial, business or public need to collect specific data, forcing companies to stick to the most essential tracking to justify their product value. Hence, companies have to start to provide more transparency around what data they collect and why they do it and integrate this communication into the product experience. Also, although companies will continue to try and attract as many eyeballs to their services as often as they can, they will be held accountable for digital addiction behaviors. Consumers (+ regulators) will expect there are ways to limit and counter behavior which is potentially destructive, similar to what some betting and gambling companies have had to do to manage gambling addiction. According to us, **this is the largest shift in consumer internet behavior we have seen since the invention of the world wide web.** "Free in exchange for data" will no longer be the assumed default way for consumers and companies to engage online. For consumers who choose not to share data, alternative business models will emerge using paid access. A completely new cohort of consumer internet companies will be created by those who navigate making privacy and data consciousness a core part of their user experience. Of course, all internet services will not be placed behind paid walls, and digital advertising is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Nor will the big internet platforms which are built upon consumer data tracking vanish in the near-term. And all trackers are not bad and infringing on personal privacy as [outlined by Stratechery](https://stratechery.com/2019/privacy-fundamentalism/?utm_source=Memberful&utm_campaign=51fe60fa86-weekly_article_2019_08_27&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_d4c7fece27-51fe60fa86-110949001). However, while there will still continue to be demand for free services using traditional consumer internet models for certain users and products, we are excited about the emerging opportunities this shift in consumer mentality creates for innovative comp

articles.title: #1 How To… Run Effective Board Meetings
articles.text: At Creandum, we back teams and ideas at an early stage. To support founders along this journey, we introduced a new **#How To...** series of events. We invite role models from our network to share personal experiences with the goal to inspire and support members and friends of the Creandum family. Our **#1 How To...** event gave personal insights into running effective board meetings, together with [Vania Schlogel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/vania-schlogel-26354641/), Founding and Managing Partner at [Atwater Capital](https://www.atwater-capital.com/). Vania is part of the #creandumfamily as Chair at [Epidemic Sound](https://www.epidemicsound.com/) and has an outstanding track record of running boards, including [LEONINE](https://leoninemediagroup.com/). Life has been an exciting journey for her mixed with ups and downs, which she didn't shy away from sharing. Prior to starting her own fund, she collected a wealth of experience at firms such as Goldman Sachs, KKR and as Chief Investment Officer of Roc Nation (Jay Z's investment arm). Here are some of Vania's key takeaways for founders and board members: **When you're first starting off as a founder:** 1. **Pick your board wisely:** You're about to enter a long-term relationship! Make sure to look for a diverse group of individuals with different functional and geographical backgrounds. The board at Epidemic Sound, for example, constitutes a variety of experts - early and later-stage investors as well as industry experts. This has allowed for invaluable discussions and diverse perspectives along the company's growth trajectory. 2. **Build informal relationships beyond the board room:** Take your board outside the office to connect on a more personal level over lunch and dinner. This will help form a stronger bond and build trust over time. Once you can build on these relationships, sharing realities' ups and downs will be easier. It will also help understand push back as feedback rather than critique. 3. **Be transparent:** Don't turn your board meetings into marketing campaigns. Share not only the good news but also the bad and ugly bits. "_**Transparency is like a muscle that needs to be built up but it will prove invaluable."**_ Expect a lot of constructive criticism and don't shy away from asking for help. Make sure to present challenges alongside recommendations or scenarios, so your board can give more valuable input. 4. **Communicate regularly:** Provide your board with monthly updates. Don't wait with big bangs until quarterly board meetings. Focus your regular updates on what's most important - the top 2–3 ups & downs will usually be sufficient. 5. **Keep networking:** You never know when and where you might meet your next potential board members. If you're still at an early stage aim for senior advisors to bridge the time before you introduce an official board. **Running and chairing a board:** 1. **The liaison & plug-in point:** as a Chair, you are the link between management and the board. Managing both parties efficiently and keeping them connected brings tremendous value to everyone involved. 2. **Do your homework:** Live your role as an informed board member, asked for previous board materials when your first join, always check pre-reads and stay on top of industry news. This includes subscribing to newsletters (yes, and reading them!). Informed questions from an investors' perspective help founders take a step back from daily operations and look at the bigger picture. 3. **Challenge the team**: Master the "good cop, bad cop game" and challenge the team respectfully (you don't want management to go into turtle mode either). Encourage candid discussions and dig deeper if you feel board meetings only touch on glossy business highlights. 4. **Governance structures matter**: Recent hiccups in a number of tech companies keep proving the need for solid governance structures. The board has a duty to ensure they're in place, and increasing diversity on boards is likely to help achieve a better service. To find out more about what to do before, during and after board meetings and how to get the most out of your board, read more [here](https://blog.creandum.com/getting-most-out-of-your-board-as-a-seed-or-series-a-entrepreneur-e79e6b0f51b4). If you're looking for guidance with your board deck, also check out Creandum's board deck template [here.](https://blog.creandum.com/board-deck-template-4dbaf77969ab) Stay tuned for our **#2 How To....** event and shoot us a message with topic suggestions you want to learn more about → hello@creandum.com! Last but not least, a big shout out to Vania for sharing her personal insights so generously with us in Stockholm!

articles.title: Why healthcare & tech are a long-lasting relationship
articles.author: Staffan Helgesson
articles.text: _The healthcare market is facing a massive transition at the moment. Telemedicine, remote monitoring and self-tracking are at the forefront - leaving a slow, intransparent and inefficient sector behind. Global VC funding of digital health companies in 1H 2019 was [USD 5.1bn compared to USD 4.9bn in 1H 2018](https://mercomcapital.com/product/q2-2019-digital-health-healthcare-it-funding-and-ma-report) - indicating the increasing interest in the space. Globally healthcare is a massive market being approximately 10% of GDP in Sweden and all the way to 18% in the US._ _At Creandum we believe in the power of technology to radically transform industries for a better future. Hence, we are taking an active part in fueling the advancements in digital healthcare by having backed already three game-changing companies in the digital health sector KRY (LIVI), Careship, and Virta._ _With the Creandum Fund's investments in [Firstvet](https://firstvet.com/), we are taking it even one step further since we believe telemedicine goes beyond humans. Aliens? No. Pets! That's why we're thrilled to announce the [€18.5M Series B round of FirstVet](https://techcrunch.com/2019/11/06/firstvet-series-b/), the video appointment platform revolutionizing the pet care industry. As an early partner (Creandum Funds led the A-round), we're excited to continue the journey with this Swedish originated disrupter. The B-round was led by Omers Ventures with the main objective of further accelerating international expansion after the company has already conquered the Scandinavian and UK markets._ Of course, we love to have a justification for using more [puppy gifs](https://blog.creandum.com/creandum-backs-firstvet-puppy-gifs-c5d95098f52), but what are the real benefits of digital healthcare companies like FirstVet or [KRY](https://www.kry.se/en/) and why do we believe they are here to stay? ## A set of hypotheses underline this belief: **1. It's On-Demand** First, there is no doubt that digitizing doctor or vet appointments through telemedicine makes for a smoother, more accessible and efficient journey for both the patient and the doctor. In an era where you can have anything from watching your favorite movie to eating the best Sushi at home at the time that best fits your busy schedule, we think healthcare should be too. Convenience is key irrespective if you are furry or not. Mobile is the solution, given global penetration of mobile phone usage has reached [almost 70%](https://www.statista.com/statistics/284202/mobile-phone-internet-user-penetration-worldwide/). KRY masters this for humans and FirstVet for pets (and their owners) and makes access to professional doctors/vets available at any time no matter where you live. **2. Empowerment of the patients** The digitalization of healthcare enables patients to become more involved in their own patient journey. In particular with the rise of wearable smart devices (fitness trackers, pulse trackers, etc.), it turns patients into leaders being able to control their health themselves. Power to the patients! As our Investment Manager Sanna has previously concluded, this is especially interesting in the space of[chronic diseases](https://blog.creandum.com/why-tech-should-focus-more-on-chronic-diseases-3864047f995a) where self-tracking and remote monitoring helps enable continuous treatment. Instead of trying to summarize the symptoms you have had the last 6 months on the yearly 15 minutes doctor's appointment on average - self-tracking provides data points that form a solid foundation for decision making - facilitating treatments for both patient and doctor. **3. Individually tailored medicine** Due to the new solutions to track individual health, the amount of data will eventually lead to more preventive and personalized healthcare. Digital health tools mean more and better data on personal metrics that can be collected and shared with physicians to allow them to analyze the results, and adjust their management accordingly to the individual, making medicine more tailored to their specific needs. Perfect for our society moving away from one-size-fits-all products in search of products tailored to suit their individual needs, preferences, and lifestyle choices. **4. Big Data fuels medical innovations** The newly available amount of health-related data could potentially prove a treasure trove for scientists trying to improve public health. The data gathered by wearables and digital health tracking apps will provide clinical studies with a larger research foundation - hopefully leading to medical advances and innovations. Blockchain will play an instrumental role in this development - keeping electronic health records accurate and safe. **5. Lower costs of healthcare provision** While it would be reassuring to imagine digital healthcare was designed for the altruistic purpose of keeping people healthier for longer, the ultimate aim of using digital health to manage illnesses and chronic conditions is to cut providers cost by reducing the amount of administrative tasks, doctor's appointments, emergency room visits and even hospital admissions that people with such illnesses need. Summing up, what makes the digital healthcare revolution so interesting for Creandum is that it's a win-win for everyone: Patients, pets, pet-owners as well as their healthcare providers. We hope to back more companies like FirstVet and KRY who aim to disrupt healthcare by making it more accessible, efficient and all in all, better. _Are you building an exciting startup that has the potential to become a billion-dollar company in the digital health space? [Ping me](https://www.creandum.com/team/staffan-helgesson) and let's have a chat!_

articles.title: Caroline Ingeborn joins Creandum as Entrepreneur-In-Residence
articles.text: At Creandum we strive at working with the best entrepreneurs in the world. Therefore, we are very excited to welcome a new entrepreneur to our #Creandumfamily - **Caroline Ingeborn** - who will join our team as an **Entrepreneur-In-Residence** **(EIR)**. An EIR is a part-time member of the investment advisory team helping Creandum to evaluate investment opportunities for the Creandum Funds or develop new investment themes to focus on. In exchange, as an EIR at Creandum, Caroline will have a platform and be part of an exciting ecosystem to figure out and develop thoughts around her next startup. Caroline not only has had immense success as CEO having built and grown the kids' app company [Toca Boca](https://tocaboca.com/) with millions of users worldwide, she also brings valuable experience from building a start-up both in Scandinavia and in the US. As Caroline is currently transitioning out of Toca Boca we had a brief talk on her past experience and what she is looking for next: 1. _Toca Boca was such an amazing success but also an odd one as it started as a corporate venture. Tell us briefly how it got started and where it is now?_ _Toca Boca was founded out of the Bonnier Group in Stockholm by Björn Jeffrey and Emil Ovemar who set out to make apps for kids with a toyetic aspect, something we call digital toys. It is hard to replicate as it was the perfect storm of a team of two with a vision, talent, and high ambitions in combination with management at the Bonnier group who fully supported their vision._ _Today, the Toca Boca group consist of two brands; Sago Mini for kids age 2–5 and Toca Boca for kids age 6+. Together the two brands reach almost 24 million monthly active users across platforms. The company is growing fast and is profitable with the new owners investing in the brands' future._ _2. What are the most important learning from growing Toca Boca?_ _There's so many, but the two most important ones are:_ _**1. Vision, mission and values matter a lot**._ _At Toca Boca believing in the power of play focusing on quality, play and diversity early on was a great decision. However, it took us a long time to really understand what this meant to us and how to work with it. Two reasons why this is very important and beneficial:_ _First, once you have set your mission, vision and values all of the decisions that you have to make on a daily basis can be tested against those. That makes decision making easier, more efficient and fun._ _Second, it makes business sense. We have seen a direct relationship between doing things according to our values and increased growth although this strategy was questioned a lot by other people in the kids' industry._ _On a personal level, it is also what has motivated me a lot to grow Toca Boca since I could fully stand behind those values._ _**2. Know when it is time to move on.**_ _At Toca Boca, we experienced a big shift in the market in terms of spending behaviour of parents in the app store that meant we needed to change our business models. Unfortunately, we hesitated and waited a long time to move to a new business model even though we knew this was happening. Eventually, it meant that we had to pivot in a bigger way when we moved. Luckily, we were able to do this successfully but next time I hope to act sooner when market conditions change._ _3. Having worked both in Europe as well as in the US, what do you think of both start-up ecosystems and where do you see the biggest differentiators?_ _I think there are more similarities than differentiators. These days, the Nordics and probably most of Europe, are on a par with the US with high-quality teams, product ideas and ambitions. A difference though is that the scale in the US is bigger. For example, I see large pre-seed rounds that I rarely hear about in Europe. Teams are larger and move more aggressively on growth. The scale also means that there are so many more people in the ecosystem, which leads to opportunities for specialization that Europe cannot support. Funnily though, one thing where the US is exactly like Sweden, despite the scale, everyone knows everyone._ _4. How do you think you can help the founders of young companies we're working with at Creandum most?_ _For a long time, I thought the challenges we had at Toca Boca were very unique, but of course, this is not true. I have found that having a sounding board can be very helpful, especially when they have been on similar journeys. Some explicit things I am looking forward to help other teams with are:_ _Turn a product into a business. Creating a product that millions of people engage with is very hard. Ensuring that it is also a sustainable business is equally hard._ _Understand and learn from my lessons on how to lead and scale cross-functional teams across locations while at the same time scaling oneself. It is completely different from leading a single functional team._ _Become Mission-driven. It sounds simple in theory, but it is ridiculously difficult in practice. It is also never "done" but needs to be continuously nurtured._ _5. What kind of areas excite you most when you think about your next startup?_ _Coming from the kids' space, at this moment, I am going to cross the spectrum completely to focus on a space that I have loosely defined as 55 to 100-year-olds. I don't know what this will entail yet but I am super excited to find out. If there is anyone out there interested in this space or already doing something, [ping me](https://www.linkedin.com/in/carolineingeborn)!_ _6. How do you think being part of Creandum will benefit you and help you develop new ideas?_ _I have known the Creandum team for some time and I am excited to join this group of stellar people. I'm sure I will benefit from their platform and ecosystem but it's also amazing to have access to great sounding boards as I develop my ideas. I look forward to honest constructive feedback to help me move forward and become better faster._ _Creandum is thrilled to h

articles.title: How to raise your next funding round
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Often I get asked questions around how to plan the next fundraising and how to best approach VCs. I summarised my thoughts on some of the key steps in a fundraise below. Tipps are mainly geared towards **Seed and Series A**, but many aspects also applicable for later stages. You can see this as a rough guideline / fundraising ABC, but as always, every round and situation is different (so don't blame me if it didn't work ;P). ### I. How should I plan my fundraise? 1. Take a step back: Is VC money actually the right thing for you? Raising VC money is not the best option for every business. It depends on the type and size of the business you plan to build. Remember, larger VCs typically search for companies that aim to become bn$ businesses. They look for founders that want to go down the high-risk route and shoot for the stars. For some businesses, it's more attractive to build lean, lower-risk well-running cash cows. From a financial perspective, both can be similarly attractive routes to founders. Take this example: Huffington Post was acquired for $314m and the founder received about $18m. Techcrunch was sold to the same buyer for $30m, yet the founder made $24m. Think about what is right for you (+ read more[ here](https://hackernoon.com/do-not-raise-vc-funding-3-reasons-against-it-7c5f6d4efbec)). That being said, if it's right for you - a VC can be a fantastic catalyst and partner to help you build the next big thing. 2. Set goals: Why do you want or need to raise a round and what do you want to achieve with it? Know what you need the money for. ### II. When is the best time to start fundraising? 1. Seed stage: As soon as you need it and know what to do with the cash (i.e. what hires you want to do, how to spend on marketing) 2. Series A and later: Latest 6 months before you run out of cash account 2–4 months for the full process (+ min. 2 months buffer). Once you have received the term sheet calculate 4 weeks for legal due diligence, drafting agreements and closing. Getting the term sheet can take time. In the fastest cases, you get it within a couple of days/weeks, but that's rare. It can take weeks to get appointments with your preferred VCs and you don't want to go with just any option. You want to fall in love with the "right" VC for you. As in real life, things can go wrong or unexpected events can happen during a process, even for the best performers. Hence, plan in buffer time, it will prevent you from running out of cash and it gives you a stronger negotiation position. 3. Series B and later: Anytime you have achieved your goals since your last round (e.g. grew revenue multifold within a year). Or you have great growth momentum or a good plan on how to make good use of more money to scale even faster. Latest 6 months before your bank account is empty. 4. In general, high performing VC backed companies tend to raise every 8–18 months. ### III. What do I need to prepare? 1. Material: A pitch deck and a financial plan (historic data and forecast, ideally as an excel) is the least you should have. Be well prepared with backup data on your most important metrics (e.g. conversion rates, retention cohorts). Invest enough time to build a well-thought-through and visually appealing pitch deck. Consider to get help from one of the designers in your team or pay a designer from Upwork if necessary (it's worth it). 2. Get feedback for your pitch deck from other entrepreneurs or befriended VCs, do several feedback rounds to improve it. It‘s your key marketing material that needs to spark an investor's interest within the few couple of minutes he spends screening it. 3. Know the legal s***: This is only relevant for the later stage of the fundraising, but make yourself familiar with term sheets and standard terms to get ready for discussions. Get legal advice from a professional lawyer (specialized on venture deals) to review term sheet, investment and shareholder agreements. And yes you need to spend money on this, but it's worth it. ### IV. How much money should I raise? 1. Rule of thumb: Make a realistic plan for how much money you need for the next 18–24 months. Add 10–20% buffer on top - plans are either way always wrong ;) 2. Common early-stage round sizes that we see today in Europe - Pre-seed/angel round: €300k–1m - Seed round: €1–4m - Series A: €8–15m 3. Remember: Bigger is not always better. If you are too ambitious in your funding size goals it can backfire and VCs might decline. You don't want to return a couple of weeks later saying that you are raising less. The hurdle to make a VC reconsider within a couple of weeks is much higher than convincing them the first time. ### V. How much should I dilute per round? 1. In Seed and A rounds: Expect to dilute 18–25% per round depending on how much you raise and how big the market interest is. 2. B rounds and later: can be slightly less than in Seed and A, expect a range of 15–20% in the B and less later on. ### VI. How should I reach out? 1. Research: Compile a list of funds, which are relevant (!) for you. Ideally, it should be a minimum of 20 funds. Check that these funds are investing in your stage, have the right size and match your geography and sector. 2. Prioritize: Rank the funds in order of who you would prefer most: Top 5, 5–10,10–20 and 20+ 3. Approach the funds in waives: a) Test the water: Start with 1–2 funds that are not in your top 5. It will help you to see how VCs perceive your pitch. You will get better in pitching over time (VCs tend to ask similar questions, makes it easy for you to prepare and finetune your answers). You want to maximize the chances of your most preferred funds. b) Time to thrive: Reach out to your top 10 and go down the list until several ones are hooked. c) Don't get comfortable too early: Most VCs will initially tell you that they love your idea. Don't get to flattered by that early interest - it is not a commitment. Continue to run your process with other funds. 4. Get intros: No matter wheth

articles.title: Speed interview with Cake founder Stefan Ytterborn
articles.author: Staffan Helgesson
articles.text: At Creandum, we believe any industry can be disrupted by the right entrepreneur at the right time. Stefan Ytterborn is clearly one of them. He is a textbook example of a serial founder: After successfully establishing the no.1 brand for ski helmets, [P.O.C.](https://www.pocsports.com/) (yes, P.O.C. stands for Piece Of [Cake](https://ridecake.com/)), he is now turning a new industry upside down with his now seventh (!) company: Stefan is designing and producing electric motorcycles under the delicious new short-form of P.O.C: Cake. At our Annual Berlin Dinner, we've speed-interviewed him about the drivers of his daily motivation, his biggest learnings and advice for founders. **1. Why did you start your latest company Cake?** When you think of the motorcycling industry, a roaring, aggressive, macho and dirty world likely comes to mind. It's also a complex and conservative culture full of excluding aspects and behaviours. My ultimate mission with Cake is to turn this upside down. The first time I encountered an electric motorcycle, 7 years ago, I realized it's time for a change in the motorcycling space. I saw it as a new challenge, went out and got 15 electric motorbikes, everything that was in the market at that time, to learn about existing products. Seeing this potential for innovation motivated me to develop a new and better product for the emerging needs of future customers. With Cake, we're thriving to inspire a new breed of users towards zero-emission, combining responsibility with excitement. **2. What makes you a good entrepreneur?** I've always been driven by curiosity and the longing for bringing purpose and change to the world. Paired with my high level of impatience, I guess there simply was no better career path for me. I just couldn't live without the speed and dynamic you're navigating towards your targets as an entrepreneur. I enjoy being in control of my own success. To sum it up, my personal formula of entrepreneurial success is purpose, quality, performance and innovation filtered in style. **3. What gets you out of bed every day?** My unstoppable ambition is my engine that keeps me going day after day. You should think about your vision and purpose, not only for your company but also for your personal life. Clearly defining it is crucial to keep the fire burning. I wake up every morning to bring meaning and innovation to our users and to some extent, to the society at large. If there's no purpose behind your actions and ideas, they won't fly. **4. What's the biggest learning from founding seven companies?** Rely on your gut feeling. Learn to trust your instincts. It may imply uncertainty and doesn't guarantee a good outcome but neither does a purely rational decision. As an entrepreneur, you're faced with decision-making all day long and most of the times you need to act quick. Hence, my advice is to spend a fair amount of time to learn to listen to your inner feeling and continuously work on making snap judgements. **5. First P.O.C., now Cake - What is your advice to building successful global brands?** Purpose and perseverance are the most evident. Sticking to that with consistency, continuity and clarity, is key. **6. With cake and previous products, you have received endorsement and appreciation from some of the world's largest celebrities (Madonna, Kanye West, just to name a few). What's the trick?** It's not my primary intention to appeal to celebrities. However, the fact that we are able to attract them is an amazing asset I´m extremely grateful for. It's a great boost for attention, recognition and aspiration. However, on a personal level, I´m much more energized by receiving approval by someone who's a product expert in the categories we're navigating in and truely has the skills of judging the product and its performance. My explanation for winning the heart of any kind of customer is simple and has been my key compass throughout my career: An excellent product takes care of itself. **7. What keeps you up at night?** Ambiguity. The question of when to accelerate and when to hold. The right timing is crucial for the success of your startup. **8. What's your leadership advice to entrepreneurs?** Trust yourself. Be honest to yourself. Bombard your idea with criticism. Work it through and then clean it up. No one but you, the entrepreneur, has spent more time turning things around and will, therefore, stand strong when confronting potential partners, investors, customers and other stakeholders.

articles.title: Creandum backs Laka
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Turning an industry upside down
articles.text: If you happen to operate in the world of startups there are two things you hear more or less daily: "change the world" and "disruption". This is the mantra of Silicon Valley. Build something from the ground up in a unique and different way and thereby completely change an industry or a market. It's a very compelling idea, but the reality is that most startups aren't true disruptors. They rather have an incremental impact on an industry. Over the last decade, we've seen a handful of companies do this; Airbnb within temporary accommodation industry, Uber for transportation, and Creandum portfolio company Spotify for music. Those who truly disrupt their industry, create outside returns. This is why when we meet companies who objectively aspire to change an industry we pay close attention. Today we couldn't be more excited to announce that Creandum V is investing in [Laka](https://www.laka.co.uk/), which is exactly one of these ideas. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1mmdI9BEyVERDFQmOjUQxB/e0dbff52dae9099e7bde24c8a715638d/image_220.png) ### The flaws of modern insurance. The insurance model was born in the late 17th century after the great fires of London. The first policies were therefore centered around property insurance. The business model back then is strikingly similar to what it is today. In fact, the oldest insurance company still active today was [founded in 1710](https://web.archive.org/web/20110902071509/http://www.rsagroup.com/rsa/pages/aboutus/history). (This speaks to great lengths about the _disruption_ that the industry has faced since.) Unfortunately, this unchanged model still has lots of flaws. These flaws lead to a profound distrust of insurance companies. At the heart of this issue lies a profound conflict of interest between insurance companies and the people they insure. When you get an insurance cover, you typically pay a monthly premium for the coverage you need, and if anything unforeseen happens you make a claim with the hope that the insurance company reimburses you. On the other hand, insurers make money on the difference between premiums collected and claims paid out, meaning they have a strong financial incentive _not to pay_ their policyholders. This is not trivial. Rarely do businesses become more profitable by delivering precisely against the promise of their customers, which is true for the insurance market. ### The flip. So is there a way to align incentives between policyholders and insurers? Well, Laka and Creandum truly believe so and it comes dow to....no monthly premiums! Instead of charging monthly premiums, customers commit to sharing the total cost of claims when something happens. Laka targets communities of customers who basically aggregated their individual risks into a pool, and equally share the cost burden when something unforeseen happens. As for Laka, instead of collecting a misaligned spread between premiums and claims, their business model involves charging a percentage on top of monthly claims. The end result is a beautiful and transparent insurance model that incentives Laka to process and pay claims as quickly and accurately as possible...and by the way it also becomes ≈40% cheaper than traditional insurance. Laka is starting out within the specific insurance vertical of bike and bike equipment across the UK, and people love them. They have thousands of customers across the UK and an unprecedented [4.99 out of 5 's](https://smartmoneypeople.com/laka-reviews/product/cycle-insurance) customer satisfaction! On the back of this Laka will soon expand to new geographies (hold tight ), as well as adding new insurance products to their offering shortly. We couldn't be more thrilled to partner with [Tobi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tobiastaupitz/), [Ben](https://www.linkedin.com/in/benallenuk/), and [Jens](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jenshartwigde/) on this journey, together with our friends at [LocalGlobe](http://localglobe.com/) and [Yes.vc](http://yes.vc/). <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2FoWwh3BkVbumeA%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&display_name=Giphy&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FoWwh3BkVbumeA%2Fgiphy.gif&image=https%3A%2F%2Fi.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2FoWwh3BkVbumeA%2Fgiphy.gif&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="Laka...flipping the insurance industry upside down...starting with bikes! " height="244" width="435"></iframe> For more information on the funding and the team's expansion plans check out [Laka's blog](https://blog.laka.co.uk/2020/02/06/announcing-our-recent-funding-round/) or [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/laka-cycling-insurtech-raises-new-funds-from-localglobe-and-creandum-2020-2?r=US&IR=T).

articles.title: Hotter Than Hot Flashes
articles.excerpt: The Menopause Market
articles.text: Today, the taboo of talking about menstruation and fertility is slowly starting to break (at least in some parts of the world). Encouragingly, this leads to increased [investments in female health](https://www.forbes.com/sites/reenitadas/2019/09/24/is-technology-pink-investments-in-femtech-to-cross-the-13-billion-mark-in-2020/#2eb29e475205). Yet, this area still accounts for only a small part of the total health funding. Additionally, the majority of funding has gone into women's reproductive health, focusing on periods, contraception, and fertility. As these are "top of mind" areas to the target group of digital natives, this probably does not come as a surprise. However, we are about to enter an era where women who have become used to leveraging digital solutions to manage their health are now entering menopause. But suddenly they have to deal with it themselves, or if they are lucky, get an appointment with a family doctor who very likely has little or no knowledge of the process. Menopause still has a very limited place in public life. We at Creandum believe that it is time for menopause to enter the 21st century. ## "Is the market big enough?" When looking at a company, this is one of the most commonly asked questions for the typical VC firm. In a handful of cases, the market is intuitively very big, and you would think how absurd it is that it still may be underserved. The menopause market is definitely one of those. In the abstract, the idea of a period in life which 50% of the population has to pass, albeit with different levels of symptoms, should be enough to give an instinctive feeling of how much leverage may exist. On top of that, women are [living longer and longer](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/life-expectancy-of-women-vs-life-expectancy-of-women), and by [2025 there will be over 1 billion women](https://www.forbes.com/sites/reenitadas/2019/07/24/menopause-unveils-itself-as-the-next-big-opportunity-in-femtech/#6fb9b7b86535) in the world going through menopause, a staggering 12% of the entire world population. Symptoms of menopause can vary but the three (of a total 34!) most common ones are hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and insomnia, [with up to 85% of women](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4890704/) experience hot flashes. Only in the UK, the associated costs for sick-leave [amounted to 7.3 MGBP](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/07/21/menopause-costs-economy-millions-every-year-bosses-do-not-understand/), and the number is probably largely underestimated due to stigma and consequent silence. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/42iSW2pedC6ZjWj2URbOhI/144099434d6aeb663c3cc13413631890/image_217.png) Big market potential - check. Second most asked VC question: Is it good timing to look deeper into this market? At Creandum, we absolutely think so for several different reasons: ### 1. The health-conscious and digitally savvy Generation X is approaching menopause Generation X is [more health-conscious](https://www.statnews.com/2017/04/03/generation-x-health-care/) than the preceding generations. This age group also represents a large amount of [spending power](https://blog.euromonitor.com/generation-x-a-small-but-mighty-generation/), especially women, who make most of a households' purchase decisions. Moreover, Generation X is digitally savvy and used to solving problems with smartphones. We expect this group to push for changes within menopause health care, with willingness to spend money and openness to try new solutions, be it digital or something else. ### 2. More women executives in the workforce - employers better deal with it The number of female managers and executives is increasing. The [Fortune 500 has more female](https://fortune.com/2019/05/16/fortune-500-female-ceos/) CEOs than ever before, and with more women in the workplace awareness for menopause is inevitably increasing. How women are able to go through this transition impacts both the employee's well-being and the company's performance. Some companies offer specific health support for their employees during the transition, and others have started to include menopause as a reason for absence to increase transparency and openness. Over time, we expect menopause awareness to continue to increase, in turn generating a growing demand for new solutions. ### 3. Scarcity within menopause professionals and relevant treatments remains According to the [New England Journal of Medicine](https://hub.jhu.edu/gazette/2013/june/news-menopause-medicine-training-needed/), medical graduates and primary care practitioners do not get enough training to support women during menopause. In addition to that, clinics specialised in [menopause are scarce](https://www.theguardian.com/careers/2019/may/02/menopause-health-has-few-specialists-and-a-lot-of-myths-can-tech-change-that). If you eventually get to see a doctor there are limited options for treatment to select from and the most common, hormone replacement therapy, is not considered safe for everyone to use. In areas where there is a demand but a lack of supply - we all know what is bound to happen - new solutions emerge. So far cultural silence has suppressed demand, but based on the reasons mentioned above it is highly unlikely the status-quo will remain. ### 4.
