Product success is not equal to building the perfect product. The product or service exists within a larger system - the business. It does not only have to be loved by its users, but it also needs to support a scalable marketing and sales model, as well as a sustainable business and pricing model. Further, it needs to align with any internal operational constraints you may have (at iZettle anything related to Payments came along with a lot of compliance to consider)._ _**2. Be humble and quickly test for success.**_ _In product development, there is rarely one right answer. Let the end-user solve the points that you are debating internally. You don't have to A/B-test every little decision or dismiss your own opinion, but instead, identify your most impactful decisions and use your intuition to form your base hypothesis on what to do. Be upfront about what success looks like and what action to take if you don't see success - sometimes this requires brutal honesty. Do it to reach a better decision quickly, instead of getting stuck in an endless debate._ _**3. Build simple tools that scale from day one.**_ _Don't put all your faith in tools and frameworks, but make sure you have a few simple ones in place early to help scale your business as it grows. Ultimately, you want to maintain the speed of decision making and adaptability that are intrinsic to most start-ups. Empower your people to deliver value - you want the people closest to the problem to solve it - you won't have time for it as a founder. Build a strong vision and constantly communicate it. Have clear and transparent goals (including a north star). Product principles can help delegate hard decisions, providing your teams with confidence on how to move forward. Accountability for goals and commitments should be crystal clear, not as a system of control, but rather as a way to extract learnings, from both wins and failures._ _**3. Why did you decide to leave your CPO role? What are you up to now?**_ _I have had a plan to start my own company for quite some time. Leaving the CPO role now was part of that longer-term plan, as well as building a venture in an industry other than FinTech. I'm still in the inspiration phase and excited to join Creandum to get to know many different industries. I have recently become quite interested in education, and I've always had an eye on the energy sector. These two are vastly different but what unites them is the potential impact they could have on society's general wellbeing._ _**4. How do you think being part of Creandum will benefit you in sharpening your company building goals?**_ _I left iZettle with a set of startup ideas that derived from where I was at that time: Opportunities in adjacent spaces to whe

articles.title: Time to cool the planet
articles.excerpt: Creandum’s perspective on Climate Tech
articles.text: **7 years and 103 days.** The famous clock in Union Square in NY that had been tracking the time of day since 1999 was reset to show a new countdown: the very limited time we have left to take meaningful action and avert the irreversible consequences of climate change. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?type=text%2Fhtml&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&schema=twitter&url=https%3A//twitter.com/theclimateclock/status/1307752210609123330&image=" title="" height="281" width="500"></iframe> The global pandemic has done the first step to help (temporarily) decrease emissions by an [estimated 5–10 % in 2020](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2020/coronavirus-climate-impact-green-recovery?linkId=100323270) (the largest drop since WWII). **Now** **it's on us to make sure we use the slim time frame we have left to drastically reduce emissions (by at least removing as much carbon as we emit) and limit global warming to well below 2°C** - the target set out in the Paris Agreement to avoid climate breakdown. At [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/), we believe software will play a crucial role when it comes to tackling the Climate Crisis. Many entrepreneurs share that view and have set out to fight the crisis hands on. We tried to understand what is happening in Climate Tech - broadly speaking, tech solutions that help reduce greenhouse gas emissions - and map the market. ## Three forces driving innovation to fight the climate crisis. There is a global cry for solutions to save our planet. The urgency behind this fight has triggered three shifts in the market that are driving climate-positive agendas and are working to decarbonise our economy. **1 - Investors: Pools of capital are increasingly flowing to environment-focused companies.** A growing pool of VCs, PEs and corporate investors is dedicating parts or entire funds to climate-conscious businesses. The list is long, but to give you a flavor: - [Amazon launched The Climate Pledge Fund, a $2bn internal VC fund](https://www.wsj.com/articles/amazon-to-launch-2-billion-venture-capital-fund-to-invest-in-clean-energy-11592910001) focused on technology investments to fight climate change (just months after Jeff Bezos committed $10bn of his own funds to a climate-friendly effort named the Bezos Earth Fund). - TPG founded [The RISE Fund](https://therisefund.com/) with $4bn under management to specifically invest in companies that measurably drive social and environmental impact. - [Pale Blue Dot just launched a $53m preseed and seed fund](https://techcrunch.com/2020/06/16/european-vc-firm-pale-blue-dot-plans-to-fund-40-planet-positive-startups/) to back climate positive ventures. - YC launched a dedicated request for [startups working on Carbon Removal Technologies](http://carbon.ycombinator.com/). **This is translating into an increasing number of financing rounds in environmentally-focused ventures.** According to Dealroom, from 2013–2019 $60 bn of early-stage capital was invested globally into startups tackling the climate challenge. In 2019 investments amounted to $16 bn. This equated to approx. 6% of total VC capital invested that year (and was up from $418 million in 2013). Recent examples include [Ecovadis](https://www.wsj.com/articles/cvc-earmarks-200-million-for-esg-ratings-provider-ecovadis-11578569401) ($200m to accelerate the adoption of sustainability ratings), [Climeworks](https://www.privateequitywire.co.uk/2020/09/02/289158/investment-climeworks-reaches-chf100m) ($75m round for their carbon direct-air capture & removal technology) and Berlin-based [Planetly](https://www.eu-startups.com/2020/04/planetly-nabs-e5-2-million-to-help-companies-become-climate-neutral/) (€5m seed for B2B software helping to calculate and reduce a company's footprint). **2 - Governmental agreements and regulatory changes are coming into force.** **Governmental policies and regulations** increasingly **** obligate countries and companies to combat global warming and to track, report and reduce carbon emissions. More than [40 countries](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/04/02/climate/pricing-carbon-emissions.html) have adopted methods to put a price on carbon through direct taxes and/or cap-and-trade programmes (A system in which the government sets an overall limit on yearly carbon emissions. Companies that exceed those levels can purchase emission permits from other companies with low emissions). Some examples: - the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS). A cap and trade scheme that is mandatory across many sectors, covers [11,000 businesses responsible for 45% of the EU's emissions](https://ec.europa.eu/clima/policies/ets_en). - China, who has been experimenting with cap-and-trade programs since 2011, is planning to gradually roll it out nationwide starting this year. - Britain's Climate Change Act was amended in 2019 and now requires the UK to reach [net-zero emissions](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-becomes-first-major-economy-to-pass-net-zero-emissions-law#:~:text=The%20UK%20today%20became%20the,80%25%20reduction%20from%201990%20levels.) by 2050 (i.e. removing as much carbon as they emit). Sooner rather than later, regulation will force nations and corporations to introduce and abide by net-zero strategies. Tools to help them accomplish these goals in an efficient, scalable and reliable manner will be highly sought-after. **3 - Business leaders are taking proactive strategic and operative measures.** Companies are facing increasing scrutiny from consumers, employees, and investors to take climate action (such as [BlackRock](https://www.ft.com/content/8809032d-47a1-47c3-ae88-ef3c182134c0), which recently punished 53 of their portfolio companies for climate inaction). As a result, a number of companies have produced ambitious plans to decarbonize their operations and supply chains. Typically, these strategies focus on a company's goal to reach net-zero emissions and entail: 1. **Increasing transparency**, such as through publish

articles.title: Getting from Seed to Series A
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Transitioning from an initial Seed investment to the Series A round is a critical step for the long-term success of many ventures. How many companies make it? What are the strategies to get there? Some insights from the Creandum funds portfolio: ### Conversion from Seed to A A while ago, Dealroom published an interesting report on this journey and it inspired us to take a deeper look at the Creandum fund's portfolio. [Dealroom's research](https://blog.dealroom.co/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/The-Journey-to-Series-A-in-Europe.pdf) showed that the conversion rate from Seed to Series A varies widely by seed investor. On average, only 19% of European startups reach Series A after raising their seed round, whereas for the top investor quartile, the median conversion rate is 40%. <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?type=text%2Fhtml&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&schema=twitter&url=https%3A//twitter.com/dealroomco/status/1093159421319016448&image=" title="" height="281" width="500"></iframe> After seeing this report, we got intrigued and wanted to analyze how this looks for the Creandum funds' portfolio companies. Approximately half of the Creandum funds' initial investments are seed. We took the [methodology](https://blog.dealroom.co/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/The-Journey-to-Series-A-in-Europe.pdf) of the Dealroom report (seed = first round between $1–4m made from 2012 until the end of 2018) and applied it to the Creandum seed portfolio. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/TmvJKWlhSPLCgOkZOVtXN/2934d01a621195766eb3be5f173b1cd6/image_183.png) Over that time frame, **75%** of the portfolio's seed companies raised an A round (>$4m) within 36 months. The Dealroom methodology leaves out seed rounds below $1m and larger $4m, if we also take these into account, the conversion ratio in the portfolio is **70%**. Kudos to the portfolio companies . Another interesting insight was the **median amount raised**. Two key findings: - The median A round of the Creandum funds' portfolio companies was $7.8m (2012–2020), ~25% higher than the EU average of $6.2m - Looking back at the last 4 years only, there's a positive trend indicating that A rounds are getting bigger and the median in the portfolio was $11.5m. ## What are the success factors to get from Seed to Series A? Getting to Series A stage is at it's core about finding product market fit (or strong signals of it). It's the key step in between finding an idea (Seed stage) and having a scalable functioning business (Series B+ stage). With that comes the interest of investors for your Series A. From my view the 3 simplified key points for getting to raise a successful A are (keeping it very short, you could probably write a book on this): - Iterating towards product market fit: This is the key. The stronger the signs for PMF the better - Team: having a strong core team in place + showing that one is able to attract and hire great talent as well as running a functioning organisation - Fundraising: getting in front of the right investors with the right attention and running a well prepared process (yes, this matters) In order to look at this from the **entrepreneurs'** perspective, we asked some of our portfolio founders, who raised strong Series A rounds, what the key factors were in them getting there successfully. ### 1. Product/market fit - **Heini Zachariassen, Vivino**: "Know exactly who your user is and understand exactly what problem that user wants to be solved - focus 100% on solving that problem and aggressively ignore everything else." - **Jordi Romero, Factorial**: "To crack growth acceleration and to break down geographical barriers, figure out exactly what to sell and to whom. At Factorial, before our Seed round, we would have to craft each customer and it felt like there was friction everywhere in the process. Eventually, we evolved the product, pricing and our message to the point where customer acquisition accelerated significantly. Not only did our revenue grow to cover most expenses but it also allowed us to calculate real CAC and payback periods. These metrics are great for validating your claims." - **Mathis Büchi, Taxfix**: "From Seed to Series A, companies have one job: to find product-market fit. Product market fit at this stage means to make people happy at scale (with decent unit economics). For us, it was important in these early days to rigorously iterate on product and distribution strategies until we could show that we are on to something big." ### 2. Listen to your users - **Moritz Claussen, cargo.one**: "Always speak to the user, no matter what you are trying to solve. Retro the shit out of things, it's the only way to constantly improve." - **Christian Wiklund, UnitQ:** "Get out and test your product as early as possible. Quick iterations and listening carefully to what the users tell you is key." **3. Organizational backbone, aka team & operations ** - **Moritz Claussen, cargo.one**: "Hire only the very best people and never compromise. It's all about a strong and functional company operating system. There is nothing more important than a company cadence that allows for ownership and accountability in the team." ### 4. Asking for help - **Christian Wiklund, UnitQ:** "Leverage your network and investors for introductions. Creandum has been amazing in supporting us and it is important that you ask for help. First-time entrepreneurs are less "needy". Perhaps because they don't want to show "weakness" or be a "nuisance". Second+ timers do the opposite and will leverage everything they can out of their VCs. A small pro tip: Don't be shy about asking future potential VCs for help! They are more than willing to chip in and it is a great way to build the relationship!" ### 5. A good fundraising strategy - **Jordi Romero, Factorial:** "It was key for us to invest in a good fundraising process. We worked very closely with our seed investors to vet potential new investors, opened all the doors via cold email

articles.title: Handing over the reins to your first Product Team
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.text: If you're the founder of a product-centric company, the product is your baby. In the beginning, it demands most of your brainpower, but once you start to scale the business, you need to leverage your time and pass this responsibility on to someone else. A key step, but probably one of the most difficult. As there are many product-centric companies in the [Creandum funds' portfolio](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/), we've dedicated our latest Founders' Discussion (a monthly roundtable) to this topic to share learnings and best practices. To add some more experience to this challenge at scale, our new [Entrepreneur-In-Residence, Leo Nilsson](https://blog.creandum.com/leo-nilsson-8526e010aae6), former CPO of iZettle joined. He has been on both sides of the conversation, taking over responsibility from the founders, but also handing it over to other people. Here is a summary of the key learnings of this session to help you manage this important step well and take your business to new heights. ## 1) When is the best time to hand over the reins? Hiring too soon can cause unnecessary financial stress while waiting too long can put your business behind. **** There's no perfect, one-fits-all timing as it largely depends on the nature and state of the company and the product. BUT there are three key milestones to watch out for: - **Short term satisfying PMF:** You've achieved a level of product-market fit you're satisfied with (at least in the short term). - **Expansion plans:** You want to expand the product line into new territory. You have visions of new products and getting them into new locations. This type of expansive thinking requires a dedicated product person to lead the way. - **Lack of time:** You need time to focus on other aspects of the business. You might be a phenomenal product developer, but the company needs you elsewhere, such as making important decisions, pitching to investors, or hiring. A day only has 24 hours, and you can't change that. So don't deceive yourself about the time you really have left to lead this department. ## 2) What skills to look for? No matter the title you're looking for (CPO, head of product, product manager, you name it), your first product hire will be a key asset for your company. So what skills should this person bring along? The list could be endless, but we've narrowed it down to four important traits to consider: - **Very strong product love:** The first thing to look for in a candidate is an obsession with the details about great products. How much do they know about our product? What do they like or dislike about it? - **Commercially driven:** You need more than someone who has a good eye for design and flow. You need someone who can develop your product proposition to win market share. - **Strong visionary:** It's not enough to just understand your vision. You need to find someone who truly believes in your vision. - **Experience in scaling products:** Find someone who knows what it takes to build a team, move fast and expand. **Pro tips:** - Senior hires will save you a lot of time in the long term. - Don't look for a whizz kid - You can't replace the founder, so don't even try to find a twin. - Your hire doesn't need to possess _every_ product skill. Over time you will build specialization for example with dedicated UX or design professionals. ## 3) Where to find them? Hiring a product leader in Europe is not easy. You might think you have to go to the US to recruit from the large technology businesses over there. Good news: This might have been required five years ago, but meanwhile, the quality of European product leaders has caught up. However, it's still a good idea to look for people who have worked for companies that - are living by the typical US, product-centric values; - have a user-centric culture. Some US giants who are leading the way here include Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Netflix. Also worth mentioning are Uber, Adobe, Dropbox, and Slack, which are all US companies with development departments in Europe. In Europe, some of the most product-centric companies are [Spotify](https://www.spotify.com/uk/), Transferwise, King, Supercell, [Klarna](https://www.klarna.com/uk/), N26, Revolut, Monzo, and [Kry](https://www.kry.se/en/about/). ## 4) What makes a good product team? Once you have made your first product hire, what should you look for in the team? Below is a list of what we've encountered time and again in stellar product teams in fast-growing companies: - Problem-solving centricity; - Strong processes and solid organizational skills; - Outcome focused; - Working towards a business goal; - Fast-moving; - Data-driven; - Collaborative. An extra tip that Leo emphasized in our conversation: Get your product team to "learn cheaply and tackle risks upfront - before the team starts coding." ## 5) How to maintain the relationship? What part of the product development process remains with the founder? How can you ensure it's going in the right direction and not spiralling out of control? A few key thoughts here: - Align on a "Northstar" with your product leader, a shared goal to work towards. - Stick to a stringent product development review process. - Give input and discuss the most crucial questions. - Constantly evaluate product results and decide whether to continue in this direction or if you need to change it up. ### Extra resources - If you're looking to develop talent from within, a great program to grow your talent is the [Reforge Program](https://www.reforge.com/all-programs) (it's digital and be enjoyed from anywhere!) - strongly recommended by Leo and several other founders that joined our conversation. - On product roadmaps, check out [this blog by Brian Cheng](https://medium.com/@brianplackischeng/part-ii-closed-your-round-high-five-b12ce9be90d5), CEO of [Careship](https://www.careship.de/). Stay tuned for more helpful resources to be shared shortly by our product expert, Leo. And if you have any reflections on the

articles.title: Voi
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.excerpt: Europe’s leading micro-mobility company’s ride to success
articles.text: What started as [a much-debated hype](https://www.ft.com/content/028e6b74-f7a8-11e8-af46-2022a0b02a6c) two years ago has now proven to be a real business model. Demand for clean micromobility is increasing as consumers look for new alternatives to move around big cities [in a convenient, sustainable, quick and safe way](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/news/gentler-greener-quieter-welcome-city-future/). In response, [cities are clamping down on cars](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200429-are-we-witnessing-the-death-of-the-car), accelerating the path of the e-scooter market to become a multi-billion dollar industry. When the Creandum funds invested in **[Voi](https://www.voiscooters.com/)** in early 2019, long before Covid-related safety concerns fueled the trend towards individual transport, we shared the vision of Voi founder [Fredrik Hjelm](https://twitter.com/fredrikhjelm4?lang=de), that **"cities should be pleasant places to live, work and travel in - where transport does not pollute the air, jeopardize people's health or cut them off from their environment."** In 2018, Voi was __ the first European e-scooter player that launched onto the market but following the US trend, it was clear that it would become a very crowded industry. [Looking back at our investment hypothesis](https://blog.creandum.com/riding-to-the-top-with-voi-bae7bf976023), we came to the conclusion that that in order to lead the micromobility movemen_t_ in Europe, _**"...the winner will be defined by speed, working closely with city regulators, best product in terms of hardware and app, integration with other transportation means and access to capital."**_ Two years later, Fredrik and his team have not only built a profitable subscription business, and are known as **"Europe's preferred operator"** with [the highest fleet efficiency](https://www.wiwo.de/unternehmen/dienstleister/analyse-in-grafiken-sind-e-scooter-eine-erfolgsgeschichte/26565066.html) but they can also tick all of our required boxes: ## Speed We continue to be impressed by the pace at which the team is iterating and improving Voi's product and operations. Since its inception in 2018, the team has executed at unparalleled speed and is now active in more than 50 cities in 11 countries. (And this despite reducing their operations from 40 to 5 cities for a couple of weeks in March during the first Covid-induced lockdown.) While Voi remains the clear winner in its home region, the Nordics (where it was recently named **["Startup of the Year 2020"](https://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.voiscooters.com%2Fblog%2Fvoi-is-awarded-startup-of-the-year%2F)**) and a strong player in Germany and Switzerland, the company also successfully gained the lead in the potentially largest market, the UK. Voi is about to more than [treble the size of its UK fleet](https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/electric-scooter-e-scooter-hire-rental-london-060032544.html) as it expands to 16 British cities, **[making it the UK's leading operator](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/technology/2020/12/01/thousands-electric-scooters-fill-uk-city-streets-voi-raises/)**, covering 80% of the market. ## Working closely with city regulators Central to Voi's business model so far has been working hand-in-hand with local authorities - a move that has seen it **[score over 2/3 of city license tenders across Europe](https://techcrunch.com/2020/12/01/voi-the-european-micro-mobility-rental-company-raises-160m-additional-equity-and-debt-funding/)**, including recent wins in Birmingham, Liverpool, Bern and Cambridge. ## Product Voi has distinctly differentiated their product offering by focusing on **[sustainability](https://www.voiscooters.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Voi-Technology-Sustainability-Statement-.pdf) and [safety](https://www.voiscooters.com/blog/putting-safety-first-in-the-uk/)** - the company's key priorities - and those initiatives have paid off: By introducing swappable batteries, integrating more sustainable fleet management infrastructure and switching to renewable energy to power their operations wherever possible, Voi has reduced the already minimal environmental impact of e-scooters even further. ![Source: [Voi Sustainability Statement 2019](https://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.voiscooters.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2019%2F09%2FVoi-Technology-Sustainability-Statement-.pdf)](https://miro.medium.com/0*RP8hpfoJS4rjfgCd) But the innovation doesn't stop there: [Voi is now also turning to artificial intelligence (AI)](https://venturebeat.com/2020/11/11/escooter-startup-voi-uses-ai-to-detect-pedestrians-and-sidewalks/) to enable its vehicles to detect pedestrians and sidewalks; they have recently announced a partnership with Irish AI startup [Luna](https://luna.systems/). ## Integration with other transportation means Partnering with other mobility providers is key to making the use of scooters as frictionless as possible and expanding the user's choice between mobility alternatives. Voi has closed a number of those **strategic partnerships**, such as a collaboration with [FREE NOW](https://www.voiscooters.com/blog/free-now-germany-integrates-voi-e-scooters-into-its-app/) in Germany, with [SBB](https://www.handelszeitung.ch/unternehmen/auf-zurichs-strassen-rollen-bald-mehr-e-scooter-sbb-ist-partner) in Switzerland and [BlaBlaCar](https://techcrunch.com/2020/05/26/blablacar-partners-with-scooter-startup-voi-to-launch-new-blabla-ride-app/) in France. **"_At Voi, we strongly believe that changing traffic for good can only be achieved through joint efforts." -_ Claus Unterkirchner, Voi's General Manager DACH** ![In June 2020, Voi announced their partnership with car-sharing company FREE NOW.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1pYVDGqAxrIqdcEqzxEzaK/15820101d0b8a725011b98bf339666a4/image_182.jpg) ## Access to capital Despite Voi's strong business model, access to capital is needed to expand to more markets, double down on user acquisition and differentiate software and hardware

articles.title: The decade of B2B marketplaces
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.excerpt: And what we are looking for
articles.text: _B2B marketplaces are disrupting traditional linear supply chains by removing friction and letting buyers and sellers operate in a more efficient way. They've been around for a while, but we believe **the timing for them to really break through is coming now**. While 2010–2020 has been the era in which SaaS achieved B2B mass adoption and large IPOs (Atlassian, Dropbox, Slack, Zoom etc.), **the next decade** will be for B2B marketplaces to play catch-up. Creandum has been backing companies in this broader space for a while, such as [cargo.one, CarOnSale, Syft, Distribusion](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/)..., and we're excited about what's ahead._ ### The current pandemic brought inefficiencies to light People have always thought that online marketplaces would disrupt B2B commerce, even in the early days of the internet. Yet, online commerce disrupted the B2C space first. One reason for this asymmetric adoption is the single (B2C) versus many (B2B) decision makers in a transaction. Another one is that B2B transactions usually have higher stakes and associated risks. Thirdly, B2B marketplaces often target old-school industries that have been struggling to find the right digitization mindset or skills. A shifting mindset in the B2B world over the last two years has led to more and more businesses adopting online marketplaces. In addition, due to Covid-19, supply chains have been massively disrupted due to movement barriers and new digital habits. We see this as a catalyzer for the break up of offline B2B legacy and an accelerated transition. We think the illustration below that went viral captures this quite well. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4XBrxgkBZaNmiv93AShxPH/d1585b910ce277d0cc5ce5b861fb2ab3/image_177.jpg) Although Covid-19 was the urgency trigger, further underlying trends have enabled the rise of B2B marketplaces. According to a [recent study](https://www.rolandberger.com/en/Publications/B2B-Marketplaces-are-blossoming.html), 91% of B2B purchasing decision makers prefer to buy online once they have decided what to buy. Furthermore, advancements in integrated payments as well as the proliferation of API infrastructure across industries is increasingly pushing the online share up. To put this into perspective, most of the global annual B2B spend is still offline and represents [2–3x](https://www.applicoinc.com/blog/rise-specialized-marketplaces-ecommerce/) the current size of the B2C market. But, B2B eCommerce is forecasted to reach $[1.8 trillion and account for 17% of all B2B sales in the US by 2023](https://www.forrester.com/report/Forrester+Analytics+B2B+eCommerce+Forecast+2018+To+2023+US/-/E-RES145710). With the increase in inbound interest and signups for B2B marketplaces, our belief is that we are just at the very beginning of this trend. ### Geographic overview of EU B2B marketplace landscape When looking at the geographic overview in Europe, B2B marketplaces often originate in markets native to their industries. In Germany, for instance, marketplaces for industrial parts proliferate due to the manufacturing-centered economy. The marketplace's proximity to suppliers and network density are advantages when growing the supply side. There are exciting companies across the whole continent, but Germany and the UK stand out in terms of the quantity of B2B marketplaces. ![_This map is not exhaustive (!). If you think a B2B marketplace company is missing that we should add: [submit here](https://forms.gle/bnmnk3U86oeiAn2A7)._](https://miro.medium.com/0*WGAmiFw7PxcLWnJO) ## Success factors and what we are looking for Offering superior convenience, service or access to specific or a variety of goods and services is a given for building up a successful marketplace. But what are the early indicators of success to look out for and monitor? To give an overview of what Creandum is looking for, I summarized some of the key factors that we evaluate. Obviously, some metrics will not be available or meaningful yet if the company is still in its early days, and while this is trying to generalize, every case is unique. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1ThQ4KDEK14wrzCHmnvLVg/527d54667221c740587f85f89324a4b3/image_179.jpg) ### Market characteristics: - **Market size:** Assuming a commission-based model, we look for a combination of 3 things: 1) GMV market size 2) Take rate 3) Contribution margin Achievable take rate and contribution margin vary widely between different markets and models, so the most honest and comparable metric for me is potential gross margin market size. To check whether your market size is large enough for VC, I've built a small calculator. [Link to the spreadsheet to play around here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1nvH_wg20URZphBVLX_GJ61bEOE14cjKNr0KorJ6qpk0/edit?usp=sharing). Note that take rate can comprise multiple charged streams that add up to each other - e.g. pure commission (with x% contribution margin) and additional service 1 (y% contribution margin) and service 2 (x% contribution margin) - and one needs to look at the weighted total take rate and margin. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3RJ9kmt6YV1ccokYH1fwcr/6114e05aee819b5b72f9880a08329384/image_180.jpg) - **High fragmentation of the demand and supply side:** resulting in a better chance of breaking through the initial demand/supply side power imbalance, increased value of the platform, and network effects. What is high? A few thousand potential participants on each side of the marketplace and limited concentration of revenues for the top buyers or sellers. - **Go-to market dynamics:** efficient acquisition and the operational complexity of go to market per side of the marketplace. Mostly acquisition is done through direct sales, but even more attractive if buyers bring sellers or sellers bring buyers onto the platform. In the ideal case both, buyers and sellers both bring each other onto the platform. - **Market transparency:** Non-transparent markets where the marketplace el

articles.title: Creandum’s 100th backing: Kive
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.excerpt: The smart asset platform for creators
articles.text: This is an honor. I'm not only talking about the honor of announcing [Creandum's 100th company](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/), but also that [after 17 years in the VC industry](https://blog.creandum.com/inside-the-dusty-brains-of-an-early-spotify-investor-looking-at-how-we-were-right-and-wrong-7938abcd36e1), I still get the opportunity to meet the most inspiring, innovative and thoughtful individuals out there, with crazy ambitions to build products and services that change the way people work, live and play for the better. And our 100th backing is no exception. For those of you who work in the creative industries, you know the painful headache of messy digital libraries, siloed files, and manual workflows all too well. Current tools to manage digital creative assets lack functionality for collaboration, are labor-intensive, and demand countless hours that creatives _should_ be using to actually create. More importantly, they are not built by the people who will use them. ### Enter [Kive](http://kive.ai) - the next-generation asset platform for creators Kive is a shareable, self-organizing content library located in the cloud that lets you interact with your assets from any device and recognizes specific elements, including human emotions, environments and lighting, but also actions, faces, types of shot (such as close-ups), time of day and thousands of others. Think Pinterest for professional creatives, but faster, multiplayer first, with fine-grained search and much nicer to use. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5xQPxhYsO4oWv0GjaVR1xW/9def529562c0835db8f3bcae6effc19c/image_175.jpg) _**Our hypothesis:**_ _As some of you may know, **a well-known Creandum first principle when evaluating early-stage companies is to simply consider user love as a proxy for the adaptation of the product by the market** (think [Spotify](https://blog.creandum.com/inside-the-dusty-brains-of-an-early-spotify-investor-looking-at-how-we-were-right-and-wrong-7938abcd36e1), [Vivino](https://blog.creandum.com/why-we-are-investing-in-vivino-ad17a4587ff7), [Kry](https://blog.creandum.com/kry-fills-all-the-boxes-of-our-healthcare-checklist-4caa51fe3b37), [shapr3D](https://blog.creandum.com/creandum-%EF%B8%8F-shapr3d-427b46b955c6), Depop, etc.)._ Talking to some of the end-users of Kive's beta product, we could quickly tick all the boxes: The platform creates real value by **saving users "hours, if not days" of work**. **The product is carefully refined based on user feedback** and engagement - a process that will help Kive offer its products to a broader market and segmented audiences in the future. The founder's **laser focus on early user deligh**t already fuels word-of-mouth marketing among creative professionals. Users value the **thorough understanding of the creative processes** "that can only come from someone who has experienced the problem themselves". _This leads on to the second fundamental principle for evaluating early-stage opportunities: **The importance of the team.**_ Well, Kive doesn't have a team (yet!), but **[Olof Lindh](https://oloflindh.com/)**, the founder, makes up for it. He impressed us off the bat. I left our first 30-minute scheduled meeting after two hours. Olof is thoughtful and incredibly eager to learn. His track record as a creative leader is second to none in his field, and it's inspiring to see how he has approached the new learning curve of building a high-performing organization destined for fast growth. Olof has very high standards when hiring, but is at the same time self-aware and keen to improve. ![Kive founder and film director Olof Lindh.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/GvATgYrwUcNR8P12l8rPI/63bd4706a56362a7799fb0eb8bedcd24/image_176.jpg) ### Created for creatives by creatives. Next to starting his venture, Olof is an experienced and successful film director. He is represented by [ICONOCLAST](https://iconoclast.tv/de) and [B-Reel Films](https://brf.co/). And as a passionate, lifelong, self-taught hacker, in his spare time - mainly nights and weekends - he developed Kive. Yes, he developed the entire beta platform himself, 100% bootstrapped. And that's probably the biggest secret behind our conviction at this early stage: **he is a founder intimately acquainted with the problem and raring to solve it.** We are beyond excited to back Kive at this early stage and for the Creandum funds to add it as the 100th company to their portfolio, all the more so as Kive shares our Nordic roots, and we are delighted to accompany Olof on his journey from creative genius to corporate leader. If you are a filmmaker, designer, architect, publisher - you name it - and want a beautiful tool to make your work easier and to boost your creative processes, I think Kive is right for you. Did I mention that **[Kive is hiring](https://kive.ai/jobs)**?

articles.title: Creandum backs SafetyWing
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Building a global social safety net
articles.text: You're probably reading this while working from your living room or kitchen, or maybe you've chosen a sunny get-away location. Accelerated by the pandemic, [remote work has become the new normal](https://blog.creandum.com/the-future-of-work-is-here-but-something-is-missing-d95f1afa119f) - at least for knowledge workers. ven as the vaccine gets distributed, a high amount of workers won‘t jump at the opportunity and start commuting again. [According to recent Gartner research](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-07-14-gartner-survey-reveals-82-percent-of-company-leaders-plan-to-allow-employees-to-work-remotely-some-of-the-time), a large majority of executives say they intend to let employees work remotely either fully or at least part of the time. 36 percent of companies say they're willing to hire workers who are 100 percent remote and live anywhere, which is a number I believe will only grow over time. But as an employer, how do you attract, manage, and retain them? At [Creandum](http://Creandum.com), we strongly believe the shift to remote work is one of the biggest changes to ever happen within knowledge workers and will require a new stack of tools to support this new reality. That's why in early 2020, we proactively set out to map the market for remote work solutions, looked at different verticals and talked to any interesting venture from this new breed of tech companies. Through this work, we realized the infrastructure of remote work is still being created. Outside of figuring out the governance of hiring an employee in a remote location (solved by startups like Remote.com, letsdeel.com and oysterhr.com), we realized companies also were looking to offer consistent company benefits, which become even more important when you compete globally for talent. ### Enter SafetyWing, providing cross-border benefits for remote employees. [SafetyWing](http://safetywing.com/) offers comprehensive cross-border healthcare insurance for remote workers across 170 countries in the world with more benefits coming soon. Employers get an intuitive interface to switch on and off benefits across the world for a fixed price per employee, while behind the scenes SafetyWing has built a robust and complex insurance solution across multiple risk partners. With SafetyWing, employers can create an amazing, consistent employee experience that's competitive within all markets. In addition to this, the company offers unique travel insurance built specifically for digital nomads, which serves the growing self-employed contractor market. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/2MjFe4XSpehTNXCla2fyuq/bcf0769b450c5984e4c4b0a968926ff7/image_173.png) SafetyWing CEO [Sondre Rasch](https://www.linkedin.com/in/srasch/) is someone we had known for four years as he went through Y Combinator with his previous business - a freelancer platform called [Superside](https://www.superside.com/) where he discovered the pain of offering benefits to workers spread out across the world. Joined by two co-founders, [Sarah](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarahbeyahte/) and [Hans](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hans-nyvold-kjellby-84975162/), SafetyWing set out to solve this specific problem, and also completed YC two years ago, and we've been following their journey ever since. 2020 was a tough year for many companies, but as you may expect the need for SafetyWing's products really exploded as part of Covid lockdowns. ![SafetyWing founders Sarah, Hans & Sondre.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6uZP9wHVFxFbIE1rrtaMb9/8ed927a750f47d75b4f7cf5d57aca5ab/image_174.jpg) Besides the movements in remote work, for years we've had big believers in how the insurance market is being redefined through technology. A few years ago we tried to understand the broader opportunities within insurtech and back then identified three themes we've been going after. The first one was redefining the actual experience of being a policyholder, which is what the life insurer [Yulife](https://yulife.com/) is doing through their mobile companion app encouraging you to live a healthier life. The second one was innovation at the very core business model of insurance, as seen with [Laka](https://laka.co/gb/home-copy?utm_expid=.Kx5qqpNPSSCoGuvOXkpszQ.1&utm_referrer=) and their community-based insurance where members share the cost of all claims and Laka earns a markup from this. The third one was serving new and growing insurance markets with modern technology DNA, which is really where SafetyWing comes in. They are one of the only companies in the world who deeply understands the needs of their customers and who can offer a product on par with the expectations of them. Hence, cue all celebration and excitement emojis as we're incredibly proud to be partnering with SafetyWing and for Creandum to lead the company's $8m Series A round. We believe SafetyWing will be one of the most important companies of the remote work movement of the next decade, and we're grateful to be part of their journey ahead. Want to join SafetyWing on this journey? [They are hiring](https://remoteok.io/remote-companies/safetywing) - remotely of course!

articles.title: Vivino
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.excerpt: From a free wine scanning app to the world’s largest wine marketplace
articles.text: **Interview with [Vivino](https://www.vivino.com/DE/en/) founder and CEO [Heini Zachariassen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/heini/)** If you like to drink wine, you‘ve likely come across **Vivino**, the ultimate destination for discovering and buying wines. **[The Creandum funds led Vivino's Series A round in 2012](https://blog.creandum.com/why-we-are-investing-in-vivino-ad17a4587ff7)** and since then, I've been privileged to be part of their board, working closely with the founder Heini Zachariassen. Today, the platform counts more than 50 million customers, but following **[Vivino's recent $155M Series D](https://techcrunch.com/2021/02/03/vivino-raises-155-million-for-wine-recommendation-and-marketplace-app/)** funding round, the company is now planning to further strengthen its position as **the leading wine marketplace in the world**. I had a (virtual) glass of wine with Heini to learn more about how the company dealt with the massive surge of new customers in 2020, how they transitioned from a free wine label scanning app to a successful marketplace and how he thinks about the company's long-term growth. (Full video interview at the bottom of this article) **Heini, despite being an avid wine drinker, you didn't have any professional experience in the wine industry. What motivated you to start a company in this space?** Not having any professional experience may have been the secret to Vivino's success. I approached the topic from a _**user angle**_. I realized there was a big problem for casual wine drinkers, like me, who are not experts and who simply felt overwhelmed standing in front of rows upon rows of wine on supermarket shelves. My ambition to solve my own problem definitely kept me going in the beginning. "**I think a simplified mindset and a completely new approach is the best way to disrupt an industry**." ![Vivion Founder and CEO Heini Zachariassen](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6DlZGOgxf67f8PiA4ZNasY/79368727d1744fb4fa02ff13624b447b/image_171.jpg) **Today, Vivino is the largest wine marketplace in the world and it's particularly popular among millennials. What do you think is the core reason that you've got such a great product-market fit?** Nailing the product-market fit is a lot about swimming with the stream, following what's happening in the world. We could see a clear market trend in younger consumers' mobile habits. With everyone using apps like Yelp and TripAdvisor, **mobile rating** has become the new normal. We jumped on that trend because it made a lot of sense to have that for wine as well. The integration of crowdsourced ratings allowed us to really scale the company, as crowd intelligence offers a competitive advantage over individual wine experts. A professional sommelier will do approximately 20,000 ratings every year. At Vivino, we get **100,000 ratings a day**. The proportions are just really different and we can easily scale the model even further. That's the beauty of digitalizing certain things. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6RMsec0RyVR44kHwNHqrbb/675ed73f5d905f95698dbf5497d8bb38/image_172.jpg) **What started as a wine scanning app without a revenue model (that is still growing massively via free word-of-mouth marketing) turned into a real money-making business. How did that evolve over time?** The moment I started to speak to investors, I had one slide in my pitch deck that clearly stated the business case: "You're going to scan a bottle of wine, and then you're going to be able to buy it." That business model just made a lot of sense right from the beginning. However, it's really easy to put it on a slide and wow the investors. **The real challenge is to actually do it.** It turned out that just because a user scans a bottle, it doesn't mean they want to make an immediate purchase. We had to dig deeper to find out when our users _**do**_ have the intent to buy. Over time, we built some new search and explore features, added recommendations, and more. That really got the ball rolling. We focused on making the app as frictionless as possible for the users, getting more data, and growing the community. Once you really own the users, it's much easier to convert them to e-commerce customers. **Why did you move to the US in 2012, [shortly after the Creandum funds led your Series A round](https://blog.creandum.com/why-we-are-investing-in-vivino-ad17a4587ff7)?** The philosophy back then was, **"If you want to win the world, you need to win the US"**. If you look at the largest consumer brands, they're almost all from the US, or even all from Silicon Valley. From a business perspective, it also made a lot of sense, as more than half of our user base was in the US. Today, things are different: Half of our turnover is coming from the US, but less than a quarter of our users are based there. In other words, the Americans are an incredibly interesting and **very profitable group of customers**. **2020 provided a great boost to e-commerce in general. How did you keep up with that massive surge over the past 12 months? And how will it impact your business in the long term?** In the past year, we never had a boring moment. We more than doubled our business in 2020, compared to 2019. I'm proud of the team's performance but I can't deny that it was a rough period. We experienced different stages: 1. **Panic.** Everything seemed to pause for a moment so I decided to hit the brakes. No hiring. No marketing. Let's just take it cool for now and see what the heck this is. 2. **Growth and problems.** Around March 20th, sales started to pick up faster and faster. That was also the moment when the first processes started to break. Our customer support couldn't keep up with the rapidly increasing demand. And with customer support flaws, our supplier process was in trouble, too. Deliveries were delayed and even more customers kept calling. A vicious circle. 3. **Solutions.** To break that circle, our solution was to focus on hiring and training new customer suppo

articles.title: Making Sense of One Year in VC
articles.text: There are no rules when it comes to a career in venture capital. Everyone has their own style, way of thinking and methodology. And **[what is required to break into VC](https://twitter.com/axeliaklein/status/1309409992492175362) might not be the same things that make you a good investor.** This contradiction can be pretty challenging for anyone who is looking to not only break into the scene but also someone learning to master the craft, and even if you have experience in the startup ecosystem, e.g. as a founder, you will inevitably need to change your mindset or how you work at some point along the way. I am celebrating my first (amazing!) year at **[Creandum](https://creandum.com/)** and thought now would be a prudent time to reflect on my biggest learnings and extract some recommendations for anyone following a similar path. ## Five learnings to not underestimate: ### 1. Feedback cycles are long, make sure to perfect your process Before starting in VC, people kept telling me that one of the hardest parts of the job is the very long feedback cycles. While intellectually this made a lot of sense given the nature of early-stage investing, I still could not really wrap my head around it. Coming from two operational roles, one as a Chief of Staff and the other as a founder, I was used to short deadlines and instant feedback. After >1 year in VC, I can definitely relate to this struggle, however, I do think there is a lot to be gained from a) thinking about your style, b) considering how you can perfect it, and c) finding ways to recognise your progress. For me, this manifests itself as a **monthly reflection**. I literally have a 1 hour sit-down with myself in which I evaluate where I am at in different aspects of the VC deal cycle: sourcing, selecting, specific domain knowledge, connecting with entrepreneurs, or winning deals. If there are certain parts I want to improve, I break them down and make them measurable with goals - maybe I improve my specific domain knowledge by writing a new blog post, or strengthen the firm's brand to win more deals by posting content (hint, hint). True, this will not make you (or me) a great investor per se, but it will make the progress more clearly defined, and with some luck, this will also lead to great outcomes. ### 2. Being new to VC can be confusing, so get a mentor or two (Warning: VC brag) One of the most fantastic things about starting a career in VC at Creandum has been that we have **clearly defined collaboration systems between partners and non-partner investment team members** (thanks [Staffan Helgesson](http://@shelgesson)!). Besides the outspoken goal of you getting a chance to actively work with all of the partners, you are assigned a mentor specifically dedicated to your progress. Given that there are no rules or frameworks illustrating how the work of a venture capitalist should be, this has been immensely helpful. And while your firm or the firm you are looking to join might not have the same setup, you can still look for mentors - perhaps in a more senior colleague, or even outside your firm. I have learned plenty of crucial things from some of my best buds in VC (you know who you are!). So to summarise: Find someone or a few people you admire and then try to extract as many learnings as you can from them. ### 3. VCs collaborate - so should entrepreneurs This was one of the things that surprised me most about joining a VC firm - how much time you actually spend talking to people outside your firm. I usually refer to this group as my extended colleagues. Yes, true, there is competition amongst different firms to win deals. **But all of the most talented non-partner VCs I know are also those who are willing to share their knowledge on exciting deals and domains**. The key here is to find those people you can trust and feel comfortable sharing with - which is sometimes easier said than done. Here I don't have any golden rules as it is a process similar to "selecting" your closest friends, i.e. something that will be very individual. Based on this insight, I was somewhat surprised at how limited sharing between founders seems to be, for example on how it is to work with certain VC firms, partners, or juniors. Granted, founders make up a larger group of people, but if you are running your own company, finding a few peers who can give you advice on the in and outs of VC will be extremely valuable. At least, that is something I wish I had as a founder. ### 4. VCs have chaotic days but nothing compares to being a founder or an early employee ![The crazy days of startup founders (and how sometimes investors can help). Credit: [VC Starter Kit](None)](https://miro.medium.com/1*gi1L7IAn6Oda2ANJrwQBHA.gif) You sometimes hear that working in VC means you are never done. That there are always more companies to meet, better tweets to write, or more Clubhouse sessions to join. However, as much as this is true (and to this day I have met few people in VC who work fewer than 60–70 hours a week on average), it will never compare to running your own business or being an early employee at a start-up. **This is true for two different reasons:** 1) You can "control" the timeline yourself, meaning you can essentially decide if you want to win a deal or not. If you want to win the deal, you usually have to work **very** fast for a few days, but the pace of iteration is often still in your power. 2) Your customers do not demand your attention constantly. VCs' "customers" are founders and LPs. And even if you work very closely with both these stakeholders, you will still not have the same level of constant need from your customers and users. As a founder, if things go wrong - be it tech, HR, sales, or marketing - everything eventually ends up in your lap. This means you have to be "on-call" 24/7. In my current role, I have the greatest respect for the time strain this puts on the founder's life. ### 5. Shifting your mindset from why not to why yes This is probabl

articles.title: Scaling Culture
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.text: **How to define, develop and maintain culture in fast-growing companies** "What's your team culture like?" - A question I'm sure many of you are familiar with from hiring interviews, no matter if you're a startup founder or a VC partner. All textbooks say it, a solid company culture is essential to the success of any business as it has a profound impact on its employees and reputation, and directly affects organizational growth and many other business aspects. But how do you really define, develop, and maintain culture in young and fast-growing companies? We discussed this important topic with some of the founders from our [#CreandumFamily](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/) and [Meltwater](https://www.meltwater.com/)'s Executive Director/EVP Americas & Board Member [Kaveh Rostampor](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kaveh-rostampor/), who was one of Meltwater's first employees. He has played a crucial role in maintaining a great team culture while scaling the organization to 3000+ people. Continue reading to learn more about our 8 key learnings that we distilled from the discussion: **Why do we need company culture?** Speaking to hundreds of founders on a monthly basis, I've noticed there are generally two distinct attitudes towards company culture: 1) Those who consider culture as essential and the glue that binds a team together, and 2) those who think it's *ahem* bullsh*t. This leads straight into learning #1... **#1 If you don't think culture is important now, you will later (and wish you had cared about it earlier).** Culture binds the organization together. Essentially it's what people say, what people do and how people treat each other rolled into one neat concept. This concept is built upon your team's values. These values represent the way they think and make decisions, and are therefore paramount when you start scaling. _Founder tip: Nouns make horrible values, whereas formulating values as verbs or instructions makes them actionable, e.g. "Your job isn't done until the job is done" (Nike) or "Make someone smile" (Amie)._ Once you start scaling, decision-making will have to be delegated to other team members. Without a strong culture and instruction-based values, you run the risk of decisions being made that might be misaligned with the founder's original vision or mission. The benefits are also clear in the numbers: [A long-term study of over 200 firms](https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnkotter/2011/02/10/does-corporate-culture-drive-financial-performance/?sh=8d885987e9e9) found that good company culture increases revenue by 4X and that 47% of people actively looking for a new job pinpoint company culture as the main reason for wanting to leave. ### When's the right time to start thinking about culture? It's _never_ too early. NEVER! In fact, the Airbnb founders wrote down their cultural values before they hired a single person. This is because... **#2 Whether you like it or not, all organizations have some kind of culture that defines them.** Broadly speaking, there are two types of organizational culture: 1. **Founder-derived** essentially refers to top-down value sharing, i.e. the founders already have an idea of which values they want the organization to be defined by. Founder-derived values are reinforced by two main actions: i) setting behavioral examples, and ii) only hiring people who already share those values. 2. **Employee-derived** values are brainstormed and agreed upon by a wider team. At [Meditopia](https://meditopia.com/en/), they tackled this by holding a company-wide culture workshop in which every employee was asked to define their personal values independent of Meditopia and subsequently identify what it is that keeps them there, what they would like to change and what not. Afterwards, a smaller team of volunteers synthesized the data into tangible values and a culture concept. Of course, a democratized process of defining your values empowers your employees and you end up with a culture that everyone believes in. But it naturally doesn't scale as your organization grows and eventually it has to be centrally managed. **#3 It doesn't matter which method you use; what's critical is doing it early on and ensuring your values and approach remain consistent as you scale.** ### How do you maintain culture when scaling? Maintaining the culture is one of the most challenging aspects. When you're small enough that you as a founder are doing the hiring, it's easier, as you just hire people who share your own values. [Amie](https://amie.so/) is a great example from [Creandum's portfolio ](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/)— The founder Dennis wants candidates who have nuanced thinking and are product-centric, so he shapes his interview questions accordingly. He sees first-hand not only what they respond with, but how they reach that conclusion and articulate it. However, as you begin to scale, hiring becomes a function of speed. And when you delegate hiring decisions, you run the risk of bringing people in who don't truly share your company's values, and it's not fair to expect them to "learn" them later on. So... **#4 Don't hire people who don't fit into your culture. If in doubt, don't hire, even if you want to fill the position quickly. It will come back to bite you in the long-run.** [33% of employees don't believe their company's core values align with their personal values](https://officevibe.com/guides/state-employee-engagement). This can be prevented by careful hiring, so here are some tips from our founders: 1. Introduce selection criteria based on values into your hiring process. Score candidates on each. 2. Hire for culture across all levels, whether it's an internship or a C-level position. 3. Be crystal clear about the company culture during interviews and onboarding processes. Ensure your interviews are two-way streets whereby the applicant can ask culture-related questions. They might identify that they aren't the best fit before you do! 4. Leave hiring-ma

articles.title: Deliver it now
articles.author: Carl Fritjofsson
articles.excerpt: Creandum backs next generation grocer Dija
articles.text: At Creandum, we have a sweet spot for big markets. With an ever-growing world population, the food market is undoubtedly one of them. The first food investment made by the Creandum funds was [Linas Matkasse](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/), one of the original meal kit delivery services, that [inspired today's market leader Hello Fresh](https://www.forbes.com/sites/victoriapavlova/2019/08/31/hellofresh-expands-to-sweden-the-cradle-of-meal-kit-services/?sh=1433edd7a1fc). In 2012, we backed [Vivino, today's biggest wine marketplace](https://blog.creandum.com/vivino-from-a-free-wine-scanning-app-to-the-worlds-largest-wine-marketplace-e7c65a3bb65c), and in 2016 [the funds invested into the grocery delivery service Cornershop](https://blog.creandum.com/doing-it-like-uber-but-in-latam-and-in-groceries-cornershop-raising-a-21m-series-b-ac836950e7f0) that became Uber for groceries. Another four years later, with new customer habits and needs emerging, we scanned the entire European continent to find what the next-generation online grocery business can look like. And we're pleased to confirm: We found it! The idea of saving time by ordering your groceries online instead of having to trek to a supermarket, push a shopping cart down aisle after aisle, then wait in the checkout line, is not something new. But the pandemic for obvious reasons certainly caused a shift in consumer behaviours making online groceries truly mass market. How can tech further innovate this model? What do customers demand from the next generation of online grocery delivery services? It's actually fairly simple. Customers want to get the products they ordered at the time they need them. This means FAST delivery and NO REPLACEMENTS. ### Meet [Dija](http://dijanow.com). No matter if you have an impulsive need for chocolate, need to top up your basics, urgently need a few extra avocados for your guac, or plan a big dinner party [Dija](http://dijanow.com) will deliver to your door within 10 (!) minutes guaranteeing stock availability. Dija is able to do this by redefining the entire grocery stack. They operate a network of purpose-built hyper-local "dark warehouses" across the city which gives them the ability to deliver with an incredible speed. Each hub will carry more than 2,000 products from trusted grocery brands and gives customers the ability to stock up on anything you would expect from a grocer. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5kF2Bv5042LwvG0ZAYVdaC/65912f2fc449e7f572b409e36ab381c9/image_167.jpg) Love at first sight. As a VC, we speak to many founders every day. We are often impressed by founders in a first meeting but building conviction as an early-stage investor requires time and effort in terms of analysis and getting to know the team. However, our first meeting the Dija founders [Alberto](https://www.linkedin.com/in/albertomenolascina/?originalSubdomain=uk) and [Yusuf](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yusuf-saban-41062862/) was different. They confirmed the Disney myth that there is such a thing as love at first sight. We were instantly amazed and truly in awe. **Why?** Alberto and Yusuf have the most relevant background experience you can think of for pursuing an opportunity like this. They combine executive roles from Deliveroo where they've seen what on-demand at scale looks like. They also built not one but two different type of online grocers in the past with immense operational learnings and understandings of the market. Finally, the two founders are some of the most ambitious and bold people we've ever met. Nothing is too big and the upside is literally infinite, and their hyper-speed of execution is the ultimate testament to this. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/74Siga67xUdWMJmaYIg46R/3fe633228476a5388825a051a3d61df3/image_168.png) Today, we are beyond excited to add [Dija](http://dijanow.com) to the #CreandumFamily and couldn't be more proud to join our friends at [Blossom](https://www.blossomcap.com) and [Index Ventures](https://www.indexventures.com), in Dija's $20M Seed round. Want to be part of shaping the next-gen of groceries? Dija is hiring! Read more about their latest launch in London on [Techcrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/03/04/dija-launch/) or [Sifted](https://sifted.eu/articles/dija-launch-london/). <iframe src="https://cdn.embedly.com/widgets/media.html?src=https%3A%2F%2Fgiphy.com%2Fembed%2F2cLgxSMKkALVm%2Ftwitter%2Fiframe&display_name=Giphy&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2F2cLgxSMKkALVm%2Fgiphy.gif&image=https%3A%2F%2Fi.giphy.com%2Fmedia%2F2cLgxSMKkALVm%2Fgiphy.gif&key=a19fcc184b9711e1b4764040d3dc5c07&type=text%2Fhtml&schema=giphy" title="Never carry your grocery bags again!" height="431" width="435"></iframe>

articles.title: Europe’s Leadership in Climate Tech
articles.text: > "Digital technologies are a critical enabler for attaining the sustainability goals of The Green Deal in many different sectors." - The EU Green Deal We at [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/) and [Speedinvest](https://speedinvest.com) couldn't agree more. Across Europe, we are observing the emergence of a flood of innovative businesses that promise to have a positive impact on climate (Read more about the driving forces [in my latest blog post](https://blog.creandum.com/time-to-cool-the-planet-creandums-perspective-on-climate-tech-1d863dd983f4)). In the process, they are taking advantage of substantial business opportunities and contributing to our economies at large. Taken together, these trends are positioning Europe to be a global leader in Climate Tech. ## Bridging the Gap Between The European Green Deal and Climate Tech Innovators Europe published [The European Green Deal](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_19_6691) in 2019 - a set of policy initiatives to turn climate and environmental challenges into growth opportunities with the overarching aim to make the EU's economy sustainable. That means zero net greenhouse gas emissions across the continent by 2050. The Green Deal defines initiatives across eight pillars. These pillars include sustainable building/renovation, energy, clean & circular economy, smart mobility, agriculture, biodiversity, zero pollution and sustainable finance. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5D3aNa6plGWOBo5qRqeuJJ/565685a57a102fe06b89b855e1202d8c/image_163.png) Together with our colleagues at Speedinvest, we took a closer look at these pillars and their action plans in detail (check out the [Green Deal's Roadmap here for more inspiration](https://ec.europa.eu/info/publications/communication-european-green-deal_en)). We realized that each pillar was already opening up a multitude of startup and investment opportunities. Our combined mission is to amplify the visibility of these opportunities. We hope that this will inspire more companies to get started in line with the pillars defined by the Green Deal and further cement Europe's role as a global leader in our efforts to defeat the climate crisis. This is why we teamed up to build the largest landscape of European Climate Tech ventures. ## Europe's Most Comprehensive Climate Tech List - Do you want to be featured? We've done the initial legwork and identified **more than 800 Climate Tech companies across Europe**. Now we need your help! Until the **31st of March**, we are crowd-sourcing a list of Climate Tech ventures across Europe in line with the pillars fleshed out in the European Green Deal. The final result will be the most comprehensive market map of the sector. View our current list - which will be updated on an ongoing basis -here: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/29FLOHaX5QZYEwLHkl2QuH/f9a31ddaad1b8768acc41de8c00e3eff/image_164.png) ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7kJ2vMUvBpmVGOS9QHvucy/0dcbd09473ffae055eedeafcc657c047/image_165.png) **Are you a Climate Tech startup and want to be added to the list?** ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1wFtbDUMErprUGbEwM2pUL/1716462310944a06ee688eef74989efa/image_166.png) If you would like to request changes to the list or want to share your ideas, please reach out to [ines@creandum.com](mailto:ines@creandum.com) or [andreas@speedinvest.com](mailto:andreas@speedinvest.com). **###** _At [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/), we believe software will play a crucial role when it comes to tackling the Climate Crisis. Many entrepreneurs share that view and have set out to fight the crisis hands-on. If you're one of those founders, driven to build a more sustainable and innovative planet, [please reach out](https://www.creandum.com/contact/)._ _[Sign-up](https://bit.ly/3chVFFf) to get the latest Creandum news, insights and resources right in your inbox._

articles.title: Creandum backs SEON
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.excerpt: Democratizing fraud-fighting
articles.text: ### You need a gun to break into the US capitol - but only a laptop to break into an online bank Before the digital age, criminals needed a good mask to hide their identity and a gun to rob a bank. Today, all they need is a laptop. In October 2020, for example, [fraudsters impersonated BP and Total by creating similarly-named entities to receive trade finance from the National Bank of Oman.](https://www.gtreview.com/news/asia/fraudsters-impersonated-bp-and-total-to-obtain-finance-singapore-court-rules/) Online consumer activity has soared over the last years - not only due to covid. At the same time, advances in digital technology have enabled more technically sophisticated forms of identity fraud. To be blunt: Any company will be the target of fraud attempts at one point. Hence, at Creandum, we strongly believe that **fighting fraud will be one of the most important tasks in the years to come**. At the forefront of this topic is the British/Hungarian company [SEON](https://seon.io/). Cybercrime is undoubtedly on the rise and identity fraud is [at epidemic levels](https://www.financierworldwide.com/qa-managing-identity-fraud-risks#.YC1tWHdKjOQ). The number of people with guns versus the number of people with laptops posing a fraud risk is dramatically changing (at least in Europe). Fraudsters create their own websites, email addresses and online profiles, such as LinkedIn profiles, for the identities, they would ultimately use. In some instances, they completely fake identities or steal legitimate photos from unrelated individuals to build up the company's online presence. However, we aren't lacking cybersecurity companies to tackle those problems. The anti-fraud market is a very crowded place, but dealing with fraud is usually seen as a complicated project and something only huge companies really have the capacity to deal with, as it usually includes opaque pricing, long sales processes, complicated integrations, and inflexible, binding contracts. Often the customer needs an urgent solution, but the market is not geared to fulfil that need. ## With SEON, this is different + better. SEON is building the leading risk data engine, helping businesses of all sizes that have an online presence to fight against fraud. SEON stands out for several key reasons: - **Advanced technology:** SEON's solution is far more advanced than what is out there so far. It operates in real-time, with no stale data and zero false positives - a paradigm shift from previous proprietary databases to true real-time fraud prevention. - **Democratizing access:** SEON enables easy implementation of their anti-fraud tool. Within an hour, you connect your systems with an API, which makes it super easy to try the solution. No more month-long projects with onsite consultants and huge setup fees. - **Full flexibility:** You pay as you go and neither need to commit to big sums nor to long contract durations. SEON is confident enough in its product to not require any lock-ins to secure customers coming back. - **Whitebox solution:** SEON built a compelling fraud prevention platform consisting of two components: 1. An "intelligence tool" draws on data from across the internet to establish customers' digital footprints, based on a single email, IP, phone number, or location. 2. A "sense platform" decides on each fraud case, weaning out false accounts and preventing fraudulent transactions from taking place. Customers can decide if they want to go all-in and pay for the entire data engine and sensing platform, or only work with the data and interpret it themselves. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3wpSgc0nYot4YoKmKxKYBj/e81b254380389a0a1a07e4e4b27d019a/image_161.jpg) ## Does this mean SEON is focused on small companies only? Certainly not. SEON's new approach to anti-fraud leads to an almost **infinite number** of use cases around understanding who your user truly is, in order to prevent fraudulent activity. SEON's flexible solution unlocks efficient go-to-market dynamics that enable the company to go after both mid-and long-tail markets. SEON has already validated its model and is currently serving customers across the globe - from large enterprises to SMEs. SEON operates industry-agnostically with a focus on fast-growing verticals such as neo-banks, esports, iGaming, forex and crypto trading - but also airlines and online communities. Among their clients are well-known companies such as Patreon, KLM and Eurobet. ## Our Hypothesis _At Creandum, we believe cybercrime will be one of the most serious threats of the 21st century. The risk of identity fraud is unfortunately only likely to increase, meaning any business that serves customers online needs to be incredibly vigilant and proactively address this issue. This includes 90% of the Creandum funds' portfolio companies. Granted, technology is used as a means to commit fraud, but it goes without saying that it is also critical in the fight to prevent it._ We believe, enterprise software will more and more be democratized. Accessing solutions via an API - without heavy frontloaded consulting projects will be the way to go to market for the winners. SEON is proving just that. ![SEON Co-founders Bence Jendruszak and Tamas Kadar](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1ukqOVe4wTVIB8gwNs9QkF/72352cf5c8ba1ce2b7ce7f1aea6f1771/image_162.jpg) With SEON, we've found an anti-fraud solution that's effective, affordable, flexible, intuitive, and clearly proves its ROI. We are super excited to work with the SEON team to democratize the anti-fraud market and prevent the bank robberies of the 21st century. **We are excited to back the founders [Tamas](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tomkadar/) and [Bence](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bence-jendruszak/) - who spend their time between their London and Budapest offices - and their team!** Be part of their journey: [SEON is hiring](https://careers.seon.io/) in London, Budapest and remote! More on [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/03/17/fraud-p

articles.title: Creandum Series A Deck
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.excerpt: Template by Creandum
articles.text: A good deck is an important factor in maximising your success for raising a Series A. It's your key marketing material and should spark an investor's interest within just a couple of minutes. Building a good deck is essential. [Here is our Series A Deck Template as a Google Slides presentation](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/17slkHITrl44d42ytmNTLKeVqpWFalNj7akigkOhRVHs/edit?usp=sharing). This deck was designed as a guide to help you build your Series A deck. Every company is different, so I encourage everyone to deviate from this template and elaborate your own personalised Series A deck that represents your company even better. Feel free to make a copy to use as a template and share. You can, of course, use this as a rough guide for other stages (e.g. Series B), in particular the core structure of the deck, which should remain similar. In a seed round, you'd have fewer details and metrics to show and in a Series B, you'd typically add extra info and metrics in an appendix. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4TqeseYnZciRvRRPoKDDFA/df3099186ffde0e0f154dab7170eb355/image_152.png) ### Structure of the deck A Series A deck normally consists of around 20 slides plus sometimes an appendix (~5 slides). The range is typically 15–30 slides in total. I would avoid going beyond 30 pages to prevent it becoming too lengthy. We recommend the following structure to cover the important boxes VCs want to check when reading through the deck: - Cover + exec sum - Problem - Solution - Product - Market - Company today (metrics & financials) - Team - What's next - Appendix This is an order I recommend, however the flow can vary depending on your business. If there is one dimension that stands out and is remarkably more exciting, you should consider putting it earlier in your deck. One example of this is the market section: If your market is massive and growing very fast (and there is already VC excitement around your market) it might make sense to put one slide about the market directly after the problem section or to even start with it after the exec sum. Some components such as user testimonials or deep dives on parts of the business model have no fixed spot but, in general, the earlier the reader understands the core of the business, the more likely it is that your traction and achievements will create excitement. ### Building the deck - Put the right effort into building your deck, get multiple rounds of feedback on it from your existing investors and other entrepreneurs. - Make it look nice. Have a designer in your team help with that or consider spending a few $ on a freelancer to polish it. If your deck has very poor design, what will an investor think your product looks like? - If you want to make it really nice, consider Figma for polishing or building your deck. Some of the best decks I see are the result of the power of Figma.
