Pitch is also a good option that more and more founders are using instead of PowerPoint or Google Slides. ### Cover + exec summary - Every deck needs a cover, choose one that resonates with the industry. - Not every pitch deck has an exec summary, but I think it's good to have one to be able to convey your strongest pitch points early on and in a few bullets, highlight some key investment attractions, e.g. how strong your growth is, how large the market is, how awesome user love is, etc. If your audience can already see by slide two that your company is exciting, they'll read all the other slides more diligently instead of skimming through, looking for the highlights. Make sure this slide is concise and contains just a few bullets with short sentences. It's not about explaining your whole deck in one slide, but showcasing the key attractions. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4aauUi44FigSw2F4dycTNO/9c700ba5e4cee5d184b6ce38a40cbeb5/image_153.png) ### Problem + Solution - To allow your business to shine later on, it is important to thoroughly explain the problem to the reader of your deck and outline how you will solve it. - Help the user understand how big the pain point and problem is by backing its severeness up with specific statistics/data and intuitive illustrations or graphics. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4IAUR40pb3Mz30rgpKbGPB/89741d150b715a77866abcb99e4739aa/image_154.png) ### Product - The product section is a part that we at Creandum are particularly eager about. We believe that letting your product speak for you is a match ball to prove your potential. A beautiful product with customer love can compensate for financial infancy and is a strong reference to how the product will develop in the future. - Explain and showcase the product with pictures, outline its core functionalities and explain how they add value. The reader should be able to quickly understand what your product does and get an impression for look and feel. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/1v1vGr4fpQAVTy8f23eefe/fa40c17a1a164e127d2bc2bf3a5a337c/image_155.png) ### Market - Market size is a core component for VCs to evaluate if the opportunity is "big enough" for their focus. Generally the market should have the potential to allow for building a (multi-) billion $ company. My colleague, Carl, has written [a good blog on this topic](https://medium.com/startup-grind/your-market-size-is-only-a-fraction-of-what-you-think-it-is-f31f79cd1e95) and I've created [a small calculator](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1_SdUSs--3tCrQ8ZfUTC_J0yaKar3ofgTPtn_J0xUQKU/edit?usp=sharing) for working out whether your market size is large enough for VC. - Show the total addressable revenue market size. Avoid only stating broad (often inflated) industry market sizes. Ideally, you have a bottom-up calculation behind what you show. - Give your perspective on market development and future size, in particular if you operate in a market that is just emerging. - Mention important market characteristics if applicable (e.g. highly fragmented structure). ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup1

articles.title: Creandum backs Osu
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.excerpt: The payment app for the self-employed
articles.text: ### Empowering the self-employed via seamless instant payments When it comes to payments, changes in customer behaviour occur in waves once a new technology is introduced. In 2011, [we backed iZettle](https://blog.creandum.com/the-izettle-story-with-cofounder-magnus-nilsson-19e4761143) to empower every offline merchant to accept card payments via POS. Over the years, card payments have been adopted rapidly, and iZettle enabled millions of merchants to run their business more smoothly. Today, we are very excited to announce another wave of payment disruption for microbusinesses, thanks to [Osu](https://www.payosu.com/). We see that [PSD2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_Services_Directive) with open banking technology is once again enabling businesses to improve the payment experience and handling. Open banking uses mobile banking authentication to facilitate an automatic money transfer. _**The advantages are:**_ _1. The **cost** of a bank transfer **is absolutely nothing**_ _2. The level of **security is high** due to the biometric authentication requirement_ _3. The **payment is instant** with no holding period_ _4. Open banking payments are **10x more convenient** than entering an IBAN_ So far, open banking technology has mainly been used for online, low-frequency and high-value transactions whereby the traditional 2–3% payment fees hurt the merchants the most. Physical, e-commerce and marketplace sales are still dominated by card transactions as they are fast, and keep store queues short while online sales conversion rates remain high. Higher merchant payment fees are motivated by tokenization and other checkout innovations. However, if we look more closely at which transactions are still mostly cash-based or reliant on manual bank transfers, we discover the millions of micro-businesses across Europe. With Osu, we are proud to back the Swiss Army knife for sole traders. [Noam](https://www.linkedin.com/in/noam-nevo-78896022/), [Alon](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alon-zion-64550438/) & [Daniel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/daniel-scott-il/) built the perfect mobile app solution for professionals such as personal trainers, roofers, taxi drivers, or osteopaths to manage their business and never worry about payment fees or chasing banking transfers ever again. Osu charges a SaaS fee, thereby giving the merchants back 100% of their revenue and much more. Instead of troublesome IBAN transfers or withdrawing cash for every session, with Osu the customers have a much better experience. ![Osu founders Daniel Scott (CBO), Noam Nevo (CEO), and Alon Zion (COO/CPO)](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4MCNNoZK6234AZOXZ6ACs5/bf053aa02ab710c8e8206e68b448e013/image_150.jpg) _**Osu works as follows:**_ _1. A payment link or an invoice is shared in any digital channel (e.g. via message or email)_ _2. The customer opens the link and selects their bank_ _3. Their banking app opens automatically and asks for payment authentication_ _4. The payment is successful and an invoice is automatically generated and assigned to the payment_ ![The super smooth Osu app experience](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/6MmV8pVV5d3er1aYv3QLcQ/cafaa7921980e41e9da667ca61e50d4f/image_151.png) On the customer's side, there is no additional app needed, there is no additional account needed, and the process takes less than 15 seconds. For merchants, Osu is not just facilitating the payment. The app uses the collected customer information to offer a neat CRM system and later also calendar features, bookkeeping, and taxation services. Merchants do not need to set up an Osu bank account. They can stay at their business account of choice and use Osu as a layer on top to run the business. We believe that microbusinesses - and sole traders in particular - do not need 15 different SaaS subscriptions to run their business. We believe they need Osu. At Creandum, we like to see companies that do not simply force merchants to use a radically different infrastructure, but rather facilitate more business, easier business, and faster business. **Today, we are excited to add Osu to the [#CreandumFamily](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/) and lead their $3M seed round. Want to be part of the next payment revolution? [Osu is hiring](http://careers@payosu.com)!** _[Sign up](https://bit.ly/3chVFFf) to get the latest Creandum news, insights and resources right to your inbox._

articles.title: Backing Craft
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.excerpt: The only writing tool you need
articles.text: Imagine needing only one tool to create well-drafted texts, beautiful presentations and well-thought-out newsletters. **** Imagine switching between on- and offline seamlessly. And being able to share notes and documents easily for unlimited collaboration, across mobile, tablet and desktop. Imagine doing all this with a _joyful feeling of support from an app that helps you shin_e. And with an app that is _perfectly connected to your other tech stac_k. **Craft is rewriting the future of note-taking.** [Craft](https://www.craft.do/) is a mobile-first, cross-platform, modern writing tool with full feature parity across platforms. Users can both consume and _**joyfully create**_ visually compelling documents on desktop and with purpose-built apps on mobile devices, big and small. Craft excels by bringing a range of features together in a compelling UX that works and syncs flawlessly across all platforms. The tool is natively _**connected**_, meaning it allows users to keep data in whatever separate tools they've already invested in. And push content from Craft to those, as well as - in the future - easily pull data back into the craft documents. It excels in creating and sharing notes but is aware of - and interoperable with - other contexts. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3pcUizLfHqFlITHvuXOZW0/cc3b900f16a51405ebe69a7c0b36931d/image_148.jpg) **Here's our top list of reasons for loving Craft** - **Its ease of use and slick interface** The difference is especially palpable on touchscreen devices. - **It works like magic to make anything you create look beautiful**The tool grows on you: before you know it the shortcuts help you even quicker create beautiful content. - **Data storage and privacy**Craft is offline-first (your data is always available), which means you can view and edit your notes anytime, anywhere. You can choose between: ** Craft's own servers (100% real-time sync and collaboration) ** Third-party cloud- or your own file system (100% control your data) - **Integrations and data portability** Craft allows you to transfer your data to other services with one click or tap on the screen. Today these are writing tools or task managers, but this is an area where Craft will continue to lead innovation and differentiate. _In short, **Craft makes it possible to create stunning results with low effort.**_ We are not the only ones amazed by Craft: Just four months after the initial product launch, Craft has converted thousands of users into brand advocates and managed to build a strong community that enjoys the ["exquisitely well-thought-out and elegantly designed"](https://www.macstories.net/stories/macstories-selects-2020-recognizing-the-best-apps-of-the-year/) multi-device capabilities. Even competitors are lining up to build partnerships with Craft. **So who's behind this revolutionary creative tool?** Enter Hungary. It would appear that Creandum is developing a sweet spot for this part of Europe as of recent. After backing [Shapr3D](https://blog.creandum.com/creandum-%EF%B8%8F-shapr3d-427b46b955c6?source=false---------0) and [SEON](https://blog.creandum.com/democratizing-fraud-fighting-creandum-backs-seon-539468e5ccdf), Craft marks our third bet in this market (and we're sure it won't be the last). The company was founded by serial entrepreneur [Balint Orosz](https://www.linkedin.com/in/balintorosz/), who previously founded Distinction which was acquired by Skyscanner. Equipped with his small-but-stellar team of engineers from top tech companies such as Prezi and Skyscanner, natural product intuition, and world-class product design sense, Balint has already been able to deliver a lot with little. We have seldom seen a founder so deeply dedicated to the problem he is solving and thoughtful about how to find the best solutions. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/79gjJrJdGLnxlMR3qsqSE1/df04c8888e7645a23987653f778233e0/image_149.jpg) Today, we're thrilled to call Craft part of the #CreandumFamily. The Creandum funds are in good company as they lead Craft's $8M Series A round with additional participation from InReach Ventures and the Skyscanner founder Garreth Williams. Craft will use the fresh capital to further refine the product's connectivity features and make it integrable into as much of the user's workflow as possible. Want to be part of Craft's dynamically growing team? [They are hiring](https://www.craft.do/careers) (remotely)! Read more on [Techcrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/01/collaborative-ios-app-craft-docs-secures-8m-led-by-creandum-and-a-skyscanner-mafia/) or [Forbes Hungary](https://forbes.hu/uzlet/craft-startup-exkluziv-creandum/). Want to hear more about why we are so bullish on the Central-Eastern European startup scene? Together with Simon, I'll join Startup Hungary's Event [First Monday](https://hopin.com/events/creandum-at-first-monday?utm_source=Newsletter+1&utm_campaign=f513385428-March_2021_campaign&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_daf4d8392b-f513385428-#schedule) on April 12th to discuss how international VC works, our Budapest-based portfolio and going global from CEE. [Register here](https://hopin.com/events/creandum-at-first-monday?utm_source=Newsletter+1&utm_campaign=f513385428-March_2021_campaign&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_daf4d8392b-f513385428-#schedule).

articles.title: Abacum — the next generation of financial planning
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Spreadsheets - the joy or pain of almost anyone working in financial departments. Yes, even though we live in the digitized, hyper-productive world of 2021, many finance teams still spend 70% of their time manually updating financial models in tedious, old-fashioned, non-collaborative sheets and forms. And we don't only see this in big incumbents. In fact, many young companies such as those in the Creandum funds' portfolio still lack more automated, native collaborative solutions. We strongly believe it's time for a change and are thrilled to lead [Abacum](https://www.abacum.io/)'s $7m seed round. In many mid-sized companies, finance teams use a mixture of Google Sheets, .csv files, a disconnected tech stack and a lot of copy/paste. Especially in fast-growing companies, data is outdated after a few months or even weeks and requires lots of manual work to update it again. Collaboration on this happens in a highly inefficient way via email, spreadsheet versions and lacks a central, trackable place (imagine trying to find where your tech lead shared the main assumptions for a board forecast). Time to say goodbye to spreadsheets and hello to Abacum. ### Becoming the backbone of finance teams. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3jEtS3C9GAxnpjDVP1i4RR/234fa2fb624a2a3ba681eb8d2eea012e/image_146.jpg) Having experienced these problems themselves many times in their previous roles - both in the finance industry and CFO in different scale-ups -[ Julio ](https://www.linkedin.com/in/juliomartinez1982/)and [Jorge](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jorgelluch/) have deep insights into building a game-changing product for the mid-market. At the core of it is **real-time data** and **collaboration**. Abacum can integrate any other software used in different parts of the company (accounting, CRM, HR, ERP, etc.) into its platform. It keeps all teams and departments in sync by automatically updating forecasting models, and budgeting and performance reports with real-time data. The product fosters collaboration across the company for more interconnected decision-making, making it easy to comment, track, interact & more. At long last, collaboration on financial and operational data is seamless and intuitive. Combine this with a truly slick and user-friendly product, Abacum takes away a lot of the tedious, manual tasks and empowers finance teams to _actually strategically think_ _about_ and interpret the data they are working with on a daily basis, thereby boosting their productivity and efficiency to new levels. More than that, the platform becomes the single source of truth for financial data. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/14tXjRXJ5AE5WzcYXssxvu/af34192ef08802b41e9829f8cafa73b0/image_147.jpg) ### Coupled with this superb, well-thought-out product, the team behind Abacum quickly earned our conviction. Julio used to be Founder & CEO at InnoCells, launching several ventures and brings along extensive investment banking experience. His co-founder, Jorge, is a European Space Agency Engineer and then CFO/COO at three of Spain's most successful tech companies: TravelPerk, Wallapop and Privalia. But it's not just the two founders and their deep industry insights that impressed us at first sight. The team has already proven strong early-stage hiring, having brought in a wealth of senior talent from top US and European companies including N26, Stitch Fix, Turo, TravelPerk or Ideo. In less than a year since its launch, the team has built a slick product, absolved the Y-Combinator program, and more than that, demonstrated great initial traction and customer love from its first clients in the US as well as in Europe - such as Typeform, Cabify, Ebury or Garten. Today, we are delighted to add Abacum to the [#CreandumFamily](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/) and lead their $7M seed round and team up with existing investors and friends at K-fund, PROfounders and YC. Also joining the round will be angels and founders such as Justin Kan (Twitch Co-founder, CEO), Maximilian Tayenthal (N26 Co-founder, CFO), Thomas Lehrman (GLG Co-founder, CEO), Avi Meir (TravelPerk Co-founder, CEO) and domain-experts such as Jenny Bloom (Zapier CFO and former Mailchimp CFO) and Mike Asher (CFO at Neo4j). The company will use the new capital to further develop the product and expand the team in Barcelona, the US and remote! Want to join a in the making? [The team is hiring: more here](https://medium.com/r?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.notion.so%2FWe-are-hiring-240cee3897fa4ae08f1484ab472bb2ec). Read more on [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/08/yc-backed-abacum-nets-7m-to-empower-finance-teams-with-real-time-data-and-collaboration-tools/). [Sign up](https://bit.ly/3chVFFf) to get the latest Creandum news, insights and resources right to your inbox.

articles.title: Speedinvest & Creandum Report: The Growth and Future of Climate Tech Startups in Europe
articles.text: This decade will be mission-critical to the future of our planet. Humankind has ambitious goals to meet in order to stop climate change. We at [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/) and [Speedinvest](https://speedinvest.com/) believe that technology will play a huge role and we see Europe paving the way for Climate Tech innovation. To get a better understanding of the current state and trends in the sector, [we decided to map out the Climate Tech landscape in Europe](https://www.speedinvest.com/blog/europes-leadership-in-climate-tech) according to the eight categories defined by the [European Green Deal](https://ec.europa.eu/info/publications/communication-european-green-deal_en). ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/771N6j6V09aQDdCiJ0IL5H/fcebd99bb378792f590eee530d94178b/image_140.jpg) We built a foundation using sources such as Crunchbase, Dealroom and our respective deal flows, and crowdsourced additional companies with your help. In the end, we recorded more than 1,100 companies that are chasing substantial business opportunities in the sector. We compared the list to our internal deal flow and other sources in the field to understand the current state of Climate Tech in Europe and how Europe's startup scene is positioned to impact climate change in the coming years. ## Questions we answer: - What region and countries are taking the lead in European Climate Tech? - Which pillars of the European Green Deal are most represented in our list? - How does our list compare to other data sources? - What specific tech trends are we seeing? - What are Speedinvest and Creandum looking for in startups? ## Western Europe in the Climate Tech Lead To get an overview of activity by location, we split the continent into four regions: Northern, Southern, Eastern and Western Europe. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/20QyNNcVWxCkoMKLnBKU8/84d8287be4146aad264227ae5854c076/image_141.jpg) Most Climate Tech startups on our list are located in Western Europe (53%), followed by Northern Europe (36%), Southern Europe (7%) and Eastern Europe (3%). When we look at specific countries, Germany is leading the way (24%), followed by the UK (15%) and France (9%). ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7a6zqVHpxQuiu8wIgcfoMK/2543f7e78904f5b477c9085197348188/image_142.jpg) When it comes to VC funding, Sweden ($3.7bn) and Germany ($3.4bn) are the countries where the Climate Tech ventures on our list have attracted the most funds between 2006–2021. The number for Sweden is primarily a result of huge funding rounds for one company - Northvolt ($3.3bn). With this outlier removed, Germany leads, followed by France ($1.7bn) and the UK ($822m). ## Energy and Smart Mobility lead our list of Climate Tech companies While many on our list operate across several of the eight pillars of the European Green Deal, Energy companies (suppliers of clean and secure energy) are in the lead, representing 26%. In second place, Smart Mobility with 18%, followed by Food (16%), Zero Pollution (12%) and Clean & Circular Economy (11%). The categories with the fewest companies, according to our list, are Sustainable Building (7%), Biodiversity and Sustainable Finance, each with 5%. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/5GlD4bxSj0U8AuSSiGlIL/c71ee8f48e8ab595bde97a2a4b917b43/image_143.jpg) Energy has also attracted the most VC funding with $5bn, dominated by large players such as Northvolt. Energy is followed by Smart Mobility with $3.7bn in financing (Flixbus, BlaBlaCar, Volocopter, TIER, Lilium). ## Does the Climate List align with what we see at Creandum x Speedinvest? Diving into our collective Climate Tech deal flow According to PwC, global Climate Tech has experienced a rapid increase in investment over the past seven years (2013–2019), **growing by more than 3750%**. In line with the increasing number of startups in the space. Not surprisingly, the number of Climate Tech pitches received by Speedinvest (see below) has increased significantly year over year for the last decade. Creandum has seen a very similar trend. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7nDAbmZFM6m3CIaPxuIE1/06f5941137f35ced25e9f6a23b192d5c/image_144.jpg) Over the past four quarters, our deal flow has been dominated by startups from the UK (17%), Germany (14%) and France (12%). Combined, the Nordics account for about 13%, in line with where our network is the strongest. ![](https://miro.medium.com/0*2IJLV9tdJm02-VGo) A majority of Europe's top 15 startup hubs are located in these countries (London, Berlin, Paris, etc.), [according to EU Startups](https://www.eu-startups.com/2020/11/top-30-europes-biggest-startup-hubs-in-2020/). And Dealroom and PwC have named Berlin one of [the world's largest Climate Tech hubs](https://www.statista.com/chart/23099/venture-capital-funding-raised-by-climate-tech-startups/), in terms of VC funding raised ($0.9b). While more than 1,100 companies is a great start, it's admittedly still a limited data set. Nevertheless, we believe it's a valuable startup point to understand what's going on, and where future opportunities lie. ## 5 trends we see driving Climate Tech in Europe In addition to this data, Speedinvest and Creandum compared notes on what we see in our respective deal flows and founder conversations. We were quick to align on five key areas of opportunity that we observe and will continue to monitor closely over the next year(s). **Carbon software** While our climate list claims only 5% of companies fall into the category of Sustainable Finance, 2020 was for us the starting point of many carbon software solutions. Typically, these companies measure, monitor and help reduce the CO2 footprint of companies and individuals. Some players in this field are [CarbonChain](https://carbonchain.com/), [Earthly](https://earthly.org/), [Tomorrow](https://www.tmrow.com/) and Speedinvest backed [Planetly](https://www.planetly.org/). More recently, we've seen the emergence of more vertical players that focus on reducing emissions specificall

articles.title: The new wave of productivity
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: _How can new productivity products still achieve more output with less input? The new generation of solutions trends towards the fusion of applications. Sharing what we're looking for in this category._ The global pandemic had a drastic impact on how we approach work and productivity. Out of this recalibration, there are big questions raised on the consequences of hybrid teamwork as well as work from home. Decade-long working style habits have been subject to reflection. The overarching question being asked more than ever is: How can we as a company, team, and individual be most productive? We are excited about the productivity space (Creandum backed companies such as [Amie](http://amie.so) or [Craft](http://craft.do)) and believe it's a great point in time to look closely at the upcoming generation of productivity. ### What to do vs. how to do it In the productivity space, there is a common misconception that productivity equals smart working. Looking at Apple's App Store, 5 of the top 10 productivity tools are note-taking and to-do apps. But in fact, the word "productivity" originates from industrial production measuring the ratio of input vs. output. When we apply this to office work, that would only encompass the efficiency of tasks and not the process of tackling it. In our belief most often the much harder step comes beforehand when one has to decide **what** to do and in which order. This decision problem is labeled with the effectiveness of work that kicks in before the individual productivity. ### Urgency vs. importance When thinking of the order and agenda we set for our tasks, we are most often driven by external stakeholders and deadlines. In VC for example, I often need to "clear" the calendar for important due diligence tasks with tight deadlines, and consequently, push back less time-sensitive ones - like writing the next blog post! The Eisenhower method (given to us by the US president who perhaps had quite a busy calendar to handle) displays these trade-offs and provides a framework to structure your to-dos effectively. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/70GtR32j9qFhAmm4HNOURq/df210e29ddb536f0854dd138e6ab5fae/image_137.jpg) The most overlooked and undervalued quadrant is the important/not urgent section. It is often the difference between sustainable long-term success or chasing deadline after deadline with limited progress. The difficulty in transferring important to-dos from the notebook to the calendar is real. The magic of finally getting the underlying decisive tasks done by scheduling them right away in a calendar was one of the key hypotheses for our decision to [back Amie's pre-seed round](https://sifted.eu/articles/amie-creandum-dennis-muller/). When deciding on _what to do,_ there are different factors and tools that influence the decision-making process: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/3Q3OkoGoKLZdvdQhJCYeKn/113eeee643ae79893f9ce531c62b9006/image_138.png) As we can see, [Amie](http://amie.so) fixes the overlooked intersection of the WHY and the WHEN. Amie does not immediately help you do more; it does, however, help you do more of what really matters to you. Amidst the current trend of creating super apps and fusion of use cases, we expect more players to move towards the middle by integrating collaborative working tools (Craft, Evernote), calendar integrations (Superhuman, Slack), or becoming the underlying agenda-setting and work progress tool for businesses (Asana). One big area where we see still potential is help in prioritizing work and private events and time allocation. Especially in settings where "the office" and the home are the same place, and where work and leisure happen at the same time, the struggle of prioritizing tasks becomes omnipresent and is no longer tied to geographical locations or temporal boundaries. ### More with less After allocating resources (mostly time) to certain tasks, the next challenge is getting the most value out of the activity with the least effort. Now we are talking about all the tools that boost our productivity by either increasing the output or saving on inputs. For theses the gain/pain is equal to the attractiveness of the product and the ease of selling the product: ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/9gPrrnAk3Tt7mN9LVkaNN/cc852068533389ec989885fda0a4d5b2/image_139.png) ### The SaaS productivity dilemma Arguably it should be fairly easy to pitch users tools that have such a rational direct effect on performance. But productivity products often come with one big dilemma. The more they create touchpoints and interaction (normally the dream of high retention), the more they take the most important source of efficiency: **Focus.** Even [Tim Cook recognized](https://techcrunch.com/2019/04/23/tim-cook-wants-you-to-put-down-your-iphone/) that constant Apple Watch vibrations might not create the highest quality of life, and silenced notifications himself. A new playing field of quality over quantity in engagement is created. This is why we are on the hunt for beautiful products that can boost productivity with high-value interactions and not only quantity. Spending less time for a better value than an incumbent player is the spot that provides great value and can get users to switch their work/productivity habits from today. ### What we look for Productivity is a space with many solutions out there, the key for us is to see how you stand out and how you will create superior user love. Here are a couple of points that we consider essential and look for: - **Unique insight**: what's the unique insight around workflows, processes, and habits that make your product desirable? - **What's your entry point?**: Productivity products often overlap with other used solutions (legacy or not) and most are trying to expand over time. There are many entry points to productivity depending on the area/solution, so you need to have a strong hypothesis on the right entry point and potential expansion or focus. - **Easy to

articles.title: Creandum expands its investment team
articles.author: Staffan Helgesson
articles.text: ### A new Partner based in Stockholm and a new Principal based in London At [Creandum](https://www.creandum.com/), one of our most important roles is supporting the entrepreneurs we work with as best we can. This entails making sure we always have their back - in good times and in bad. In order to truly understand our founders' challenges, it's critical that we have a thorough understanding of the operational efforts behind building great companies. That is one of the reasons we are beyond excited to announce **two new members** to the team: **[Sabina Wizander](https://www.creandum.com/team/sabina-wizander)** and **[Gemma Bloemen](https://www.creandum.com/team/gemma-bloemen)**, who will join as **Partner** and **Principal** respectively. Sabina and Gemma both have an outstanding track record when it comes to proving their profound operational expertise: Sabina spent her last four years working at the Creandum funds' portfolio company **[Kry](https://www.kry.se/)** that [recently surpassed a $2B dollar valuation](https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/27/kry-closes-312m-series-d-after-use-of-its-telehealth-tools-surged-100-yoy/). At Kry, Sabina held [different senior management positions](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sabinawizander/) ranging from Director of Business Operations, Chief Commercial Officer, and most recently, Chief Strategy Officer. She joined Kry shortly after spending a couple of years in Creandum's own team as an Investment Manager from 2015 to 2017. In that time, she worked closely with our General Partner Fredrik Cassel and was heavily involved in [Kry's seed round led by the Creandum funds](https://blog.creandum.com/kry-fills-all-the-boxes-of-our-healthcare-checklist-4caa51fe3b37). Sabina was also part of the Berlin task force established to open up Creandum's office there. As the 19th employee at Kry, Sabina played an essential role in scaling the company to become today's European digital health category leader. Prior to that, she was with McKinsey in San Francisco, supporting some of the large tech companies there. Sabina, who holds a Master's degree in Engineering, was also part of the core team shaping McKinsey's view on future technologies together with prominent advisors such as Hal Varian and Eric Schmidt. ![In addition to strong operational and analytical skills, Sabina was already impressing us back then with her fearless go-getter attitude which manifested itself in many ways, not least when throwing herself on a plane to take part in her first Burning Man and build networks globally.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7ESBYVmyonON1zHAqpnOtg/5af38dbd2f2bc6cfb87a762e32a44d54/image_135.jpg) Given her history with Creandum, her dynamic and passionate personality, and our conviction that her heart beats for social change, innovation and impact-driven companies, we're delighted to have her back in the team as **Partner**. Sabina will be based in Stockholm but will explore different industries all across Europe, like the rest of the team. Our new **Principal**, Gemma Bloemen, joins us from **[Elder](https://www.elder.org/)**, the UK's leading health tech marketplace. As Chief Operating Officer, Gemma was deeply involved in steering the company's overall strategy and worked closely together with the CEO on many aspects of the business, including their [Series B fundraising process in 2019](https://tech.eu/brief/elder-raises-8-2-million-series-b-to-provide-personalised-in-home-care-to-aging-population/). Before joining Elder, Gemma was part of scaling **Uber** during its most formative years growing the local UK team from 20 to 250 people. Prior to that Gemma spent a number of years at McKinsey. Originally from The Netherlands, she has lived on four different continents and holds degrees from Yale and INSEAD. We've got to know Gemma as an extremely ambitious and curious extrovert, who enjoys working with entrepreneurs from different industries. As an angel investor herself, she's been proactively supporting founding teams, sharing her expertise in operations and people/recruitment, and is no stranger to strategic planning and goal setting. She has a soft spot for marketplaces, digital health, and sustainability, and has always been a champion for diversity and inclusion. At Uber, she co-chaired Women of Uber in 2017, and, along with much else, we are looking forward to seeing her supporting other companies to further their diversity efforts. The Creandum funds have over many years already invested in a range of companies from the UK ecosystem, such as [depop](https://www.depop.com/), [Tide](https://blog.creandum.com/better-business-banking-creandum-invests-in-tide-dbb661c33eb2), [Laka](https://blog.creandum.com/turning-an-industry-upside-down-creandum-backs-laka-c0c53cfcd2ed), [Argent](https://blog.creandum.com/the-beginners-guide-to-argent-58356efcea42), [Dija](https://blog.creandum.com/deliver-it-now-creandum-backs-next-generation-grocer-dija-f3feeb44a84e), [YuLife](https://blog.creandum.com/insurance-with-a-heart-announcing-creandums-backing-of-yulife-4cd96ef02567), [Osu](https://blog.creandum.com/backing-osu-the-payment-app-for-the-self-employed-d5eaf5022f5), and others, and we're tremendously excited to have Gemma as our first Investment Team hire based in London to further strengthen our activity on the ground. She will be working in close cooperation with the firm's wider investment advisory team in Creandum's other key hubs Stockholm, Berlin and San Francisco. ![When Gemma is not meeting or supporting entrepreneurs, she's out with her new dog Gimli.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4TMgbdsaYkb4eXZYit9tzA/1f10f14459656722de8026921b387ed4/image_136.jpg) The whole team at Creandum is thrilled to be working with Sabina and Gemma over the coming years in our continued mission to be the premier venture firm for Europe's most ambitious entrepreneurs. To both, we wish you a very warm welcome to the #CreandumFamily!

articles.title: Looking at the Spanish tech ecosystem from an international perspective in 2021
articles.author: Peter Specht
articles.text: Creandum recently announced [Abacum's seed round](https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/08/yc-backed-abacum-nets-7m-to-empower-finance-teams-with-real-time-data-and-collaboration-tools/), which marks the fund's second investment in Spain after [Factorial](https://factorialhr.com/) . We are optimistic about the Spanish tech scene and think the ecosystem is on a great path to becoming an important hub in the European startup landscape. Two years ago, we did a [deep dive](https://blog.creandum.com/looking-at-the-spanish-tech-ecosystem-from-an-international-perspective-533c8f4514f2) into the Spanish tech ecosystem from an international perspective. In this piece, we will revisit this and further explore the role of local and international investors, key geographic hubs, and the startups emerging within them. ### Recent development We have seen very positive developments in the Spanish ecosystem over recent years, such as: - **Increase in the availability of Spanish early-stage capital,** especially for seed rounds. In recent years, Spanish VCs have been raising their second or even third funds, and early-stage fund sizes are growing. K Funds, 4 Founders Capital, Big Sur Ventures, Kibo Ventures and Samaipata's latest funds are great examples of that. First-time fund All Iron raised the [largest debut fund in Spain](https://sifted.eu/articles/all-iron-ventures-fund/) to date last year, and [Target Global](https://techcrunch.com/2019/09/24/pan-european-vc-fund-target-global-is-opening-an-office-in-barcelona/) opened an office in Barcelona. It's safe to say that the early-stage VC scene is booming and we have been lucky to invest alongside great Spanish funds. - **International investments flowing into the market**Next to local early-stage capital, international capital plays a key role in the ecosystem, and more international investors have been keen to make bets in Spain. **Over 80%** of the seed and series A rounds in 2020 included international investors. This indicates international investors' confidence in Spain and VCs investing via zoom only has increased accessibility. But we'll touch more on international investors later. - **Strong development of Spain's key hubs - Barcelona and Madrid**Unlike many other cities in Europe, the startup landscape in Spain is not dominated by one hub, rather there is a co-existence of hubs. Barcelona and Madrid are at the center of the tech scene and attract entrepreneurs, talent, and local and international investors. We also see other tech centers develop next to these two key hubs, such as Valencia and Andalusia. - **Role models leading the way**With the first Spanish unicorns, the floodgates are starting to open; Spain is slowly breaking out its €100M status quo exits. Glovo, Cabify, Idealista and Spanish-rooted Flywire lead the way to billion-dollar valuations. Together with companies like JobandTalent, TravelPerk and Typeform, they serve as a breeding ground for entrepreneurial talent and strengthen the local "halo effect". We increasingly see former employees of these scaleups choosing to go on to found their own ventures. __ For example, Sifted recently wrote about the Glovo "mafia", Abacum's co-founder Jorge was previously at TravelPerk and Wallapop, and Teo and Pedro from Circular worked together at JobandTalent. We've previously seen this halo effect in European hubs like London, Stockholm and Berlin, and are excited to see a similar development in Spain. Moreover, joining or founding a startup has become a serious possibility for students after leaving university. - **Fundamentals in place:** a) low cost of living with attractive costs for great talent b) good technical and business universities (ESADE, IE, IESE, Politècnica Madrid/Catalunya etc.) c) vibrant tech hubs and scene (BCN/MAD) Despite considerable progress, the number of unicorns and success stories are naturally not yet at the level of Europe's major hubs. But we're confident that companies like Factorial, Onna, Paack, JobandTalent etc. are on a great trajectory and will serve as role models for young entrepreneurs. ## What's still missing? From the perspective of an international investor, we have a observed a few challenges that the Spanish landscape faces: ### Lack of local growth capital Similar to our conclusion two years ago, there is still a lack of local growth capital available. Although local early-stage capital has become more widely available, growth capital for series A, B or C+ is still highly dependent on international investors. We believe that for the Spanish ecosystem to truly mature, more local growth capital needs to be available. ### Laggard copycat behavior A multitude of Spanish startups have been known to replicate business models originating from the US or Northern Europe. We see a triangular movement; starting with innovation in the US, then startups in Northern/Western Europe apply the business model to the European landscape, which gets replicated for the Southern European or LATAM market by Spanish ventures. Below are a few examples of this triangular movement: Robinhood was founded in the US in 2013, in 2015 Trade Republic brought the model to EU, and copied in Spain in 2018 by Ninety Nine. We see a similar pattern for neobanks: Chime launched in the US in 2013, Revolut in Western Europe in 2015, and Bnext and BNC10 in Spain in 2016 and 2018 respectively. In delivery there is a clear triangulation between Grubhub, Delivery Hero and Glovo. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7CjMDhnFe8p7k2DxHlwvjs/bc657c7dba06d6391494c25c2fc9a4ad/image_131.jpg) Although Picasso once said "Good artist copy, great artists steal" and Steve Jobs added that Apple has always been "shameless about stealing great ideas", questions remain as to how much innovation originating from the Spanish tech scene has the potential to be a European or global category leader. We would love to see even more companies from Spain being the "first" ones coming up with business models or executing

articles.title: Depop — organically opening the hearts and wardrobes of Gen Z
articles.author: Fredrik Cassel
articles.text: _[Depop](https://www.depop.com/), the fashion marketplace for the next generation, has just been acquired by Etsy for $1.625B. Since [the Creandum funds invested in Depop at Series A stage](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/depop/company_financials) in 2015, it's been a rare pleasure to be part of their mostly self-funded growth journey. Etsy is a unique partner for the next stage of Maria Raga and the team's development of the Depop brand and community._ Depop's growth story is an unprecedented one. With competition raising ever-larger amounts and allocating a substantial share of it to paid and influencer marketing channels, Depop's organic growth rate is still upwards of 90%, even last year, almost a decade after the company was founded. Similar to Spotify or Instagram, Depop has managed to build a platform that attracts its users - the vast majority is under the age of 25 - on a daily basis. This is very different to most other marketplaces and makes Depop something much more important. Unlike many of its peers, Depop is not only the go-to point for transactions, _**it's actually a destination for daily inspiration and, most importantly, interaction around unique fashion**_. The social commerce trend might have other origins, but Depop took it to the next level: While in many instances social commerce means to ‘follow what an influencer buys', at Depop it's all about the interaction between buyer and seller (60% of users do both) - liking, commenting or getting the same love or feedback on what you sell. The boundaries between commerce and connections, consumption and production, and even entertainment and entrepreneurship have blurred for its audience. To quote [Maria Raga](https://www.linkedin.com/in/maria-raga-045b712/?originalSubdomain=uk), CEO of Depop, from today's press release: _**"Our community is made up of people who are creating a new fashion system by establishing new trends and making new from old. They come to Depop for the clothes, but stay for the culture."**_ ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7v0adrF3ihxAHxi0HfA2ze/df9d4a1ed6e5e8268d25bbc48b141bd8/image_126.jpg) Creating this level of engagement with both buyers and sellers doesn't happen overnight or by coincidence. Rather, it's a combination of many right decisions year after year, guided by a set of fundamental principles. Here are a few: 1. **Create an Authentic product** Simon Beckerman started Depop with some unique insights and, more importantly, a _feeling_ for what the next generation of consumers would be inspired by. Some stellar moves in the early days meant he could bring along well-known online profiles, defining and inspirational to the target audience, who made Depop _theirs_. It wasn't about paying them to shoot a video with the app, it was helping them to use the app and enjoy it as an extension of their online persona. The core users found something authentic. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/2u93bqEtK5F97icvWJWdLd/2ace6e55d0754e653573533d1bf7e034/image_127.jpg) **2. Care for the community** One of the secrets to Depop's success was that the team built and grew the platform as the community, not as outsiders looking in. They always put the users' needs and desires first. This includes boosting the most meaningful sellers, i.e. those who create content that represents the diverse, next-gen, recycled fashion brand and will help attract and retain new users particularly well. Almost without exception when I came by the office in the early days, preparations were underway for a photoshoot with an important seller or a meetup with a particular part of the community. **3. The products are ‘the product'** Finding and attracting the right sellers, the right brands, and making sure they upload the right (fashion) products that embody the Depop brand is a manual process. It has been amplified with tech over time, but it requires significant effort and attention from the Depop team. ![](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/ctq6HENycdc26pV9pj1d2/1f02632b880c7e5477ad8048ff13571f/image_128.jpg) Mastering this, and realizing that this is as much a part of the (tech) product roadmap as any improved functionality or feature in the app, is in my opinion the fundamental key to success and the completely unique path to market that Depop has. There's simply no way that money spent on paid marketing, no matter how much, can generate the same quality traffic as a user who comes to Depop after following a product for sale published somewhere else. And equally important - this user is much more likely to like what's offered there and stay for a long time. **4. A uniquely strong culture and leader** As Simon transitioned away from the CEO role, Maria Raga grew right into it, in the most amazing way. Maria joined as VP Operations in 2014 and took over the head coach role two years later. ![Maria Raga, CEO of Depop. Foto by [Dominik Tryba](https://introduce.berlin/).](https://miro.medium.com/0*6SxntevtNNqa52K2) The way Maria has taken the best of what Depop was born with and built its culture and organization into something incredibly unique and resilient is the most impressive company culture-building work I've seen. It cuts through so many dimensions, starting with attracting phenomenal global talent - one of Maria's fortes. _**And equally important - being patient enough in hiring, and diligent enough in promotion, to build a STELLAR and DIVERSE team**_, representative of the diverse and fantastic seller and buyer base. And in numbers, this means growing the company's net revenue from roughly 125K monthly and total valuation from <30M when the Creandum funds invested in 2015 to more than 50x that (did I mention that the growth was rather capital efficient?) . **Depop's organic growth story is both brilliant and hard-won and we're honoured to have had the pleasure to work with a CEO as exceptional as Maria, and her team. The acquisition by Etsy marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter - we will miss

articles.title: Creandum promotes Peter Specht to Partner
articles.author: Simon Schmincke
articles.text: At Creandum, we take great pride in finding the best entrepreneurs across Europe and the US - but we are equally excited when we find a superstar colleague, who rises through the ranks of the firm in record time. Peter has undoubtedly set a new benchmark when it comes to learning quickly, working relentlessly and moving the firm forward in every dimension. Promoting Peter to Partner is a natural next step and a testament to his dedication and success. Peter joined Creandum in the summer of 2017 from Bain after spending some time at Google and various companies in the Rocket Internet universe. Joining a company that was short of fancy offices or a well-known brand name in a new region motivated Peter: building the Creandum franchise first in the DACH region and later more and more in Spain. Peter's calculated appetite for risk, driven by his fine-grain due diligence capabilities, enabled Peter to become a trusted advisor both in the firm and to his portfolio companies. His eye for detail enabled him to push the work of various colleagues early on in his tenure at Creandum - always carefully weighing up risks and opportunities. In combination with his relentless work ethic, his goal-getter mentality shined early on when he was already winning deals across Europe. ![Creandum's first office in Berlin - barely any furniture, but work mode on.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4YJRZnXyDYFI62iWciKZxW/4bf56ba1745e84952d9b645a514f8719/image_123.png) Shortly after his promotion to Principal in 2019, Peter spent six months in Creandum's San Francisco office - allowing him to build out his network across the US venture scene. Today, Peter's connection to the US ecosystem helps the whole Creandum family navigate the American investor landscape. Further, Peter also opened up the Spanish market for Creandum, as he lived several years in Barcelona and led deals in SaaS companies [Factorial](https://blog.creandum.com/automating-your-hr-payroll-why-creandum-backed-factorial-c0907919f22b) and [Abacum](https://blog.creandum.com/abacum-the-next-generation-of-financial-planning-331ed1298dcb). Read Peter's recent [deep dive into the emerging Spanish tech scene here](https://blog.creandum.com/looking-at-the-spanish-tech-ecosystem-from-an-international-perspective-in-2021-fe0fdc23bc74). Peter focuses his work on SaaS, [B2B Marketplaces](https://blog.creandum.com/the-decade-of-b2b-marketplaces-and-what-we-are-looking-for-fdd116e67138), [Productivity](https://blog.creandum.com/the-new-wave-of-productivity-f8db35f5b316) and [Mobility](https://blog.creandum.com/perspective-on-mobility-tech-whats-next-742c3fe33278) - among others. Today, he serves on the board of [Factorial](http://www.factorialhr.com/), [CarOnSale](http://www.caronsale.de/), [Cargo.One](https://blog.creandum.com/digitising-the-air-freight-industry-creandum-backs-cargo-one-cc4c47173419), [Amie](https://blog.creandum.com/disrupting-the-productivity-stack-why-we-backed-amie-91cfc4e72232), [Twaice](https://blog.creandum.com/backing-twaice-the-new-standard-for-battery-analytics-4062c2e5fd8c) and [Abacum](http://www.abacum.io/) - and works closely with the team at [Voi](http://www.voiscooters.com/) and [Cake](https://blog.creandum.com/https-blog-creandum-com-backing-cake-f65171cff77b). _Peter believed in Amie when others saw nothing. I leaned on his advice many times when I would have acted over my head. He challenges me firmly, yet so respectfully. Congratulations on your well-deserved promotion, Peter!_ _**Dennis Müller, CEO and Founder, Amie**_ ![Peter organized our first SME day at Creandum for entrepreneurs to discuss best practices with founders & execs in this space.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/4PEPVRg2BYGvJAKAzu6pWc/df2c609141daa992477a46298e7262df/image_124.png) Peter is well known across the portfolio for having very close relationships with the entrepreneurs he works with. He always puts portfolio companies first and backs them throughout their journey. _Peter not only shows up when there are suns and rainbows but also when things get tough - I really appreciated his perspective on a lot of my most difficult decisions. I could really rely on Peter and the whole Creandum team to make our Series A fundraise a massive success - it would not have been possible without the team effort._ _I am grateful for a relationship with Peter based on trust and the conviction in building a large European disruptor._ _**Tom Krüger, CEO and Founder, CarOnSale**_ Peter tries to be as helpful to the portfolio companies as possible and is a master at orchestrating the best fundraising processes. He also shares his knowledge with the entrepreneurs that are not (yet) in our portfolio, by creating for example a [Series A deck template](https://blog.creandum.com/creandum-series-a-deck-template-21a6df9c1ac4), a guideline on [How to raise your next funding round](https://blog.creandum.com/how-to-raise-your-next-funding-round-7e6bd2e027e2), or a detailed outline on how to g[et from Seed to Series A](https://blog.creandum.com/getting-from-seed-to-series-a-f866b0793cfe). _Peter is a great partner for Factorial and myself as a CEO. He has supported us from the first day and has never hesitated_, _despite the rollercoaster nature of an early-stage start-up. When it came to us finding our path to fastest growth, Peter helped at all the key moments. He's 100% committed to supporting the founders and always bets on the winning product and team._ _I'm 100% sure I'll see Peter continue to thrive as an investor and I look forward to keeping him as a close confidant of Factorial._ _**Jordi Romero, CEO and Founder, Factorial**_ That being said, Peter, we could not think more highly of you, not only as a colleague but also as a friend. And despite your tremendous success so far, it is also fair to talk about things that didn't work out yet: the establishment of Oktoberfest as an institution here at Creandum. This is something we need to have a second shot at . ![](//images.

articles.title: Traits of unicorn founders
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.text: _The original article was published on [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2021/06/15/how-to-identify-unicorn-founders-when-theyre-still-early-stage/)._ As an early-stage VC, you spend time with hundreds of fantastic startups, trying to identify the potential winners by thinking about market size, business model, and competition. Nevertheless, deep down you know that in the long run, it all comes down to the team and the founder(s). When we look at the most successful companies in the [Creandum funds' portfolio](https://www.creandum.com/portfolio/), their amazing performance is in large parts thanks to the founders. However, even after 20 years in the industry, I have to admit that analyzing the team is still the most challenging part of the job. How do you evaluate a young first-time entrepreneur and an early-stage company with little traction? At Creandum, in the past 18 years, we have been fortunate to have worked with some of Europe's most successful startup founders, such as [Daniel Ek from Spotify](https://blog.creandum.com/inside-the-dusty-brains-of-an-early-spotify-investor-looking-at-how-we-were-right-and-wrong-7938abcd36e1), Sebastian Siemieatkoswski from [Klarna](https://www.klarna.com/), [Johannes Schildt from Kry](https://blog.creandum.com/kry-fills-all-the-boxes-of-our-healthcare-checklist-4caa51fe3b37), [Jacob de Geer and Magnus Nilsson from iZettle](https://blog.creandum.com/the-izettle-story-with-cofounder-magnus-nilsson-19e4761143), [Emil Eifremfrom Neo4J](https://blog.creandum.com/some-thoughts-on-why-creandum-is-leading-neo-technologys-new-20million-investment-8e19a9137c8), [Christian Hecker from Trade Republic](https://blog.creandum.com/backing-trade-republic-commission-free-trading-for-everyone-d05486ec196b) and many more. After a while, we realized that these incredible entrepreneurs all share some fundamental characteristics. Of course, they all have lots of energy, work hard, show patience, perseverance and resilience. But on top of that, all these unicorn founders share five key traits that, as an investor, you should look for when you back them at an early stage. ## 1. They know what they don't know Many people expect a typical startup founder to be very confident and have a strong sales mentality. While they should definitely live up to those expectations, the best founders are also humble and well aware of their weaknesses and limitations as well as the potential challenges for their startup. They keep wanting to learn, improve, and grow the business beyond what average people have the energy and drive to manage. ### How do you spot that at an early stage? - They listen and reflect on key questions. They don't always go for the fastest answer. - They are building a strong team around them and have shown that by making a couple of key hires. - They understand where the gaps are and which talents and skills will complement their own strengths. - They show a constant curiosity in and outside their domain. ![_"I've always been a really, really insatiable, curious person."_ Daniel Ek, Spotify Founder & CEO.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/7z2rQluimw7Ux6dvwWvH67/af65f21284d4cd8d6535b7a9b9189443/image_118.jpg) ‘Knowing what you don't know' is key when it comes to building the right team. When we met the Spotify founders Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon in 2006, we were struck by how they [challenged, complemented and respected each other](https://www.creandum.com/stories/spotify). Their level of discussion and how much they pushed each other is something we're always looking for in co-founders. (For more insights on Daniel Ek's journey from founder to CEO,[ listen to the 20min VC podcast](https://www.thetwentyminutevc.com/daniel-ek/)) As investors, we are well aware that, in reality, we have limited influence on the success of a startup. But if the founders have an ounce of this character trait, it's also likely that they will listen to at least some key advice at pivotal moments towards building a unicorn. ## 2. Helicopter ability The most successful founders think **BIG**. However, the best ones also sweat the small stuff, and show frugality, particularly in the early days when they're operating with a tiny budget and an often nonexistent team. Founders need to be hustlers/ hard-working individuals. Much more difficult to spot, though, is their leadership potential. In other words, the ability to move between strategic, high-level thinking and operational problem solving on a day-to-day basis, and then evolve this seamlessly as the business grows. In a matter of a few years, a unicorn founder has to shift from being the hands-on jack-of-all-trades, to the hiring manager and then the CEO, all the while leading the company. Essentially showing "helicopter" ability - moving from strategy to operations and back– seamlessly in the interactions. ### How to spot these traits early - There is clarity about the founder's long-term plan and vision for the company. Early actions are aligned with a North star. - There are signs the founders are walking the talk as you see them interact with their team members. Good leaders demonstrate great communication skills, as well as clarity, transparency and integrity. - There are proof points of an eager mentality in the previous experiences of the founders. ![Sebastian, Siemieatkowski, co-founder and CEO Klarna.](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/75tqH4IiOZHhfxa5R5L688/ce1d403ca137def9ebfc455d56cc0f38/image_119.jpg) A great example is Sebastian from Klarna, who 16 years ago embarked on a journey to build today's highest-valued European fintech ever. An immigrant in Sweden, he took on side projects from an early age and started Klarna when he was 23. He has since scaled the company to 3,500 employees. Throughout, Sebastian has kept agile, kept learning, and evolved as a people's empowerer. [To learn more about his leadership journey, listen to the 20-min VC podcast.](https://www.thetwentyminutevc.com/sebastian-siemiatkowski/) A t

articles.title: Pleo: Becoming the fastest Danish unicorn ever
articles.author: Johan Brenner
articles.text: **A conversation with Pleo co-founder & CEO Jeppe Rindom on scaling his company to a billion-dollar valuation at record speed** At Creandum, we regularly bring the most interesting entrepreneurs from the European tech ecosystem together to enable them to connect and share learnings. We recently met with **[Jeppe Rindom](https://techcrunch.com/2021/07/05/pleo-raises-150m-at-a-1-7b-valuation-for-its-new-approach-to-managing-expenses-for-smbs/?tpcc=ECTW2020)**, Co-Founder and CEO of **[Pleo](https://www.pleo.io/en)** in Copenhagen, one of our key markets. He shared some of the key lessons on building a global company out of a small country like Denmark, fast and successfully scaling it to Series C and turning it into **[the country's highest-valued company](https://sifted.eu/articles/pleo-150m-unicorn/).** Jeppe co-founded Pleo in 2015 in Copenhagen to offer smart payment cards to employees, enabling them to buy the things they need for work, all while keeping the companies in control of spending. Pleo's solution revolutionized business spending by reducing administrative complexity, eliminating expense reports, and simplifying bookkeeping. The company is expanding rapidly - in the last two years, Pleo grew its headcount from 80 to 330 people and today, the company operates in six markets across Denmark, UK, Ireland, Spain, Germany and Sweden. Two years ago, they closed their Series B round led by Stripes and [have now closed their Series C round at $150M](https://techcrunch.com/2021/07/05/pleo-raises-150m-at-a-1-7b-valuation-for-its-new-approach-to-managing-expenses-for-smbs/?tpcc=ECTW2020), lifting Pleo's valuation to $1.7B - the highest Series C raise for any Danish-founded start-up ever. ![Pleo Co-Founder & CEO Jeppe Rindom](//images.ctfassets.net/vx9l0f5sup17/hriYHWwSKefD6XFggzuiB/776ca8f925cc2fa57b193f6dfd9d78f0/image_116.jpg) ## The key challenges of running a company from Seed to Series C and beyond _Since you started the company in 2015 with your co-founder Niccolo Perra, you have grown the company so quickly that it's hard to keep up with your pace. Now you have closed Denmark's largest-ever Series C round of $150M! Looking back, what were the key priorities on your journey from Seed to Series C?_ ### Product-market fit [When Creandum invested in our Seed round in 2017](https://blog.creandum.com/why-we-think-pleo-is-the-perfect-fintech-company-23ada9223270), we had a product, but we didn't really know whether it would work (even though we might have given you the impression that we were confident it would). However, we needed some capital to start running tests. We launched the product without a billing system in place and advertised it at a certain price point, but never charged the customer. We couldn't make any money at that point, but at least it gave us some sort of evidence and confidence that customers would pay for it eventually. _**In the beginning, it's all about testing.**_ ### Internationalization After checking your product-market fit, your next challenge is to prove that your product works beyond your home market. If you're starting a company out of a small country like Denmark, you don't have a choice of whether you expand internationally. So, the question becomes whether you launch into one country first, or whether you tackle several countries all at once. At Pleo, we knew that since our product caters to all industries and company sizes, we didn't need to prove that it works the whole world over. Instead, we needed to nail it in at least one other market outside Denmark. We chose to focus on the UK first since it's the biggest and the most competitive market. We raised our Series A to prepare for that expansion and grew the company from 20 to 80 people. To optimize our chances of success, we had to adapt to UK-specific needs and double down on our localization efforts. To win the market, we aimed for having the best product with a stellar customer experience and receiving only excellent customer feedback. _**If your product or service is only mediocre, your chance of winning the category is close to zero.**_ ### Economics Once you've nailed both the product-market fit and the product quality, the focus of a SaaS company begins to shift to KPIs and metrics. You need to focus on the fundamentals of your economics, track recurring revenue, and headcount. Now that we have more than 300 employees across five different offices, and more than 17,000 customers, it's extremely important to keep track of everything. _**Metrics are vital for being able to preemptively diagnose potential problems.**_ I absolutely recommend bringing in a CFO as early as possible, even if it's only a part-time role. Most startups underestimate the value of having a CFO early. ### Scaling internationally _You mentioned you have four offices now with more than 300 employees. Where do you stand on the ‘standardize' versus ‘localize' debate? How do you maintain the company culture? And what are your biggest learnings?_ Since our first fundraising round in 2017, scaling the company has been our #1 focus. _**My biggest learning is that it's a people game.**_ You realize that you will never scale without the right people and the right motivation. Given Denmark's limited population, we, in particular, had to make a choice to either take Pleo international very fast or hire people from abroad and fix problems domestically. I had worked for companies with international offices operating in different time zones and I've seen how difficult that was.
